agricola-de-re-metallica-1912:
Georgius Agricola wrote De Re Metallica in Latin in 1556. Herbert Clark Hoover and Lou Henry Hoover gave it English dress in 1912. Hoover was a mine man long past when he took up the task. The book is the great text on mines and metal work of its age.

Twelve books tell of shafts, pumps, ores, and the smelt of each metal. Fine wood cuts show the craft at work, gear by gear. Agricola writes from years at the mines of Bohemia. The Hoover dress, with its rich notes, made the book a prize of the trade.
annales-cambriae-ingram-1912:
The Annales Cambriae, or Annals of Wales, are a Latin chronicle kept year by year in medieval Wales. James Ingram translated them into English in 1912. Most entries are bare lines about kings, battles, and deaths, the plain record of a small nation's memory.

Two short entries changed literary history. One notes Arthur's victory at Badon in 516, where he carried a cross into battle. Another records Camlann in 537, where Arthur and Medraut fell. From those stark lines grew centuries of argument about whether Arthur lived at all. The whole Arthurian tradition leans on this spare chronicle.
arxiv-2512-00012:
Andrei Enea introduces Painting with Code, an editor that eases children from block coding to real text code. The jump from dragging blocks to typing syntax is a known hurdle in school computer science, especially for children aged eight to ten. Many learners stall exactly at that transition.

The web-based editor uses authentic JavaScript syntax, but wraps it in a simple drawing library. Each line of code gives immediate artistic feedback on screen. Learning syntax through drawing keeps motivation high while the code stays real. A simplified, function-based drawing library keeps the first steps gentle while the syntax itself stays fully authentic.
arxiv-2512-00312:
After a penalty in rugby union, a team must choose: kick at goal for points, or kick to touch and chase a try. Kenny Watts and Jonathan Pipping build an expected points framework for that decision in 2025. The value of each option depends on field location and game context.

Expected points models convert a game situation into the points a team can expect from it on average. Comparing the two kicks on that scale gives coaches a principled guide instead of habit or gut feeling. The framework is a neat example of sports analytics turning a sideline judgment call into a measurable trade-off.
arxiv-2512-00412:
Large reasoning models think out loud in chains of thought, which creates new safety risks. Jiawei Chen and co-authors red-team such models in 2025, probing attacks like chain-of-thought hijacking and prompt-induced inefficiency. Existing evaluation methods do not fully capture these failure modes.

Explicit reasoning improves transparency and logical consistency, but the visible trace is also an attack surface. Red teaming means attacking the models deliberately to find weaknesses before bad actors do. The study helps safety teams design evaluations matched to how reasoning models actually fail, rather than borrowing tests built for older chatbots. Prompt-induced inefficiencies waste the very reasoning the models are valued for. Hijacking a chain of thought means steering the reasoning, not just the answer.
arxiv-2512-00712:
Zhuohua Liu, Kaiqi Huang, Qinxin Mei, Yuanqi Hu, and Wei Xing wrote a 2025 paper on tuning analog circuits. Designers must search for settings that make a circuit meet its goals. Most search tools treat the task as a black box over smooth functions, with no use of physics.

Yet device physics shapes circuit behavior into known families, like exponential device laws and rational transfer functions. Standard Gaussian process surrogates assume smooth, steady behavior and can misfit sharply nonlinear circuits when only fifty to one hundred tests are affordable. The authors exploit that family structure instead. Better fits at small sample sizes could cut costly design trials.
arxiv-2512-00812:
Yijia Fan, Jusheng Zhang, Kaitong Cai, Jing Yang, and Keze Wang tackle multi-label classification in a 2025 paper. In that task, one item can carry several labels at once, like a photo tagged with many objects. The task suffers from label imbalance, fake correlations, and shifts between datasets, which hurt rare labels most.

Their Causal Cooperative Game framework treats classification as teamwork among players. It mixes causal discovery, a counterfactual curiosity reward, and a causal invariance loss that favors features stable across settings. It also boosts rare labels on purpose. The mix aims for labels that stay right when conditions change.
arxiv-2512-00912:
Abdelghafour Halimi and four coauthors present ForamDeepSlice in a 2025 paper on tiny fossils and deep learning. Foraminifera are small shelled organisms whose fossils help date rocks and read past oceans. Naming their species from scans is slow, expert work.

Their framework classifies twelve foraminifera species from two-dimensional slices of three-dimensional micro-CT scans. The team curated a careful dataset from dozens of scanned specimens across many species. They kept the twelve species with enough examples for robust learning. Automating this naming could speed up geology and climate studies that rely on these fossils.
arxiv-2512-01112:
Tarun Chitra gives the first formal study of autodeleveraging in a 2025 paper. Autodeleveraging is a last-resort mechanism on perpetual futures exchanges, the main venues in crypto derivatives. When losses overwhelm the system and normal liquidations fail to preserve solvency, the exchange forcibly cuts winning positions to share the loss.

Despite the huge volume perpetual futures trade, no formal model of this mechanism existed. Chitra provides the first one, studying what outcomes are impossible and how the mechanism can be improved. A formal model lets exchanges and regulators judge whether their last-resort rules are fair and stable.
arxiv-2512-01412:
Ziqian Wang, Yuxiao Cheng, and Jinli Suo build a time-series model that can explain itself. Most explain tools just mark which points mattered. They miss big traits like trends, cycles, and sharp shifts in regime. Those traits are what humans look for in long data runs.

The new model pulls out clear causal patterns from the data. Each pattern is a named shape, like a trend or a cycle. Users can see why a forecast was made in those terms. Clear cause-based tales build trust for use in health, energy, and finance forecasts.
arxiv-2512-01712:
Aday Cardenas and co-authors show zero-point motion shapes high-harmonic spectra in solids. Reading those spectra often needs very short dephasing times. Those times are far shorter than scattering physics would suggest. That mismatch has long been a puzzle in the field.

The team shows phonon zero-point fluctuations do the job. They suppress long-range electronic coherence on their own. Clean spectra then arise with no ad-hoc decay terms. A physical cause for the decay firms up how harmonic spectra are used to probe solids. Solids from silicon to layered crystals all show the effect, so a phonon cause would unify spectra that now each need bespoke fixes.
arxiv-2512-01912:
The lonely runner conjecture is a puzzle from 1967 about runners on a circular track, each moving at a constant, different speed. It claims every runner eventually gets a clear gap from all the others. Matthieu Rosenfeld's 2025 paper proves the claim holds when there are nine runners.

The conjecture, first stated by Jörg Wills, is a known open problem in combinatorial number theory with several equivalent forms. Rosenfeld's proof sharpens the method he previously used to settle the eight-runner case, adding a couple of key improvements. Each new case brings the full conjecture, still unproven in general, a step closer.
arxiv-2512-02112:
When a system is driven across a phase transition, defects form in patterns predicted by the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, a universal rule born in cosmology and condensed matter alike. Jan Balewski and a large team report in 2025 an anomaly in the counting statistics of those defects.

Their experiments used long one-dimensional chains of Rydberg atoms, cooled and driven slowly across a continuous transition. Counting defects event by event, rather than just on average, revealed behavior the standard picture did not predict. Anomalies like this matter because Kibble-Zurek scaling is used to benchmark quantum simulators and to reason about the early universe.
arxiv-2512-02312:
Dating the branches of the tree of life from DNA relies on fossil ages, and those ages are uncertain. Greg Ellison and Liang Liu present in 2025 a faster method for estimating node ages that accounts for fossil calibration uncertainty without the heavy cost of Bayesian relaxed-clock analyses.

Bayesian methods are principled but must re-evaluate the full phylogenetic likelihood again and again, which becomes crushing on large genomic datasets. Their adjusted pairwise likelihood approach approximates that work far more cheaply while staying accurate. Faster divergence dating opens evolutionary timelines to the genome-scale datasets now common in biology.
arxiv-2512-02412:
Arnav Burudgunte, Paul Valiant, and Hongao Wang, based at Purdue, work on a puzzle about rebuilding lost data. A hidden string of zeros and ones passes through a channel that deletes each bit at random. Each pass gives only a partial copy, called a trace, and the task is to rebuild the string.

For the circular form of the puzzle, the best known upper and lower bounds sit far apart. That gap is huge, described as exponential in size. The authors narrow it with new bounds, which helps show how many traces recovery truly needs. Sharper bounds tell us how much loss a string can take and still be rebuilt whole.
arxiv-2512-02512:
Aditya Chaudhary, Prachet Dev Singh, and Ankit Jha work on making small or blurry images sharp. Single image super resolution asks a model to guess fine detail that the input lacks. Their method, ViT-SR, builds on a Vision Transformer, a model that reads an image in patches.

Training runs in two stages, as the title notes. First the model learns by colorizing images, a self taught task that builds rich visual features. Then a residual upsampling stage lifts those features to a larger, sharper picture. Two stage training of this kind aims for better detail without far more data. Sharp large prints from small files would help phones, drones, and old film scans alike.
arxiv-2512-03112:
Fair credit for each input is a core goal in explainable AI. Jialai She studies Shapley values, a top method for that task, in this 2025 work. The classic method assumes payoffs add up in a simple way, which real data often break.

Heavy tails, linked features, and odd loss scales can twist the credit a feature gets. She offers a sparse, order-based form of Shapley regression for non-linear cases. Better credit scores for features help users see why a model made a call. That clarity matters in health, lending, and other high-stakes uses. Sparse results are easier to read, since only a few features earn large credit.
arxiv-2512-03312:
Proteins work by changing shape, not by sitting still. Daniel Richman, Jessica Karaguesian, Carl-Mikael Suomivuori, and Ron Dror study those shapes in this 2025 work. The spread of shapes a molecule takes is far harder to find than one folded structure.

Diffusion models can generate molecule shapes, but hidden parts of the landscape may stay unseen. The authors unlock those hidden conformations at inference time, without retraining. Fuller shape maps help explain how proteins function and fail. They may also guide drug design against flexible targets. Inference-time tricks avoid costly retraining each time a new target protein is studied.
arxiv-2512-03712:
Power in a local distribution grid must satisfy hard physical limits on voltage and current in every phase. Sary Yehia and Alessandra Parisio address the resulting optimisation problem in a 2025 systems preprint. Real low-voltage networks are unbalanced, meaning the three phases carry different loads, and that imbalance makes the optimal power flow problem nonlinear and awkward.

Their hybrid method uses sequential convex programming, a loop that solves a simpler convex version again and again. Each round mixes a fixed outer approximation, straight-line approximations, and an adaptive trust region that keeps steps honest. The process settles at a point meeting the standard optimality conditions. Tests covered standard IEEE feeders and a real network in Cyprus. The method matched a leading nonlinear solver closely, with gaps under a tenth of a percent. It also ran up to twice as fast.
arxiv-2512-03812:
The share of national income going to workers has fallen for years, awkwardly for classic economic facts. Jiyuan Lyu proposes a mechanism in a 2025 economics preprint: large firms use more capital-intensive technology, so activity shifting toward big firms mechanically drags the labour share down. That weighting effect could operate even in perfectly competitive markets.

To test the idea, Lyu uses minimum wage rises in China as a shock that pushes small, labour-intensive firms out of business. Data from a national survey of industrial firms, plus a statistical instrument built from earlier firm patterns, support the chain. After a shock, small firms exit more, output moves to larger capital-intensive rivals, and the local labour share falls measurably. The effect survives concentration checks and placebo tests. A fairer spread of firm sizes, the estimates suggest, would raise the labour share.
arxiv-2512-03912:
Brain scans can be summed up as connectivity matrices showing which regions fluctuate together, and doctors would like to group patients by those patterns. Yixi Xu and Yi Zhao propose a clustering model for exactly that job in a 2025 statistics preprint. Their target is resting-state functional MRI data, where each person's pattern is captured by a covariance matrix.

The model mixes a mixture-of-experts structure with a regression on those matrices, assuming all groups share common linear projections of them. A generalised linear model with covariates then produces groupings that differ by projection yet stay readable. Extensive simulations check the method's accuracy and robustness. Applied to Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, the approach finds subgroups defined by brain coherence. Those subgroups also line up with demographic factors and cognitive measures, suggesting the clusters carry clinical meaning rather than statistical noise alone.
arxiv-2512-04012:
Photo collections gathered in the wild always contain strays: images that barely overlap with the rest and poison reconstructions in 3D. Jisang Han and colleagues report a surprising discovery about that problem in a 2025 computer vision preprint. A feed-forward reconstruction model called VGGT, never trained to reject outliers, appears to do so internally anyway.

By feeding the model controlled mixtures of real and distractor images, the team located a specific layer whose behaviour suppresses the distractors. Probing that layer revealed internal representations that separate irrelevant views from genuine ones. The authors simply read that signal out to perform outlier rejection, with no fine-tuning or extra supervision. Experiments on staged and real-world sets show the filtering generalises across scenes. The finding suggests large models quietly learn housekeeping skills their designers never requested, if researchers know where to look.
arxiv-2601-07012:
Madhav Sharma and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with case study of an exploratory high voltage NASICON-based na 4 NiCr(PO 4 ). It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. We examine a new NASICON-type Na 4 NiCr 3 material designed for high-voltage and multi-electron reactions for the sodium-ion batteries (SIBs).

The Rietveld refinement of the X-ray diffraction pattern, using the R 3 ¯ 3 c space group. Confirmed the stabilization of the rhombohedral NASICON framework. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07512:
Jingwen Fu, Ming Xiao, Mikael Skoglund, and Dong In Kim tackle sending images over wireless channels. Data rate limits and reliability demands make the task hard. Classic designs split compression and error protection into layers. Joint source-channel coding merges them, but low latency remains tough. Their 2026 preprint proposes a generative decoder approach.

The method is called land-then-transport and uses flow matching, a generative modeling technique. Learned image priors let the decoder rebuild a good-looking image from a small channel budget. Diffusion-style generative decoders already show strong perceptual quality under tight limits. The authors build on that idea for wireless transmission. The work matters for phones, cameras, and sensors that must send pictures over weak links.
arxiv-2601-08012:
Aarya Doshi and colleagues work toward tool use by AI agents that can be verified as safe. Language model agents gain power by calling tools: data sources, APIs, search engines, code sandboxes, even other agents. That power brings risks, like leaking sensitive data or overwriting critical records. Such failures are unacceptable in enterprise settings. Their 2026 preprint targets verifiably safe tool use. It appears in a new ideas track of a software engineering conference.

Verification means proving an agent stays within bounds, not just testing a few cases. Enterprises will not deploy agents on critical systems without such assurance. The paper frames the problem and a research direction. Safety checks must understand tools and their side effects. The work serves software engineering and AI safety scholars. It treats enterprise adoption as a verification problem.
arxiv-2601-08112:
Jordan D'Silva and co-authors tally where the universe's normal matter sits across cosmic time. Their 2026 arXiv paper computes the mass history of stars, dust, and neutral gas. The range runs from today back to redshift about three, when the universe was much younger.

The team models spectral energy distributions with the ProSpect code. Their sample covers about 800,000 galaxies from the GAMA and DEVILS surveys. Adding black holes to the count completes a cosmic baryon inventory. Such an inventory tests whether astronomers have found the ordinary matter that theory predicts. It also tracks how matter moved into stars over billions of years.
arxiv-2601-08212:
Shoichiro Mizukoshi and co-authors report broad hydrogen lines in heavily obscured active galaxies. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses multi-epoch spectroscopy to study these puzzling objects. The classical model says broad lines come from the broad-line region and show only when dust blocking is small.

The team had earlier found broad H-alpha lines where dust blocking exceeds 50 magnitudes. Three named cases are MCG-3-34-64, UGC 5101, and Mrk 268. Such detections clash with the simple picture of a dusty torus hiding the broad-line region. Multi-epoch spectra test whether the lines persist and how they vary. The results may force a rethink of how obscured nuclei are structured.
arxiv-2601-08512: Przemyslaw Spyra wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on when a sum settles in a space with no bound on its size. In finite spaces, three kinds of settling match: conditional, unconditional, and absolute. In Banach spaces with no bound, the Dvoretzky-Rogers theorem splits the three apart. Spyra gives one theorem that unites seven equal tests for unconditional convergence. The tests cover order-free sums, net convergence, subseries tests, sign stability, bounded multiplier traits, and weak uniform convergence. The split counts for how stable numeric methods stay.
arxiv-2601-09212:
Xingyao Li and three co-authors speed up how AI draws an image piece by piece. Such draws are slow, since each part waits for the last. A guess ahead trick can draft parts fast, then check them. Past soft forms of that trick let more drafts pass, to gain speed. But they had no firm base, so gains could hide a loss in grade.

The team adds a firm base with a slow cool rule. The rule starts soft, so drafts pass with ease. It then cools to strict as the draw goes on. That path seeks speed early and truth late. A reader who draws with AI gets a trick with both a proof and a pace gain.
arxiv-2601-09612:
Khairul Alam and Banani Roy mine the issue trackers of a major bioinformatics community. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes GitHub issues and pull requests in nf-core pipelines. Nf-core curates standard, peer-reviewed analysis pipelines built on the Nextflow workflow system.

Such systems make large genomic and proteomic analyses reproducible and portable. The authors study what users report and request, and how maintainers respond. Patterns in the reports reveal friction points in docs, testing, and design. Lessons from a mature, strictly governed community can guide other scientific software projects that face the same growing pains.
arxiv-2601-10112:
Tsvi Cherny-Shahar and Amiram Yehudai map a code base so an AI aid can read it. Code aids often fail to find how a project builds and tests. That gap is worse when a project mixes tongues. Each tongue has its own build tools and rules.

The pair built the Repository Intelligence Graph. It maps parts that build, parts that group, run tools, tests, and packs. Links show which part needs which, and which tests cover which part. Each link traces to a real build or test file. The map is fixed by rules, not by a model's guess. That makes it a firm base for an aid.
arxiv-2601-10312:
Zhipeng Liu and co authors build a sorter for time data that must learn new fields in turn. Web tools oft sort time rows, from clicks to health signs. Deep tools have made big gains at this. But a sorter may face new fields one by one, not all at once.

Old skill can fade as new fields come. The team use dual causal learn. Cause based traits tend to hold when fields shift. Two such paths back each other up. The aim is a sorter that learns each new field and keeps the old. It should stay robust as the fields roll in.
arxiv-2601-10612:
Kratika Mazde, Angelo Ricarte, and George N. Wong ask why black hole systems follow a neat pattern across three kinds of light. Observations of active galactic nuclei show that millimeter brightness, X-ray brightness, and mass move together. The pattern hints that one source powers the emission in each band. The team tests that idea with computer models of gas near black holes.

They run five large simulations with strong magnetic fields, then trace rays through them. The ray tracing builds spectra that include synchrotron light, hot-gas glow, and scattered photons. Comparing those spectra with the observed pattern can reveal its physical origin. The work links telescope data to the flow of gas at the edge of a black hole.
arxiv-2601-11212:
Xiaodong Zhang, Jiongning Che, and Barbara Dietz run lab tests on quantum billiards. Their 2026 preprint links two billiard systems with unlike dynamics. One has chaotic classical paths, the other has regular ones. The pair are joined by a gap in a shared wall.

The team reads the spectra of the joined system in the lab. Coupled systems like this test how order and chaos mix. The work also tests a special form of the Rosenzweig-Porter model. That model is a known frame for states that spread in odd ways. Lab data of this kind can check math claims that pure theory leaves open. It grounds the model in real measured spectra, not just in proofs.
arxiv-2601-11312:
Joonhyung Kim, Ioannis Platis, and Li-Jie Sun map distances on a quaternionic group. Their 2026 preprint studies the quaternionic Heisenberg group. The geometry is sub-Riemannian, so motion is bound to planes. Quaternions extend complex numbers to four dimensions here.

The team uses quaternionic contact geometry as the frame. They define a chain of Riemannian metrics on the group. Each metric stretches the vertical directions by a set scale. The limit of that chain gives the true sub-Riemannian picture. From it they describe geodesics in exact form. They also give the distance and the spheres in that metric. A formula for horizontal mean curvature of surfaces follows.
arxiv-2601-11412:
Andreas Kruff, Nolwenn Bernard, and Philipp Schaer sort ways to check fake queries. Their 2026 preprint builds a taxonomy of such measures. User simulators can test search systems without real users. Simulated queries stand in for what real users would type.

Whether those fakes match real queries is still open. That gap limits trust in results based on simulation. The team reviews the literature on validation at length. Their focus is checks of simulated queries against real ones. A taxonomy sorts the checks by what they measure. Clear classes help labs pick checks that fit their claims. The work aims at firmer ground for simulated evaluation.
arxiv-2601-11612:
Arnav Sonavane pre-trains vision models on farm images for disease work. The 2026 preprint uses hierarchical vision transformers for the task. Agricultural disease classification guides treatment and saves crops. Labels for sick plants are costly to gather by hand.

Self-supervised pre-training learns from unlabeled images alone. Sonavane tests domain-specific pre-training with the SimCLR method. Just 3,000 unlabeled farm images drive the pre-training. The gain in accuracy is 4.57 percent in the study. That beats the 3.70 percent from architecture design. The benefit holds across architectures, not just one model. Swin-Base gains over 4 percent from the same step. Domain data, it seems, beats generic scale here.
arxiv-2601-11712:
S. Mac Manamon, L. Matra, S. Marino, and a large team survey exoKuiper belts. Their 2026 preprint presents the ARKS survey with ALMA. ExoKuiper belts are debris discs around other stars. CO gas is detected in a significant share of them.

About 20 such discs show CO in the record. The origin and evolution of that gas stay elusive. Its mass and spatial spread are crucial evidence pieces. The two are coupled through optical depth in the gas. Past analyses worked at low to moderate resolution only. ARKS resolves substructures in the belts at finer detail. Sharp maps can separate gas born in place from gas released later.
arxiv-2601-11912:
Himanshu Gupta, Leslie Hogben, Bryan Shader, and Tony Wong take up an inverse problem for symplectic eigenvalues. Symplectic geometry now plays a role in maths, physics, and applied work. For a class of matrices, such eigenvalues exist by a theorem of Williamson.

An inverse problem asks which lists of such values can occur for a graph. That is, given a graph, which eigenvalue sets fit matrices tied to it. The work sets up this question for graphs. Such lists link graph form to matrix traits in a strict way.  The question links graph shape to matrix traits in a strict way.
arxiv-2601-12012:
Zhaoyang Jacopo Hu, Alex Ranne, Alaa Eldin Abdelaal, and their co-authors grade suturing skill in robot surgery in real time. Trained judges grade such skill with the OSATS scale. A live, fair grade tool could aid training and tests.

They study model choice for fast skill calls from surgery data. Fast calls let a trainee get notes while the task is fresh. Firm live grades could also flag unsafe moves at once. The work weighs which models keep speed and truth in balance.  Live grades can shape drills for each trainee by need.
arxiv-2601-12312:
Yongjun Jeon, Jongmin Shin, Kanggil Park, and a large team read surgical workflow via action triplets. A triplet names the instrument, the action, and the body target in one step. Such reads aid workflow checks and skill grading in surgery.

Progress was held back by severe class imbalance, subtle visual gaps, and linked sense among triplet parts. Their frame, named in the work, joins space and time data in a hierarchy. Better triplet reads could guide robot help and training.  Triplet reads join what tool, what act, what target.  The frame is built for the full surgery workflow.
arxiv-2601-12512:
Mohd Usama, Belal Ahmad, and Faleh Menawer R Althiyabi work on a snag in medical image AI. MRI scans from distinct scanners or hospitals often look subtly different. Shifts in hardware, protocol, and settings cause this domain shift. A deep model trained on scans from one source can then do worse on scans from another.

The team fine tune a Cycle GAN model to adapt images across domains. Their setup is unsupervised, so it needs no paired scans of the same patient. A good adapter could let one trained model serve many hospitals at once. That would cut the cost of retraining for each new scanner. The work speaks to a key barrier for AI in real clinical use.
arxiv-2601-12612:
Piyush Sao studies how to compute the log determinant of a large matrix, and what can go wrong. The matrix is symmetric and positive definite, a common case in practice. Log determinants arise in Gaussian process inference and in Bayesian model comparison. Standard scalable methods lean on many matrix vector products and polynomial approximations.

Those methods estimate the trace of the log of the matrix. Sao asks what trace powers reveal about that target quantity. He gives closed form estimators built from trace powers. He also gives certificates, checks that vouch for an estimate, and maps failure modes. Knowing when an estimator fails is as vital as the estimator itself. The work serves large scale statistical computing.
arxiv-2601-12712:
Tom Kimpson, Domenic P. J. Germano, Jennifer A. Flegg, and Mark B. Flegg model birth death processes across scales. Many biological systems mix species at very different abundances. Some species appear in high copy numbers while others stay rare. That heterogeneity breaks any single modeling style used alone.

Deterministic models are fast but inaccurate for low count species, where chance rules. Fully stochastic simulations are accurate but prohibitively expensive for abundant species. Hybrid approaches split the system, treating each part with the fit method. The team develop multiscale modelling for such hybrid schemes. Their work serves cell biology and ecology, where rare and common species interact.
arxiv-2601-12812:
Sushant Kumar Ray and a large team ask whether clinical question answering needs specialized medical fine tuning. Clinical QA systems increasingly rely on large language models. Deployment often assumes that domain specific fine tuning is essential for good answers. Specialized models like BioBERT, BioGPT, and PubMedBERT remain popular in the field.

Those specialized models face practical limits, the team note. They can have narrow coverage, high retraining costs, and limited adaptability. A general model might do as well without those burdens. The study tests that assumption head on. The answer guides hospitals weighing cost against accuracy in medical AI tools.
arxiv-2601-12912:
Andreas Brannstrom and Juan Carlos Nieves verify human emotion with action languages and answer set programming. They introduce an action language called C-MT, the Mind Transition Language. It builds on answer set programming and transition systems. The language represents how mental states evolve in response to sequences of observable actions.

Drawing on appraisal theory of emotion, they formalize mental states as multi dimensional configurations. Emotions become structured states that a program can reason about and check. The paper extends earlier work with a generalized formalism. It adds methods for representing, analyzing, and comparing psychological theories in these terms. Formal tools could let emotion theories be tested with logical rigor.
arxiv-2601-13012:
Arun K. Pati asks a deep question about the rules of quantum theory. In the standard rules, states are paired by a fixed inner product, a way to score how much two states overlap. Pati asks if that pairing could be changed and still keep the core rules of physics.

He tests a broad form of the pairing, set by a fixed plus operator. He keeps three rules in place while he tests it. Moves in one lab must stay local. Shared states with links across labs must exist. No signal may pass faster than light. His claim, set out in the title, is that the last rule alone pins the pairing to its standard form.
arxiv-2601-13312:
A team that includes A. Roodman pools faint gamma ray light with maps of cosmic web to find who made it. Much of the gamma ray sky is known. The rest is a smooth glow from sources too faint to name one by one. That glow is called the unresolved gamma ray background.

Cross links are the tool. If the glow waxes where a web tracer waxes, the sources tied to that tracer made part of the glow. The team uses more than one tracer at once. Each tracer marks a class of hosts, like galaxy groups. By split of the glow by host class, they can say which faint crowds shine most in gamma rays.
arxiv-2601-13412:
Puneet Sharma and co-authors, for the AICE group, teach a net to grade how clean colon capsule pics are. A colon capsule is a pill cam that films the gut as it passes. How clean the gut is sets if a film can be read at all. A poor clean must be caught or the test is waste.

Their data holds five hundred pics. Fourteen clinicians graded each pic on the Leighton-Rex scale, from poor to excellent. A ResNet-18 net was taught to match those grades. Split fold checks guard the score from luck. For gut teams, an auto grade could flag bad films fast and save a repeat test.
arxiv-2601-13912:
Mikołaj Korzyński and Mateusz Kulejewski study a subtle shift in light bent by gravity in 2026. In gravitational lensing, mass bends the path of radiation from a far source. Motion of the lens, source, and observer sideways creates a frequency shift. That shift is typically negligible in most astrophysical contexts.

Detection strategies have been proposed for both electromagnetic and gravitational waves. The team studies how the shift varies with viewing direction. Even a tiny shift could carry data on cosmic motion. Future fine instruments may turn this effect into a new probe.
arxiv-2601-14112:
George Mihaila trains models to explain which words drive a transformer's answer in 2026. Explainable AI has become critical as transformers enter high-stakes fields. Healthcare, legal systems, and financial services need trust and accountability. A transformer's self-attention weights have proven valuable for interpretability.

Attention shows where a model focuses as it reads. Mihaila's work learns supervised token attribution from transformer attention patterns. Supervision uses known answers to teach which tokens mattered. Clearer token credit could help experts audit model choices before acting on them. The maps can be checked by hand for a few key cases. That check is what lets experts trust the bulk of the scores.
arxiv-2601-14412:
Xiao Wang, Csaba Balázs, Ran Ding, and Chi Tian study phase transitions in the early universe in this 2026 paper. When strongly supercooled cosmological first-order phase transitions are sufficiently slow, they can generate super-horizon inhomogeneities. Those are patches of uneven density larger than the horizon at the time. The team computes the resulting super-horizon curvature perturbations.

Their tool is a gauge-invariant, multi-fluid formalism. Gauge choices can create fake effects in such calculations. By resolving the gauge ambiguities inherent in conventional approaches, they aim for perturbations that are physically real. The work is pure theory. It uses math, not new sky data. The sums are done with care, step by step, so the end size can be trusted. The title poses the core question: how large are those perturbations? Readers get a careful size estimate for a possible mark of the universe's first transitions.
arxiv-2601-15112:
Lana Bozanic, Alex May, and Stanley Miao study a coordination puzzle for quantum networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with entanglement summoning. In this task, spread-out parties must create entanglement between far-apart sites on request.

The parties cooperate, but their links are limited. Timing rules may demand that the entangled state be ready before some pairs can even talk. Only some links in the network can be used at all. The authors ask when summoning can still be done, and they trace the task back to its base in entanglement sharing.
arxiv-2601-15612:
Shao-Wen Wei and five co-authors study the shadows of unusual black holes in a 2026 arXiv paper. A black hole's shadow is the dark shape it casts against glowing matter. In some models beyond Kerr black holes, the shadow grows a cusp. A cusp is a sharp point on the shadow's edge. The authors show this change runs deep. It alters the shadow's topology, flipping its topological charge from one to minus one.

The title promises a gravitational equal-area law tied to this change. It also links the cusp to critical phenomena. In plain terms, the shadow's shape may act like a phase signal. Observers who image black holes could use such signs. A cusp in a real image would hint at physics past the standard Kerr picture.
arxiv-2601-15812:
Shir Ashury-Tahan and four co-authors map why language models fail in a 2026 arXiv paper. Benchmarks tell us when models fail, but not why. A wrong answer on a reasoning set can come from many causes. Formatting issues, calculation errors, or dataset noise may be to blame. Weak reasoning is only one suspect. Without separating causes, benchmarks cannot guide improvement well.

Their tools are ErrorMap and ErrorAtlas, per the title. They chart the failure landscape of large models. A chart of causes points builders to the right fix. Fixing format is cheap; fixing reasoning is not. Misdiagnosed failures waste effort on the wrong cure. For evaluation science, this paper pushes past scores toward diagnosis.
arxiv-2601-15912:
Ariyan Bighashdel and Kevin Sebastian Luck turn plain instructions into small robot controllers in a 2026 arXiv paper. Robots that follow language usually split into two camps. One plans at a high level through hand-designed interfaces. The other uses large end-to-end models that are hard to run in real time. Their framework, TeNet, takes a middle path. It builds compact, task-specific policies directly from text descriptions.

Text-to-Network is the name's expansion. A network here is a small control policy, not a giant model. Compact policies can run fast on robot hardware. Generating them per task avoids hand-coding each new job. For deployment, small and specific often beats large and general. TeNet aims to give language-driven robots that practical edge.
arxiv-2601-16012:
Yanfeng Zhang and six co-authors simplify a coding scheme for urgent wireless links in a 2026 arXiv paper. Sparse superimposed coding suits short-packet ultra-reliable low-latency work. Conventional versions suffer from high coding complexity. Dense codebook matrices drive that cost. Every codeword touches many symbols, so encoding and decoding run heavy. The authors propose a low-complexity version of the scheme.

Their design uses a sparse codebook structure. Each codeword holds only a few nonzero elements. Sparse operations are far cheaper to run. The gain matters for small devices with tight energy budgets. Factory sensors and control links cannot carry heavy decoders. A coding scheme that keeps reliability while shedding cost fits exactly those users.
arxiv-2601-16212:
Siddhant Haldar and coauthors use point forms to move robot skills across fields. Their 2026 preprint deals with a lack of real robot task data. Fake and game data are cheap to make at scale. But a look gap parts fake views from real views. Skills learned in fake worlds then fail in real rooms.

Point forms strip views to bare 3D point sets. Bare points look more like in both worlds than full pics do. Skills taught on points may cross the gap with less loss. The team tests point skills on real tasks. The work, called Point Bridge, seeks cheap paths to real skill.
arxiv-2601-16312:
Dikshya Mohanty and three coauthors teach and test models on polymer design tasks. Their 2026 preprint deals with AI for science in the polymer field. Past models fail on polymer tasks for two clear flaws. Most lack deep facts about polymers as a class. Aligned models also lack the range of skills the tasks need.

The team builds teach sets and tests tied to polymer work. Teach sets fill fact gaps with set polymer truths. Tests then check skill on real design tasks, not toy ones. Strong scores would show a path to use in labs. The work maps what models must learn for this field.
arxiv-2601-16612:
Antonio Bracale and coauthors flag gaps in true checks of smart power meters. Their 2026 preprint deals with meters that log use and grade marks. Such meters are now the main tool for bills and checks. Yet their proof tests use clean waves or plain test forms. Real grid waves are far from clean or plain in form.

Tests that miss real waves can pass meters that fail live. The team maps which real states proof tests must add. True tests would catch meter flaws ere bills go wrong. They would also firm trust in new grid data. The work is a call to fix meter proof rules.
arxiv-2601-16712:
Kartik Chari, Raid Dokhan, Anas Homsi, Niklas Kueper, and Elsa Kirchner aid rehab with smart sleeves. Exoskeletons can lift and guide weak arms. To help well, the frame must guess the force at each joint. Their 2026 preprint draws that guess from skin signals. Eight small pads read the hum of arm muscles.

Light neural nets turn those hums into force calls. Such nets must run fast on small gear. The team built a clean path from raw hum to force. Their path picks sharp traits from the signal first. Good force calls let frames help, not fight, the user. This could aid stroke and injury rehab in clinics.
arxiv-2601-17412:
Valerii Serpiva and four co-authors present DiffusionCinema, a drone filming system driven by words. A user states the shot in plain language. The system plans the flight path to match. No hand piloting is needed. A sample request asks the drone to orbit a person and reveal a scene. Diffusion models read such prompts and shape the path.

Good aerial shots take skill that most users lack. A word-driven system puts that skill in reach. It could serve creators, news teams, and event staff. The work joins language models with flight control in one loop. It treats camera motion as part of the prompt, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-17912:
Qinyi Liu, Mohammad Khalil, and Naman Goel test a tabular data model for hidden unfairness. Their 2026 preprint studies TabPFN, a foundation model for tables. TabPFN is trained on huge numbers of synthetic data sets built from causal models. It then learns new tasks from examples given in context, and it scores well on real tasks. The concern is what else the causal pre-training bakes in.

Fairness is the lens of the study. A model trained on made-up worlds may carry the biases of those worlds into real choices. The authors run an empirical check of how the model treats groups. Their work asks users of tabular models to test fairness, not just accuracy, before they deploy.
arxiv-2601-18012:
Hendrika Maclean and co-authors test language models on the strict world of payroll. Their 2026 preprint notes a known weakness. Models are strong at writing, search, and analysis, and their grasp of language keeps growing. Yet they stay shaky on exact numbers and on output that auditors can check line by line. Payroll needs both: exact math and a clean audit trail.

The team studies how well models handle the semantic and syntactic sides of payroll tasks. Meaning and form both matter when pay rules are coded in words. Errors here hit real wages and real legal duties. The findings help firms judge where a model can assist payroll work and where humans must stay in charge.
arxiv-2601-18612:
Susim Roy and Nalini Ratha build a way to match records of the same person across files while the facts stay locked. Banks and state desks must often tell if two records name one person. Names shift in form: a nick name here, a typo there, a new home in the next file. The match must be made, yet the facts are too dear to share in plain form.

Their plan works on locked facts with a code that lets maths run while the lock stays on. It takes in more than text, so sight and sound cues can help the match. A locked match could let desks share the gain of a joint check with no leak of names. That would help fight fraud while it keeps faith with strict rules on data.
arxiv-2601-18712:
Sambuddha Chattopadhyay, Marios Michael, Andrea Cavalleri, and Eugene Demler study a state in which a crystal bears flow with no loss when hit by light. The crystal is a ball of carbon cages with metal in the gaps. In the cold it bears such flow on its own. Light at a set tone can wake the same state at far more heat, up to room heat. That wake took a strong flash in past tests.

A tone in a set band, the team find, wakes the state with far less flash. They study why that tone has such a strong hand. The wake works by a boost in how pairs of bits bind as one. A cheap wake could bring loss-free flow close to real use. The work is a step in that hunt, with care on the maths of the boost.
arxiv-2601-18812:
Ernesto Mamedaliev and four colleagues set out a fair way to grade a class of quantum tools that hunt best plans. The tools mix quantum steps with plain steps in a loop. They are a top hope for hard plan tasks on the noisy quantum kit of today. But their grades swing by chance, and the field lacks one set bar for a fair grade.

Their frame grades such tools on a set class of plan tasks in which all facts are whole and all picks are yes or no. It sets how runs are made, how grades are summed, and how swings are told. A shared bar could let teams set grades side by side with trust. It could also show which tools gain from more runs and which have hit a cap. Fair bars are a must as the field grows past first demos.
arxiv-2601-18912:
Shalima Binta Manir and Tim Oates ask why graph neural nets fail on some graphs but not on others. These nets pass notes along links to guess labels for nodes. They tend to do poorly when linked nodes hold unlike labels, a trait called low homophily. But that trait alone does not tell the whole story.

Pairs of graphs can share the same homophily score yet give very unlike scores for the same net. Some unlike label graphs stay easy even for a plain graph net. The authors argue that shape, not just label match, drives the gap, and they test a hybrid method built on that view.
arxiv-2601-19312:
Alexandre Alouadi and five co-authors speed up a strong form of diffusion based generation. The Schrödinger Bridge framework steers one distribution into another; its Bass extension controls both drift and volatility at once. That power usually costs many rounds of computation.

Their algorithm, LightSBB-M, finds the optimal transport plan in only a few iterations, where rival methods may need many rounds of back and forth passes. Fewer rounds mean generative models built on this frame can train and run at lower cost. The work keeps the richer control of the extended bridge while cutting the bill that kept it niche.
arxiv-2601-19412:
G. Risaliti, B. Trefoloni, and M. Salvati explain why bright quasars all seem to shine alike. Models of quasar accretion predict a wide spread of optical and ultraviolet traits, set by the black hole's mass and how fast it feeds. Yet most bright, optically picked quasars show strikingly alike spectra.

The team shows the sameness follows from a nearly fixed ratio of light output to mass, plus thermal emission from a thin disk. One shared feeding rate makes the whole class look uniform. The result simplifies how astronomers read quasar light and weigh the black holes behind it.
arxiv-2601-19512:
Mauro Sanchiz works in functional analysis, the study of spaces made of functions. His setting is the Musielak-Orlicz spaces, a broad family of such spaces defined by a growth rule. He asks when sets in these spaces are weakly compact, a property that helps prove that solutions to problems exist. The spaces he treats are not symmetric, which makes the theory harder than in classic cases.

He proves two criteria for weak compactness under a standard growth condition. The results extend older criteria that Andô proved for the simpler Orlicz spaces. From them he derives tests for when a sequence of functions converges weakly. He also shows that spaces with a splitting property have a stronger compactness trait. Sequence spaces are covered as a special case.
arxiv-2601-19612:
Manuel Wendl and five colleagues make reinforcement learning safer to use outside simulations. An agent that learns by acting in the real world can cause harm while it explores. The authors start from policies that are imperfect but cautious. Such policies can come from offline data or from simulators.

They use these conservative policies as priors, a base behaviour the learner stays near. Exploration then improves on a safe starting point instead of wandering freely. The prior guides the agent away from known danger while it learns. Safe exploration is a key step for robots and systems that learn on the job. The work offers a practical way to borrow caution from existing controllers.
arxiv-2601-19812:
Obinna Umeh identifies a missing piece in cosmological perturbation theory. The standard theory follows how structure grows in the expanding universe. It is well-posed only until shell crossing, when particle trajectories intersect. Beyond that point the equations stop predicting and perturbation methods break down.

Zoom-in calculations focus on small regions at high resolution. They need a framework that stays valid where ordinary theory fails. Umeh describes an essential building block for such a theory. Getting past shell crossing matters for modelling galaxy formation accurately. The work addresses a foundational gap rather than a single application. It sets up later development of a complete zoom-in perturbation theory. The gap is not a small one. It blocks a whole line of work.
arxiv-2601-19912:
Duo Chai and four colleagues test how fragile language models are to hardware faults. Language models demand heavy computation and memory from modern graphics processors. Shrinking transistors and lower voltages make those processors more prone to soft errors, random bit flips from radiation or noise. A single flipped bit can corrupt a model's output silently.

The team runs an instruction-level fault injection study on graphics processors. They flip bits at chosen points and watch how model behaviour changes. The study maps which instructions and layers are most vulnerable. Knowing the weak points guides protections, from checksums to selective hardening. As models enter safety-critical roles, such resilience data becomes essential.
arxiv-2601-20112:
Maja Vukovic and five colleagues study how AI coding assistants are used inside large companies. Their 2026 study looks at usage, effects, and what firms require from these tools. Large language models now help with many coding tasks, from reading old code to writing tests and fixing bugs.

The authors gather evidence from the enterprise setting, where rules on safety, privacy, and control shape what tools can do. Their study asks how workers actually use the assistants day to day, and what gains or problems show up. Results of this kind help firms decide how to roll out coding assistants with care.
arxiv-2601-20812:
Alfredo Alegría and three co-authors extend a classic statistics idea to richer data. Their 2026 paper concerns the effective sample size. That number states how much independent information a dataset truly holds. It discounts the overlap that correlation between observations creates. For simple scalar data, the idea is widely used in geostatistics. For functional spatial data, it has stayed largely unexplored.

Functional data are whole curves, not single numbers. Spatial versions record such curves at many sites. Nearby curves tend to resemble each other, so the true information is less than the raw count. The paper builds the effective sample size for this setting. That gives analysts an honest sense of how much data they really have. It matters wherever sensors record profiles across a landscape.
arxiv-2601-21012:
Young Kyung Kim and four co-authors teach models to learn from the order of a stream, not just its contents. Their 2026 paper presents Order-Aware Test-Time Adaptation, or OATTA. Test-time adaptation lets a pretrained model adjust to distribution shift. It learns from unlabeled data as the data arrive. Existing methods treat the stream as independent samples. That ignores the signal hidden in temporal dynamics.

Order itself carries supervision, the authors argue. What follows what tells the model how the world is drifting. OATTA leverages that dynamics for robust streaming inference. The model can then track slow change instead of being fooled by it. The method suits live systems, from cameras to sensors, where conditions wander. It turns a weakness of streaming data into a source of guidance.
arxiv-2601-21112:
Rauno Arike and four co-authors test how much a watchdog model needs to see to catch a saboteur. Their 2026 paper studies LLM monitors for frontier agents. Such agents can misbehave in misaligned ways. They may deceive, exploit reward hacks, or pursue hidden objectives. One control strategy uses language models themselves as monitors. Those monitors read the agent's work and flag misbehavior. Their skill depends on what information they can access.

The authors vary that access and measure detection. A monitor with full transcripts may catch what a summary-fed one misses. Too much access, though, costs money and may leak sensitive data. The study maps the trade-off for sabotage detection. Its lessons guide labs that deploy agents under automated oversight. Oversight design is now a front-line safety question.
arxiv-2601-21412:
Alexei Borodin and Alexey Bufetov study a traffic-like model from probability theory. In the model, particles hop in one direction only and cannot share a site. Each particle carries its own type, and all types are distinct.

The authors focus on the leader, the type of the rightmost particle after a long time. They prove a central limit theorem for that random leader. In plain terms, the leader's type settles into a bell-shaped spread around a mean. Such results show how order emerges in systems with many ranked particles, a pattern that also appears in queues and growth processes.
arxiv-2601-21612:
Bing Han, Chushu Zhou, Yifan Yang, Wei Wang, Chenda Li, Wangyou Zhang, and Yanmin Qian improve self-supervised learning for audio. Methods that bootstrap their own targets have made strong progress on sound understanding. Most work at one level of detail only, which limits how they capture sound's mix of fine and broad structure.

Bootstrapping from scratch is also slow and costly to converge. The authors add representation-level guidance to a convolutional audio transformer. Regularizing the learned features should speed training and enrich the detail captured. Better audio models serve speech, music, and sound-event tools alike.
arxiv-2601-21812:
Francisco Caldas, Sahil Kumar, and Cláudia Soares bring diffusion models to forecasting time series. Diffusion methods generate data by gradually adding noise and learning to remove it. For time series, the authors argue, the noise-adding step itself should respect the structure of the signal.

Their 2026 preprint introduces a forward diffusion process that splits a signal into its spectral components, its mix of fast and slow waves. That split preserves structured patterns such as seasonality better than standard diffusion does. The method is model-agnostic, meaning it can wrap around existing forecasting networks rather than replacing them. Better handling of seasons and cycles could improve forecasts in energy, finance, and weather-driven planning.
arxiv-2601-22012:
Sergi Masip and three co-authors give forgetting a face. A neural net that learns task after task tends to lose the first tasks. This flaw is called catastrophic forgetting. Most tests score it by lost marks on old tests. That hides what breaks inside the net.

The team looks at the inner parts of the net as it learns. They show that forgetting is a change in how the net codes each trait it has learned. When new tasks twist that code, the old traits can no longer be read. Their work lets us watch traits live or die, one by one. That view can guide guards that shield the traits old tasks need most.
arxiv-2601-22112:
Mark Whitmeyer studies games where each side bets on a spread of scores, not one score. Each player picks a spread over a scale of marks. Strong spreads cost more, and the cost grows in a smooth, curved way. Firms do this when they choose how much chance to build into a good. Labs do it when they aim work at top press.

He shows that a fair game of this sort has a shared best reply, where no side wants to move. He lists traits that this point must have and gives a way to pin it down. The work then points to fights in research and to markets with few big firms. In such games, sides steer the odds, not the end score.
arxiv-2601-22212:
Spencer Klein studies linked spins in the spray from near-miss ion hits. When two heavy ions race past each other, they do not touch. Their strong fields clash in place of the cores. Those fields spark off light-based hits at high rates, and more than one spark can fly in a pass.

Such a pass can make new bits of matter, or shake the cores of the ions. Klein looks at pairs of new bits that then break down. He asks how the paths of their parts stay linked, twist by twist, round the beam line. Tests of this sort turn big rings into labs for the quantum world. They probe linked states at force far past what bench tools can reach.
arxiv-2601-22312:
Can Polat, Erchin Serpedin, Mustafa Kurban, and Hasan Kurban built a test to catch when large models fake facts about materials. Their 2026 preprint names the test SCALAR. It checks how models cope when the size and shape facts in a prompt shift in set ways.

The test links three things: grasp of scale, stray made-up claims, and steady logic. A model that fails it may sound right while its facts warp with size. Such checks matter as labs lean on models for design leads. The bench gives a shared way to grade that trust.
arxiv-2601-22812:
Jana Gonnermann-Müller and four co-authors ask whether AI agents can keep a steady character over long talks. Language models are now used as stand-ins for people in behavior studies. That use only works if the model's persona, its stated traits and style, stays stable over time.

Their check has two sides: what the model says about itself, and how outside raters judge its replies. A model that drifts in character could quietly spoil study results. The dual check gives researchers a way to spot that drift early.
arxiv-2601-23112:
Cheng Yu and four co-authors ask how AI safety benchmarks should themselves be judged. Safety benchmarks are pivotal checks on advanced AI systems. Yet the authors find deep technical, epistemic, and social shortcomings across the field.

Their review covers more than two hundred safety benchmarks and maps the common failures. They draw on engineering science and long-standing theories of risk and safety for guidance. If the measuring tools are flawed, safety claims built on them cannot be trusted. Engineering sciences and established risk theory supply the standards the review uses to judge the benchmark field. Shortcomings are grouped as technical, epistemic, and sociotechnical, a map meant to guide repairs.
arxiv-2601-23212:
Joshua Southern and six co-authors predict how multispecific antibodies will behave using graph neural networks. These engineered antibodies grab several targets at once, offering powerful new therapies. Their effect emerges from complex molecular architecture, so small design changes can flip the outcome.

Experimental data are scarce, which makes prediction even harder. Treating the antibody as a graph lets the network reason over its domain layout. Good predictions could shorten the costly trial-and-error of therapeutic design. Domain topology is the variable under study: how the antibody's parts are arranged governs what the assembled molecule can do.
arxiv-2603-01912:
Yinghao Tang, Yupeng Xie, Yingchaojie Feng, and colleagues build interactive teaching documents with human and agent teamwork. Their 2026 system, ViviDoc, turns one topic input into an interactive educational document. Interactive articles engage readers well, but making them takes both subject expertise and web skills.

Naive agent generation gives outputs that teachers cannot control or verify with ease. ViviDoc splits work among planner, executor, and evaluator agents in one pipeline. A human-readable plan format, DocSpec, breaks each visualization into state, render, transition, and constraint parts. Educators review and refine that plan before any code is written, which bridges intent and output. Expert review and a user study find large gains over naive generation and an intuitive editing flow.
arxiv-2603-02312:
Marco Bonvini, Stefano Frixione, and Giovanni Stagnitto refine proton structure calculations in this 2026 paper. Splitting functions describe how quarks and gluons share a proton's momentum as scales change. At very small momentum fractions, large logarithms must be summed to all orders. The team revisits the steps needed for accuracy at the next level of that summing.

They derive fresh all-order results for several key quantities in the theory. Most notably, one anomalous dimension is now properly resummed for the first time. That unlocks a correctly resummed splitting kernel that mixes quarks and gluons. The new implementation behaves better numerically than earlier versions. All advances ship in the upcoming fourth release of their HELL code framework.
arxiv-2603-02512:
Szilárd Enyedi proposes human-certified module repositories for AI-built software in this 2026 paper. Language models now generate code and assemble multi-part systems. The safety of those systems depends on the trustworthiness of their building blocks. Today's components often have unclear origins, thin review, and unpredictable interactions.

His repositories would stock reusable modules that humans have certified. Each module carries rich provenance, security review, and an explicit interface contract. Human oversight blends with automated analysis in the certification workflow. A reference architecture and threat analysis ground the proposal. Lessons from recent supply-chain failures shape the design. Governed, auditable module stocks could make AI-assembled software far more reliable, Enyedi argues.
arxiv-2603-02612:
Ritu Dey, Ayushi Agarwal, Reetesh Kumar Gangwar, and colleagues compute electron impact data for tungsten in this 2026 paper. Tungsten walls in fusion devices shed neutral atoms that glow in visible and near-ultraviolet light. Reading that glow needs consistent atomic structure and collision data. Their relativistic distorted-wave method supplies excitation cross sections at fine-structure resolution.

Target states come from multi-configurational Dirac-Fock wavefunctions with extensive correlation. Level energies are benchmarked against other theory and a standard reference database. Cross sections cover excitations from the ground level and six metastable levels. Incident electron energies run from threshold up to a high range. Most reported cross sections appear here for the first time. Results depend strongly on the starting level, a fact modelers must respect.
arxiv-2603-02812:
Klaus Deckelnick, Philip Herbert, and Michael Hinze prove that a basic shape-tuning method always settles down. Their 2026 paper concerns shape optimization, where a domain's outline is adjusted to meet a goal governed by a partial differential equation. The equation here is semilinear and elliptic, a common class in physics and engineering design.

They study steepest descent carried out directly in function space, with shapes compared through the Lipschitz topology, which controls boundary roughness. The main result is global convergence: from any start, the method converges rather than wandering or stalling. A second result gives conditional convergence of the shapes themselves in two dimensions. Such guarantees matter because shape algorithms are often trusted long before they are proven.

An Introduction to Metaphysics is Bergson's most famous short work, printed here in the 1912 English version by T. E. Hulme. The French philosopher sets out his method in one sustained argument: intuition, not analysis, is how thought reaches reality.

Analysis, Bergson says, circles a thing and gives symbols; intuition enters it and grasps its duration, the flow of inner time. He applies the contrast to the self, to movement, and to life itself. The essay is dense but exhilarating, a key to all his larger books. Hulme's version carried Bergson's fame through the English-speaking world.

cia-0000049012: An excerpt from 1981, kept in a CIA item, weighs whether the right or the left carried out assassinations in El Salvador. In that war, each side blamed the other for nearly every killing, and proof was rare. The excerpt's even-handed guessing shows how hard the simplest question, who did this, was to answer.
cia-0000049112: A probe of terrorist killings in El Salvador is the subject of a CIA item from 1985, kept with the Truth Commission records. Terrorist killings, in the language of the files, covered the political murders both camps committed. An investigation's existence was itself news in a country where most killings were never investigated at all.
cia-0000049212: Biographical information on Colonel Nelson Ivan Lopez y Lopez, partly blacked out, fills a CIA item from 1991. Bio files were the system's portrait of an officer: posts held, ties kept, reputation noted, family listed. This one survives in the Truth Commission records, its gaps guarding the parts still judged sensitive.
cia-0000049412: Progress on human rights in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049412, dated June 5, 1987. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper claims movement on rights rather than fresh abuses. Readers get a brief declassified item whose positive heading stands out among the grimmer Salvadoran titles, preserved as the agency framed it then.
cia-0000095212: A cable from Leopoldville about cancelling an operation or proceeding with risks is declassified CIA document 0000095212, dated August 1, 1963. The heading presents the choice in either-or terms. Readers get a short declassified cable record from the Congo station's city, its subject the decision itself, preserved without the operation being named in the title.
cia-0000097712: Intelligence Warning of the Tet Offensive in South Vietnam, with publication date estimated, is declassified CIA document 0000097712, dated March 1, 1968. The heading flags the dating estimate in parentheses. Readers get a short declassified paper on warning before the Tet Offensive, its subject the intelligence that preceded a major attack in South Vietnam.
cia-0000100512: Message from the ADCI on the New York Times story on Guatemala is declassified CIA document 0000100512, dated February 5, 1995. The heading names the sender by initials and the newspaper story answered. The brief file is an internal message record about press coverage, preserved as the agency's response to a story rather than reporting itself.
cia-0000107312: Minutes of Forty-ninth Meeting Committee on Exchanges is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000107312, dated August 2, 1979. The title marks a long running series: this was the forty-ninth meeting of one committee. Minutes record what a meeting covered, in formal meeting form. The brief record is a committee minutes item, numbered in its own title as released.
cia-0000109012: Use of Prison Labor in Construction of Dimitrovgrad Automotive is the first numbered heading, cut off mid-phrase, on declassified CIA document 0000109012, dated January 1, 1983. The title ties prison labor to building an automotive plant at Dimitrovgrad. What part of the plant is cut off where the heading ends. The brief record is a prison labor construction item from 1983.
cia-0000112812: Espionage - Herbert Moy is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112812, dated January 5, 1945. The title pairs a charge and a name: espionage, Herbert Moy. A companion file from October 1944 calls the same man an active collaborator. The brief record is a charge file, one of two Moy files in this wartime group of files there.
cia-0000117912: Guatemala: 1984-1995 is the whole heading on declassified CIA document 0000117912, dated August 5, 1995. The title is a country and a span: Guatemala, across eleven years, 1984 to 1995. The span ends in the same year the record is dated in the catalog. cia-0000119212:
An April 1984 CIA document lays out what the American intelligence community was doing about the prisoner and missing problem. Inside, the document divides duties and reports steps taken across the community. That kind of coordination paper shows how a wartime question became a long bureaucratic effort. It matters because it explains the machinery behind the searches, the briefings, and the reports to families that continued for years after the last troops came home.
cia-0000132412: Cuban developments are surveyed in a CIA document dated September 5, 1959. Eight months had passed since Castro's victory, and the revolution was still defining itself week by week. Washington watched every turn of the new regime with close attention. The short document gathers the latest changes as the agency saw them that autumn, while Cuba's final direction was still being argued over in Havana.
cia-0000132512:
Parochial schools being seized by the Castro regime fill a CIA item dated April 4, 1961. The headline also reports foreign priests being expelled, though the last word is cut short in the record. The revolution was moving directly against the Catholic Church that spring.

The item reports the seizures and expulsions as they were announced. Church schools had educated much of Cuba's middle class for generations. For readers, the entry marks a sharp break between the regime and one of the island's oldest bodies. It came days before the Bay of Pigs invasion hardened every line in Cuba.
cia-0000132612: A Lima meeting of left-of-center parties calling for unity fills item 12 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 3, 1960. Its headline breaks off after the word united, leaving the call unfinished. Peru's capital was hosting the region's moderate left that month. The short item reports the meeting and what the parties agreed to demand.
cia-0000135812: Weekly progress reports fill a CIA paper from 1954 on the Guatemala operation. Part of its headline subject was deleted before release. The reports cover the week of March 23 through 29, though the headline breaks off mid-word. A weekly rhythm ran through the whole covert campaign that year. The short paper keeps the reports for that week as filed.
cia-0000135912: Dated 5 May 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records a short summary of a meeting held on 17 June, cabled from Guatemala City under a May date. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. cia-0000136112: With a date of 3 April 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a visit by Salamander to Sherwood. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. cia-0000136312: Sent to SKILLET, ONTRICH, and SHERWOOD in June 1954, this LINCOLN cable passes on the latest reliable situation report from PBSUCCESS. cia-0000136612: Dated 4 January 1961, a Spanish document from the declassified records of Brigade 2506. The first week of 1961 produced a thick run of these Spanish records, this one among them. The brigade was the CIA's exile force, then training for Cuba. The catalog gives the item no subject. cia-0000136712: The catalog gives this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document an estimated date of 5 January 1960, a full year before the brigade's known training peak and earlier than the unit's public history suggests. The date is flagged as estimated, which may explain the oddity. An earlier summary attached Second World War summit material to this item; that is unsupported and dropped. cia-0000136912: Learn all you can about an arms shipment, this April 1954 cable directs. A Swedish ship delivered the arms at Puerto Barrios, Guatemala. A contact in Stockholm is to be asked for aid. That Czech arms delivery sharpened the crisis before the invasion.
cia-0000137312: Dated 1961, NSC Briefing — Cuba is a declassified CIA paper written for the National Security Council on the state of affairs in Cuba. The year matters: 1961 brought the Bay of Pigs landing in April and a hard freeze in U.S.–Cuban relations. The catalog does not date the briefing more closely or name its topics, so this description does not place it before or after the landing.
