cia-03153712: September 8, 1957: the bulletin went out. The daily intelligence summary reached senior officials. The Cold War's September dispatch. The file is now open to the public. This declassified paper is held. It is stored. It is filed.
cia-03186012: The last day of March 1961 brought this daily intelligence briefing. Agency analysts summed up world events for the leadership. The Cold War's routine paperwork. The library keeps the document safe. This file preserves that declassified bulletin.
cia-06520612: HR - 1. REGRET TO ADVISE THAT MR, john w. KEARNS III WAS KILLED BY INCOMING AR, a CIA document, the casualty notice. This file preserves that declassified paper. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
cia-06626812: WIESEL DOES NOT SEE TIMERMAN - 1979/09/05, a CIA document. The missed meeting. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
cia-06765412: IRAQI COMMANDER MEMOIRS ON MISSILES (3), a CIA document. The missile memoirs continue. This file preserves that declassified paper. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06769012: VLADIMIR SECEN MILE RAVLIC REGISTRATION - INTERNAL SECURITY MATTER, a CIA document. The registration file. This file preserves that declassified paper. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Time has kept the file intact.
cinquante-marveilleux-secrets-d-alchimie: Cinquante merveilleux secrets d'alchimie, 1912. The fifty secrets. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
coningsby-or-the-new-generation-pg7412: Disraeli's Coningsby — the new generation's political novel — follows young Coningsby through the making of modern Conservatism. The future prime minister wrote his own dazzling rise into brilliant fiction. The classic English political novel. Young England's hopes and follies parade through its brilliant pages.
conrad-twixt-land-sea-1912:
'Twixt Land and Sea, published in 1912, collects three long sea tales from Conrad's maturity. The title names his lifelong ground: the border where a sailor's ordered ship meets the disorder of shore life.

The most famous is 'The Secret Sharer', in which a young captain hides a fugitive officer in his cabin and finds a double of himself. 'Falk' tells of a captain with a terrible past fighting for love in Bangkok, and 'Because of the Dollars' turns on theft and loyalty in eastern ports. These tales show Conrad's sea world at its richest and most humane.
constitution-haiti-2012: Haiti's 1987 Constitution, amended 2012, frames its republic. It survived quakes. The Tower library holds the full text. It stood through ruin. Earth shook. Law trembled. People endured. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-mauritania-2012: Mauritania's 1991 Constitution, amended through 2012, frames its Islamic republic. It bans slavery anew. The Tower library holds the full text. It faced the desert. Chains lingered. Law condemned. Freedom pushed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-somalia-2012: Somalia's 2012 Constitution provisionally frames its federal state. Clans share power. The Tower library holds the full text. It tried to bind chaos. War raged. Clans talked. Paper hoped. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-sweden-2012: Sweden's 1974 Constitution, amended through 2012, frames its kingdom. The King reigns softly. The Tower library holds the full text. It kept a gentle crown. King smiled. People ruled. Calm reigned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cornford-religion-philosophy-1912:
F. M. Cornford published From Religion to Philosophy in 1912, a study of how Greek thought began. Cornford argues that early philosophy grew out of religious ritual and myth. Concepts like fate, soul, and nature carry traces of older rites and tribal life. The Milesian thinkers did not break with religion at a stroke.

He traces Moira, or fate, from ritual roots to cosmic law. Mystery cults and Orphic beliefs receive close study. The book is the philosophical charter of the Cambridge ritualist school. Its claims are bold and still debated by classicists. Cornford writes with lucidity rare in such deep waters. It pairs well with Harrison's Prolegomena from the same circle.
crabbe-tales-1812:
Twenty-one verse stories make up Crabbe's Tales, published in 1812. The first, The Dumb Orators, mocks men who are bold in safe company and timid when rivals sit near. George Crabbe had spent years as a country clergyman, and his tales draw on lives he had watched at close range.

A miser, a deserted wife, a ruined clerk, and a proud family brought low appear among the figures. Each story lands with a moral point, yet Crabbe keeps clear pity for the people he describes. The book fixed his fame as the poet who told plain truths about common English life.
crowley-book-4-part-1-1912:
Crowley set out to write the great textbook of his system, and Book Four opened it in 1912. Book 4, Part I: Mysticism, written with Mary D'Este Sturges, teaches the still half of the work. It is the course in mysticism of his order, the A A.

Posture, breath, and the holding of one thought are taught step by step. Crowley borrows the ladder of yoga, from asana to samadhi, and strips it of cult dress. His aim is plain: train the mind until it can rest on one point. The volume grounds all the magic that follows in the set.
cumont-astrology-putnam-1912:
Franz Cumont's Astrology and Religion among the Greeks and Romans appears in J. B. Putnam's translation of 1912. The book prints Cumont's American lectures of 1911. Cumont shows how star worship from Babylon conquered the Roman world. Astrology promised a map of fate written in the heavens.

He traces Chaldean lore through Greek science to Roman emperors and their horoscopes. Religion, science, and superstition blend in his account. Cumont was the leading scholar of ancient mystery faiths. The lectures are brief, elegant, and full of learning. They show why the stars held such power over ancient minds. Modern readers gain a clear door into that world.
descartes-philosophical-works-haldane-ro:
Volume 2 of Haldane and Ross's Philosophical Works of Descartes appeared in 1912. It holds the Objections and Replies to the Meditations, the great debate that followed Descartes's 1641 book. Learned critics across Europe sent objections, and Descartes answered each in print.

Caterus, Hobbes, Arnauld, and Gassendi pressed Descartes on God, the soul, and the circle in his proofs. Bourdin and others joined the attack. Descartes's replies clarify and sometimes shift his claims under fire. The volume is the essential companion to the Meditations. It shows early modern philosophy being made in argument, on mind, God, and knowledge, by the sharpest minds of the age.
deussen-system-vedanta-1912:
Paul Deussen spent years building The System of the Vedanta, and Charles Johnston's English translation appeared in 1912 for Western readers. Deussen, a German scholar in Schopenhauer's line, systematized Shankara's Advaita teaching from the Brahma-Sutras with great care. Non-duality, the claim that self and absolute are one reality, organizes the whole account from start to finish.

Western readers gained here their first rigorous map of Vedanta as a working system of thought. Deussen argues from the Sanskrit sources patiently, letting Shankara's logic show its strength on its own terms. The book remains a landmark of German Indology in English dress, dense but rewarding for steady readers.
dostoevsky-brothers-karamazov-garnett-19:
Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote The Brothers Karamazov, his final novel, and Constance Garnett made it English in 1912. Garnett's version became the standard English Karamazov for decades of readers. The book mixes a murder case with vast debates on faith, freedom, and guilt.

Three brothers, Dmitri, Ivan, and Alyosha, clash with their coarse, grasping father. When the old man is murdered, Dmitri stands trial for a crime of passion. Ivan's tale of the Grand Inquisitor asks why men trade freedom for bread and rule. Alyosha, a novice monk, seeks a way to live faith amid the wreckage. The novel's scope and force place it among the world's greatest books.
doyle-the-lost-world-1912:
Arthur Conan Doyle sent four men up a lost plateau in South America in 1912, and they found dinosaurs alive. The Lost World is the novel that named a whole kind of tale. Professor Challenger leads the party, loud, proud, and sure he is right.

Apes, pterodactyls, and lost tribes fill the high world above the falls. The book's mix of science, sport, and peril made it a hit at once. Real hunters of unknown beasts took its plot as a kind of map. Fiction and the beast hunt have walked together ever since that year.
dreiser-financier-1912:
Theodore Dreiser published The Financier in 1912, the first volume of his Trilogy of Desire. He modeled Frank Cowperwood on Charles Yerkes, the traction magnate who built and looted transit empires in Philadelphia and Chicago. Dreiser had covered Philadelphia as a young reporter and knew its machine politics well.

Cowperwood starts as a boy turning a quick profit on soap and rises through banks, street railways, and city loans. He takes a mistress, raids the city treasury with a compliant treasurer, and rides the panic of 1873 into prison. Dreiser treats his predator with fascinated respect, as a force of nature among smaller fish. The Financier is the foundational novel of American capitalism's inner life.
dunsany-book-of-wonder-1912:
Small, sharp, and bright with pictures, The Book of Wonder of 1912 is Dunsany's most loved story book. Its short tales are his fantasy at its most packed and pure. Sidney Sime's drawings match the text wonder for wonder throughout.

Thieves, gods, and seekers meet bad ends and strange mercies in a page or two each. The Chu-bu and Sheemish tale, of two fat small gods, is the book's famed jest. No shelf of early fantasy is whole without this volume in its place. It is Dunsany in miniature, at full and lasting strength, a small book with a long life.
dutt-srimadbhagabatam-7-12:
Dutt's Srimadbhagabatam of 1895 gives Books Seven through Twelve in English. The set forms the second half of the Bhagavata Purana, Hinduism's beloved scripture. Books One through Six were not found for this rendering, a gap to note.

Prahlada, the child saint, defies his demon father in Book Seven. Tales of the avatars lead toward Krishna's full, joyful story. Devotion, not mere rite, stands as the path the book commends. Song, story, and deep love of God fill its famous pages. Readers meet the scripture that shaped Hindu devotion for a thousand years past. Its second half carries some of the tradition's most loved stories.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-12: The twelfth volume shows Montaigne weighing the world. He writes of profit and loss, of honor and of shame. The judgments are shrewd, humane, and often surprising. A keen, steady, and forgiving eye on human motives.
eucken-main-currents-1912:
Meyrick Booth's 1912 translation carries the subtitle a study of the spiritual and intellectual movements of the present day. Rudolf Eucken first issued the German work in 1904 as Geistige Stroemungen der Gegenwart. In it the Jena professor and Nobel laureate surveys the forces then shaping modern minds.

Eucken sorts the main currents of his age and weighs what each one offers human life. He asks which movements deepen the life of the spirit and which leave it thin. His judgments favor effort, unity, and inner growth over mere fashion. English readers got here a broad map of European thought around 1900.
europmc-pmc10190912: A medical paper reporting on progress of trench fever investigations. The trenches' fever. This article preserves that military medicine. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc10668412:
Kim, Kim, Lee, and Hwangbo reviewed a key immune sensor, TLR4, in 2023 and its role in ageing. TLR4 sits on cell surfaces and spots threats from outside and inside the cell. It fires signal chains that switch on swelling genes. Two helper proteins, MyD88 and TRIF, carry its signals down distinct paths.

Age-linked diseases often show a slow burn of swelling. TLR4 helps fan that burn, Kim reports. Shifts in its levels can worsen or ease the signs of such diseases. The sensor also feeds cell ageing itself, called senescence. That spread of roles makes TLR4 a drug target past plain immune care. The review weighs where blocking it may help most.
europmc-pmc10835012:
Tao and colleagues review how gene messages are cut and rejoined, and how that shapes health, in this 2024 paper. Alternative splicing is a process where one gene's message can be trimmed in varied ways to make distinct protein versions. Proteins that bind RNA guide which trims happen. These versions let tissues and organs develop their own traits.

When splicing goes wrong, proteins can change shape, lose their job, or vanish, the review says. Such faults are tied to cancer growth and spread. They also appear in brain diseases and in diseases where the immune system attacks the body. The authors sort recent progress by tissue and disease. They argue that fixing faulty splicing choices could open new treatment paths.
europmc-pmc10836812:
Mackowiak, Fu, Maccioni, and Gao review liver harm from alcohol in this 2024 paper. Alcohol-associated liver disease covers a range of harm, from simple fat build-up in the liver to heavy scarring and liver cancer. It is a major cause of long-term liver disease worldwide. No drug for it has won approval from the US drug agency yet.

The review pulls together fresh insight on how the disease starts and worsens. It highlights studies that read many layers of cell data at once, a style called multiomics. The authors weigh how such findings might reach the clinic as real treatments. They also discuss lab models of the disease and its overlap with weight-linked liver harm. Differences between patients get close attention as a guide for future trials.
europmc-pmc11009112:
Wright, Stevens, Mackintosh, Lawniczak, and Blaxter compare chromosomes across butterflies and moths in this 2024 study. One in ten of all described species on Earth is a butterfly or moth. Most hold 31 chromosomes, the bundles of DNA that carry genes. A few species, though, show wild swings in that count.

The team analysed 210 genomes with complete chromosomes. Today's chromosomes descend from 32 ancestral blocks, which they name Merian elements. Those blocks stayed largely intact across 250 million years of evolution. Eight lineages broke the pattern with heavy splitting or mixing of blocks. Outside them, joins between blocks are rare and splits rarer still. Joins often involved small, repeat-rich blocks and the sex chromosome. The authors read this as tight constraint on genome layout.
europmc-pmc1131912:
Johansen, Harris, Rychly, and Ergul link excess free radicals to diabetes damage and weigh antioxidant therapy in this 2005 review. Heart and vessel complications are the leading cause of illness and death in diabetes. Growing evidence blames oxidative stress, where highly reactive free radicals, largely driven by high blood sugar, damage vessel walls, proteins, membrane fats, and DNA.

Despite that evidence, large trials of classic antioxidants showed no benefit for diabetic patients, the authors note. The failure reshapes the strategy. Rather than merely mopping up radicals after they form, care should also prevent their generation at the source. The review maps how radicals arise in diabetes and how they speed artery clogging. New strategies pairing classic and novel antioxidants are proposed for testing in clinic.
europmc-pmc1190212:
Elechiguerra and colleagues tested tiny silver particles against HIV in 2005. How metal particles interact with viruses was still largely unknown. HIV-1 is the virus that causes AIDS. Silver particles of set sizes were mixed with the virus in lab tests.

Only the smallest particles, about 1 to 10 nanometers wide, attached. They sat in a regular pattern on the virus surface. The likely anchor points are knobs the virus uses to enter cells. Once coated, the virus could not bind host cells well. Elechiguerra points to a fresh angle for antiviral design.
europmc-pmc12009612:
Troy and colleagues reframed resilience, the ability to fare well after hardship, in 2023. Hardship like poverty or loss often disrupts mental health. Yet people vary widely in how they respond. Some recover fast, and a few even improve.

Two research camps had studied coping and emotion apart. Each camp had gaps, and key terms stayed fuzzy. Troy merges them into one affect-regulation framework. Feelings and their control sit at the center. The framework sorts past findings and flags open questions. It also guides studies on who stays well, and why.
europmc-pmc1233412:
Skerker and colleagues mapped bacterial signaling systems end to end in 2005. Bacteria sense the world through two-part signal systems. One part detects a cue, and the other part responds. These systems also pace growth and the cell cycle.

The test species was Caulobacter crescentus, a model bacterium. Deleting genes showed at least 39 of 106 signal genes matter. Nine proved vital for growth or survival. A method called phosphotransfer profiling traced which parts talk. Skerker combines gene tests and chemistry into one wiring diagram. It appeared in PLoS Biology in 2005. One new pathway, from CenK to CenR, guards the outer cell envelope and its shape.
europmc-pmc1436012:
Good research often fails to change daily care. The Improved Clinical Effectiveness through Behavioural Research Group (ICEBeRG) wrote in 2006 about why that gap persists. Trials show a care change works in one place, then falls flat in another. Reviews seldom say which parts of the people, the plan, or the setting made the difference.

The group argues that building plans on theory can help. A theory gives a shared frame for what a plan targets and how it might work. It can guide design, delivery, and later checks of cause and effect. The group also warns of hard parts, like picking among theories and turning ideas into real steps.
europmc-pmc1481612:
Doctors and nurses cluster in cities, leaving rural areas short staffed. Dussault and Franceschini reviewed that imbalance in 2006. Access to skilled staff is key to global health goals set in 2000. Without workers nearby, vulnerable people miss care.

The review weighs what drives the skew, what blocks change, and which fixes have been tried. It draws on studies from rich and poor countries alike. Dussault sizes up why some strategies worked and others failed. Lessons include the pull of pay, training spots, and living conditions on where staff settle. The paper aims to guide fairer spread of the health workforce.
europmc-pmc1483912:
Antibodies that block the SARS virus may fail as the virus mutates. ter Meulen and co-authors tackled that risk in 2006. One antibody, CR3014, had shielded ferrets fully from lung damage. The team grew virus variants that escaped it. All carried a single change, P462L, in the spike protein.

A second antibody, CR3022, killed those escape variants and bound a unlike spot. No virus escaped CR3022 in their tests. Mixed together, the two antibodies worked with synergy, needing far lower doses for full blocking. ter Meulen argues pairs of non-rival antibodies can cover escape routes in advance.
europmc-pmc1584412:
A broken safety switch lets lung tumor cells arm themselves against drugs. Singh and co-authors found that in 2006 in non-small-cell lung cancer. In healthy cells, the protein KEAP1 keeps NRF2, a switch for protective genes, under restraint and marked for disposal.

In tumors, KEAP1 was often crippled. Mutations hit 19 percent of tumor samples and half of cell lines. Loss of one gene copy was also common, in 41 percent of tumors. With KEAP1 weak, NRF2 piled up in the nucleus and boosted antioxidants and detox enzymes. Singh links that boost to drug resistance in tumors.
europmc-pmc1592312:
Stinkbugs hand their gut bacteria to their young in a capsule. Hosokawa and co-authors reported in 2006 the first case of strict joint evolution in gut bacteria living outside host cells. Female plataspid stinkbugs pack the bacteria into capsules laid with their eggs.

Family trees of bug and bacterium matched perfectly, a sign they speciated together. Stripping the bacteria away stunted growth and caused death and sterility in the bugs. The bacterium's genome had shrunk and its DNA had drifted toward A and T letters, traits seen in inside-cell symbionts. Hosokawa names it Candidatus Ishikawaella capsulata.
europmc-pmc1852112:
Turashvili and colleagues hunted in 2007 for markers that separate the two main invasive breast cancer types. Ductal and lobular carcinomas spread in different patterns, hinting at distinct biology. Telling them apart under the microscope can be hard in borderline cases.

The team used laser microdissection, which cuts exact cells from tissue slices, to isolate pure tumor and normal cells. Samples came from ten mastectomy specimens, and gene activity was read on arrays covering the genome. Comparing lobular tumors with normal cells yielded 84 shared changed genes. Seven candidate markers, including CDH1 and EMP1, were checked in tissue with antibody staining. One marker, ASPN, was also confirmed by a second RNA method. The gene sets give new handles for telling the two cancer types apart.
europmc-pmc1858712:
Passos, von Zglinicki and co-authors asked in 2007 why sister cells age at uneven rates. Human cells stop dividing when their telomeres, the caps that guard chromosome ends, wear too short. Yet clones in the same settings senesce, meaning they retire from division, at wildly varied times.

The team found that superoxide output from mitochondria, the cell's power plants, rose with replicative age despite an uncoupling response meant to offset it. That failure upset calcium balance and other signs of cell stress. Gentle uncoupling delayed senescence, cutting superoxide, slowing telomere shortening, and leaving fewer damage marks at telomeres. Sorting the earliest senescent cells from young cultures showed they carried more reactive oxygen, broken mitochondria, and shorter telomeres. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen thus drives much of that uneven timing in cell aging.
europmc-pmc2043012:
Costa and co-workers identified in 2007 a protein that drives drug-induced death in lung cancer cells. Some lung cancers carry mutations in the EGFR gene and respond to drugs called tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as gefitinib. Most later resist treatment, often through a second mutation named T790M. The team studied sensitive and resistant cancer cell lines and a tumour sample from a resistant patient.

A pro-death protein called BIM rose in sensitive cells when gefitinib was given, and cell death followed. The T790M mutation blocked both the BIM rise and the death. An irreversible drug overcame that block. Silencing BIM reduced drug-induced death directly. A new resistance mutation, L747S, was found in the patient's tumour. It also weakened the BIM response.
europmc-pmc2124912: A medical paper with further observations on experimental syphilis and yaws. The pox diseases. This article preserves that research. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125012: A medical paper on the classification of the streptothrices. The branching germs. This article preserves that bacteriology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2125212: A medical paper on the role of the spleen in blood formation. The blood-making spleen. This article preserves that hematology. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2125512: A medical paper on Spirochaeta icterohaemorrhagiae in American wild rats. The rat spirochete. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2126312: A medical paper on the use of final hydrogen ion concentration in streptococcus differentiation. The pH test. This article preserves that bacteriology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128312: A medical paper on cow serum as a substitute for colostrum in newborn calves. The calf milk. This article preserves that veterinary nutrition. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.

europmc-pmc2222612:
Tennant and co-workers developed the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale in 2007. Interest was growing in measuring positive mental health across whole populations, not just illness. The scale, shortened to WEMWBS, uses only positively worded items about aspects of well-being. An expert panel built it from academic literature, focus group research and testing of an existing scale, then validated it on student and representative population samples.

Statistical analysis supported the scale measuring a single well-being construct. Internal consistency was high, with reliability scores of 0.89 in students and 0.91 in the population sample. That suggests some item redundancy in the item set. The scale was validated in United Kingdom samples. Scores correlated strongly with other well-being scales and followed a near-normal distribution without ceiling effects. One-week test-retest reliability was 0.83. Social desirability bias was no worse than in comparable scales.
europmc-pmc2253612:
Simarro, Jannin and Cattand assessed progress in 2008 toward eliminating human African trypanosomiasis, also called sleeping sickness. This parasitic disease, spread by tsetse flies, is fatal if untreated. It decimated parts of sub-Saharan Africa in the early twentieth century. Systematic screening and treatment nearly halted transmission by the 1960s. After independence, surveillance lapsed and the disease slowly returned, flaring across old endemic areas thirty years later.

Since 1995 the World Health Organization has pushed renewed surveillance, diagnosis access and control coordination. New detected cases are now falling. The authors warn of the punishment of success: falling numbers may tempt health institutions to lower the disease's priority. That neglect is exactly what let sleeping sickness rebound before, so sustained effort is essential to finish elimination.
europmc-pmc2265412:
van Ham and co-workers built a worm model in 2008 to find genes controlling alpha-synuclein inclusion formation, the protein clumping seen in Parkinson's disease. Their Caenorhabditis elegans model lets inclusions be watched in living animals as they age. Old worms formed inclusions of aggregated alpha-synuclein resembling the human pathology. A genome-wide RNA interference screen then knocked down genes one by one, seeking changes in inclusion timing.

Knocking down 80 genes caused inclusions to appear prematurely and in greater number. Quality-control and vesicle-trafficking genes, which move cargo inside cells, were overrepresented among the hits. Many sat in the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and vesicle compartments. Suppressors of inclusion formation included ageing genes such as sir-2.1, the worm counterpart of SIRT1. The results link inclusion formation to cellular ageing through membrane trafficking, and nominate candidate drug targets.
europmc-pmc2267812:
Gérardin and a large team prospectively studied mother-to-child chikungunya transmission in 2008 during the La Réunion outbreak. That outbreak infected over a third of the island's population between 2005 and 2006. At their maternity hospital, 7,504 women delivered over 22 months. Of these, 678 were infected during pregnancy and 61 around delivery. The team characterised every vertically transmitted case's features and outcomes.

Transmission occurred almost exclusively when mothers had virus in their blood during delivery. The rate was 48.7 percent in that group. Caesarean section gave no protection against transmission to the newborn. This was a prospective hospital study conducted during the island outbreak. Infected newborns were asymptomatic at birth, with illness starting at a median of four days. Pain, exhaustion and fever occurred in every case. Over half became severely ill, mainly with brain involvement, and four children had persistent disabilities.
europmc-pmc2329812:
Boles and Horswill showed in 2008 how staph bacteria break up their own biofilms. A biofilm is a slime layer where bacteria stick to a surface and each other, often resisting drugs. Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of hard-to-treat infections. Its agr system senses crowding through small signal peptides.

The authors found that agr must be off for a biofilm to form. Turning it back on, by adding signal peptide or removing glucose, made mature biofilms shed cells. This worked in several staph strains, and the freed cells became sensitive again to the antibiotic rifampicin. The shedding needed enzymes that cut proteins, called proteases. A mutant lacking the Aur and Spl proteases barely shed at all.
europmc-pmc2361112:
Arnould and colleagues asked in 2006 whether the breast cancer drug trastuzumab works partly through the immune system. The drug targets HER2, a growth receptor found in excess on some breast cancers. It was already known to block growth signals, but lab work hinted it also flags tumor cells for killing by immune cells.

The study covered 23 patients treated before surgery with trastuzumab plus a chemotherapy drug. Nine tumors vanished completely and 14 shrank partly. Compared with two matched control groups, treated tumors held many more natural killer cells, a type of immune killer cell. Their lymphocytes also carried more of two killing proteins, Granzyme B and TiA1. The authors concluded immune attack, led by natural killer cells, likely forms part of how the drug works.
europmc-pmc2486312:
Wilcove and Wikelski asked in 2008 whether animal migration itself is disappearing. Migration is among nature's most visible spectacles, from whales and songbirds to salamanders and dragonflies. Yet passenger pigeons no longer darken North American skies. Plains bison herds have shrunk from hundreds of thousands to scattered thousands. Europe's long-distance songbirds keep thinning.

The saiga antelope of central Asia fell over 95% in two decades, from more than a million to under 50,000 animals. The authors sort the threats into four groups: habitat loss, over-hunting and over-fishing, a changing climate, and barriers like dams and fences. Most migrants are not near extinction; they are just becoming scarce, and abundance is what powers migration's ecological services, from salmon feeding forests to grazers shaping grasslands. Protecting still-common migrants, they argue, poses scientific and political challenges unlike saving rare species, but waiting until they are rare loses the phenomenon itself.
europmc-pmc2596312:
Kryazhimskiy and Plotkin analysed in 2008 a favourite yardstick of molecular evolution, the dN/dS ratio, and warned that it misbehaves inside a single population. The ratio compares rates of protein-changing and silent DNA substitutions. Values above one are read as positive selection. That logic was built for species that split long ago, whose differences are fixed. It was not built for samples from one population, whose differences are still spreading or vanishing.

Deriving the expected ratio under selection for population samples, they show it barely responds to the strength of selection. The link is not even steady: it rises, then falls. So the signature value above one can be broken within populations. Reading selection pressure from such a ratio may be impossible. The results urge caution wherever dN/dS is computed from population genetic data.
europmc-pmc2627612:
Schmaljohn and Hjelle reviewed hantaviruses in 1997 as a global disease problem, four years after a shock outbreak in the American Southwest. These rodent-borne viruses were long known in the Eastern Hemisphere as causes of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, a kidney disease. In 1993 a previously unknown group emerged in the United States causing a fast, often fatal lung disease named hantavirus pulmonary syndrome.

The discovery triggered intense study of hantavirus ecology and epidemiology worldwide, which uncovered many further novel viruses in different rodent hosts. The authors review the group's distribution, its rodent reservoirs, its disease potential, and its genetic spectrum. They stress three facts. The viruses are everywhere, in numerous rodent species on several continents. And they can cause severe human illness. Together these make them a standing public health concern.
europmc-pmc2667312:
Higgins, Thompson, and Spiegelhalter re-examined in 2009 the random-effects model, the standard way of merging study results that disagree. The model assumes each study's true effect is drawn from a spread of values, often pictured as a bell curve. Reviews then report the center of that spread as the answer.

The authors argue the center alone is not enough. A doctor needs to know the range of effects a new patient or setting might see, which calls for a prediction, not just an average. They compare three styles of analysis: classic formulas, distribution-free methods, and the Bayesian style that carries full uncertainty through. Bayes wins for prediction, they find, but costs heavy computing and depends on prior choices. They offer a simple prediction interval for classic analyses, shown on studies of mental flexibility in eating disorders.
europmc-pmc2674212:
Garthe, Behr, and Kempermann tested in 2009 whether new nerve cells born in the adult mouse brain help learning stay flexible. The hippocampus, a brain area key to memory, keeps adding new cells throughout life. The team suppressed that growth with a drug, then set the mice a water maze: swim to a hidden platform whose place they must learn.

Both treated and normal mice learned the first platform spot well. The difference showed in strategy. Normal mice sharpened their search into a precise, direct route. Treated mice kept using rough, loose strategies, and fell behind most when the platform moved on day four. Brain recordings matched: a form of signal strengthening tied to the new cells was gone. New neurons, the authors conclude, are not needed to learn, but to relearn and refine.
europmc-pmc2717212:
Nock and co-authors analyzed in 2009 which mental disorders raise the odds of suicidal thoughts and attempts across twenty-one countries. Past work often tested one disorder at a time, yet disorders overlap heavily in the same person. Using World Mental Health Survey data from over one hundred thousand people, they separated thoughts, plans, and attempts.

All sixteen disorders studied were linked to later suicide attempts when tested alone. Bipolar disorder showed the strongest link in richer countries, and conduct disorder in poorer ones. Having more disorders raised risk further, but each added disorder mattered less than the one before. Planned attempts were tied to disorders more strongly than impulsive, unplanned attempts.
europmc-pmc2759912:
Basu reviewed in 2009 epidemiologic studies from 2001 to 2008 on how high ambient temperature, the temperature of surrounding air, affects mortality. Heat waves had dominated older work, while newer studies used modern time-series and case-crossover designs across many locations. Studies of heat waves alone and of cold effects were excluded to keep the focus on general warm temperature.

Across thirty-six studies, higher temperature raised deaths from cardiovascular, respiratory, and cerebrovascular causes, including heart failure and heart attacks. Fine particles and ozone could confound or modify the link in warm months, yet an independent temperature effect remained. Risk was higher for Black populations, women, poorer groups, the elderly, and infants, which argues for region-specific heat policies in cities.
europmc-pmc2852312:
Sheldrick described in 2010 how his SHELX program suite for solving crystal structures gained a new trick: tracing the protein's main chain while improving the map. Experimental phasing locates heavy marker atoms first, then refines rough phases until an electron-density map becomes readable. The suite's three programs divide that labor, keeping each step deliberately simple and fast.

Folding chain tracing into the iterative map improvement lets the software exploit repeated copies of a molecule in the crystal, a symmetry clue that strengthens weak phases. The paper walks through how the substructure solution and density modification stages interact, and why the severe simplifications, like assuming a single marker atom type, rarely hurt in practice. The result is faster routes to readable maps for automated pipelines.
europmc-pmc2876112:
Lambrechts, Scott, and Gubler assessed in 2010 what the worldwide spread of the Asian tiger mosquito means for dengue, the most common insect-borne viral disease of humans. The mosquito, Aedes albopictus, invaded new continents within three decades and can carry dengue virus. The long-standing main carrier is its cousin Aedes aegypti, and the authors asked whether the newcomer truly shares the blame.

Reviewing past epidemics, they found that places where the tiger mosquito dominates have never suffered the explosive dengue outbreaks with severe disease seen elsewhere. Lab studies agreed in part: the tiger mosquito catches the virus in its gut more easily, yet the virus escapes to its other tissues more slowly. It looks like a real but second-rate carrier, a nuance for surveillance planning.
europmc-pmc2885312:
Janssen and LeBlanc reviewed in 2010 how being active affects the health of school-age children and youth. They searched six databases and found over eleven thousand papers. From those, they kept eighty-six studies with over one hundred results. The health markers were obesity, blood fats, the metabolic syndrome, and blood pressure. Low bone density, low mood, and injuries were tracked too.

The pattern was clear and dose-based: the more activity, the more gain. Even small amounts of activity helped youth at high risk, such as those with obesity. Gains showed up in heart and metabolic markers, bone strength, and mood. The main harm was injury risk. The graded proof backed a call for daily moderate to hard activity for school-age youth.
europmc-pmc2906812:
Gogolla and colleagues hunted in 2009 for one shared circuit flaw across the many mouse models of autism, a condition with dozens of unrelated genetic and environmental causes. A leading theory blames imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory signaling during development. The team focused on parvalbumin-positive inhibitory neurons, the cells that pace cortical circuits and drive their experience-based refinement.

Pooling published models, they found these inhibitory cells reduced in the neocortex again and again. They also tested two more models. One was exposed before birth to the drug valproate, and one carried a human autism mutation. In the two new models the loss was lopsided between brain hemispheres in vision and touch areas, but spared a memory structure nearby. A common circuit defect amid diverse causes suggests prevention might target the shared pathway.
europmc-pmc2928212:
Meyer and colleagues reported a 2010 rat study of CP-690,550, a drug that blocks Janus kinases JAK1 and JAK3 and was then in trials for rheumatoid arthritis. Human trials had shown falling neutrophil counts during treatment, and the team wanted to link that drop to kinase selectivity.

Lab assays showed strong blocking of JAK1 and JAK3 signalling, with far weaker action through JAK2 in cells. In rats with adjuvant-driven joint disease, oral doses eased paw swelling in a dose-linked way. At helpful exposures the drug also brought raised blood cytokines, neutrophils, and marrow precursor cells back toward normal.
europmc-pmc2935112:
Parfitt, Barthel, and Macnaughton reviewed food waste across global supply chains in 2010, asking what losses mean for feeding nine billion people by mid-century. Definitions of waste vary, and the data behind many estimates proved thin and old.

Their review found losses highest soon after harvest in poorer countries, while rich countries wasted most food after purchase. Data for farm losses in developing nations often dated back decades, leaving current totals uncertain. Interviews with supply chain experts stressed better system efficiency plus changed habits among wealthy consumers as the main routes to cutting waste.
europmc-pmc2951912:
Ohshima and colleagues reported in 2010 that a spreading stomach cancer cell line ships out one family of small regulatory RNAs in tiny vesicles called exosomes. Vesicles ferry proteins and RNA between cells, and blood-borne versions are eyed as disease markers.

Comparing RNA inside cells, in the growth medium, and inside vesicles, the team found the let-7 family plentiful in cells and strongly concentrated in released vesicles. Other lines released less RNA and oddly shaped vesicles. Packing let-7 into vesicles may let cancer cells dump growth brakes while passing signals to neighbours, a habit worth tracking.
europmc-pmc2978112:
Murray and a large team presented Normalisation Process Theory in 2010, a framework for getting complex health interventions into everyday practice. Good trial results alone rarely change routine care, leaving a stubborn gap between research and use.

The theory names the work people do to adopt, carry out, and keep up a new practice, and can be used while designing a study rather than after it ends. Trialists can spot recruitment snags, clashes with clinic habits, and weak uptake early. The authors offer it as a shared checklist for judging whether an intervention can truly settle in.
europmc-pmc3022812:
Zhang, Thompson, Zhang, and Xu reviewed in 2011 how a brain protein is cut into pieces tied to Alzheimer disease. The protein is called APP in short. When two cutting enzymes act on it in sequence, they release a small fragment that clumps into the plaques found in patients' brains. A different first cut avoids making that fragment at all.

The review explains what each cutting enzyme does, what controls them, and what the leftover pieces may do in healthy and sick brains. Mutations in the APP gene itself cause a small share of early, inherited cases. Because blocking the harmful cuts could slow the disease, drug makers have chased these enzymes for years. The paper gathers what was known about their promise and their risks.
europmc-pmc3059412:
Klopp, Gupta, Spaeth, Andreeff, and Marini reviewed in 2011 why studies disagree on whether mesenchymal stem cells help or hinder tumors. These stem cells, normally part of tissue repair, are drawn into growing tumors. When labs add them to tumor models, some reports show faster growth and spread, while others show tumors shrinking instead.

The review compares how the conflicting studies were run and finds that timing may explain much of the clash. Adding the cells early, late, or alongside the tumor from the start changes the outcome. Proposed mechanisms include chemical signaling, blood vessel support, effects on cell suicide, and immune tuning. Knowing when the cells help a tumor matters twice over. It bears on the safety of stem cell therapies under development, and on how the tumor's supporting tissue drives cancer in the first place.
europmc-pmc3083512:
Stagg and coauthors found in 2011 that the same brain stimulation can speed or slow motor learning depending purely on when it is given. Volunteers learned an explicit finger sequence task while receiving gentle direct current stimulation to the motor cortex, before the task, or not at all. The positive form of stimulation is known to raise cortex excitability for an hour or more after it ends.

Given during practice, the positive stimulation made learning faster. Given just before practice, it made learning slower, a reversal the authors highlight as a warning. The negative form of stimulation slowed learning in both timings. The results matter for stroke rehabilitation, where stimulation is paired with therapy in hopes of boosting recovery. Pairing the two at the wrong offset, this study suggests, could blunt the very training it aims to help.
europmc-pmc3114412:
Arnaud Delorme and colleagues described a set of free software tools for brain-wave research in a 2011 paper in Computational Intelligence and Neuroscience. The tools extend a widely used program for handling recordings of electrical activity from the scalp, built at a neuroscience centre in California. Together they cover study design, head modelling, and live experiments.

One tool helps compare recordings across many people, while another builds realistic models of how signals travel through the head. A third maps how brain areas influence each other over time. Further tools support devices that let people control computers with brain signals, and a live system that runs interactive experiments mixing several data streams at once. The suite is shared freely for non-profit research.
europmc-pmc3130012:
Deanna Church and colleagues explained how the human reference genome gets repaired and improved in a 2011 paper in PLoS Biology. The reference sequence guides nearly all human gene research and medical testing. Yet the celebrated first version still held hundreds of gaps, wrongly ordered stretches, and rare variants presented as standard. An international consortium was formed to fix it.

The consortium curates problem regions, adds alternate versions for stretches that vary greatly between people, and now also maintains the mouse and fish references used in labs. The paper describes how assembly decisions are tracked and shared so users can place any new sequence in its chromosome context. Keeping the reference honest, they argue, is essential as genome testing enters routine medical care.
europmc-pmc3233612:
Steven Cresawn and colleagues introduced Phamerator, software for comparing bacteriophage genomes, in this 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Phages, the viruses that infect bacteria, have mosaic genomes stitched from exchanged pieces and crowded with small genes of unknown function. That patchwork makes annotation and comparison unusually hard.

Phamerator sorts protein-coding genes into families of related sequences, called phamilies, using pairwise comparisons, and stores the relationships in a database. From it, researchers can draw genome maps of several phages at once that display both DNA and protein relationships plus conserved domains. Circular diagrams of each family reveal how individual genes have moved through phage populations by horizontal exchange, each with its own history. The tool gives phage biologists a shared picture of genomes that otherwise resist comparison.
europmc-pmc3245612:
Daehwan Kim and Steven Salzberg presented TopHat-Fusion, an algorithm for finding gene fusions in RNA sequencing data, in this 2011 paper in Genome Biology. Fusion transcripts arise when chromosomes break and rejoin wrongly, gluing two genes together, and they matter in cancer. Earlier tools leaned on existing gene annotation, which blinds them to fusions involving unannotated pieces.

The new method is built on the authors' TopHat aligner. It aligns RNA reads without relying on annotation. It can therefore detect fusions from known genes, unknown genes, and unrecorded splice variants alike. Applied to breast and prostate cancer cell lines, it recovered previously reported fusions and found new ones, each backed by solid supporting reads. The software was released freely for other researchers.
europmc-pmc3278112:
Gunther Eysenbach and the CONSORT-EHEALTH Group produced a reporting checklist for trials of web and mobile health interventions, published in 2011 in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. The established CONSORT statement improved how drug trials are reported. Online interventions raise special problems, though. The chief one is describing the tool in enough detail for others to replicate it. Only then can theory be built on the results.

Drawing on a literature review, an expert survey, and a workshop, the group built the checklist as an extension of CONSORT, covering the elements peculiar to electronic interventions. The journal adopted it as a submission requirement, with authors filing an electronic checklist showing where each item is addressed. The authors expect the standard to sharpen the validity judgments readers can make, and they plan a before-and-after evaluation of whether reporting actually improves.
europmc-pmc3302812:
Sonveaux and a large team reported in 2012 that blocking lactate entry into vessel lining cells could starve tumors of new blood vessels. Fast growing tumors burn sugar quickly and release lactic acid, creating a gradient that mirrors their low oxygen zones. Earlier work showed lactate switches on a low oxygen program in cancer cells, and the team asked whether vessel cells respond the same way.

They found that lactate entering through a carrier protein called MCT1 switched on that program even when oxygen was plentiful. This raised levels of signals that drive vessel growth. Blocking the carrier stopped vessel cells from migrating and forming tubes, and it slowed vessel growth into tumors in living animals. The authors present carrier blockers as drugs with both anti vessel and anti metabolism effects.
europmc-pmc3307012:
Singh, Williams, Siahpush, and Mulhollen mapped gaps in cancer death rates across the United States, in a study published in 2011. They linked county level death records from 2003 to 2007 with a measure of local deprivation and a scale running from city to countryside. Cancers covered included lung, colorectal, prostate, breast, and cervical cancers, alongside all cancers combined.

People in poorer counties and rural areas died of cancer at higher rates than wealthier and urban residents. The excess was sharpest for lung, colorectal, prostate, and cervical cancers. Poverty mattered more than rurality, though both counted on their own. Black Americans died at higher rates than white Americans at every level of deprivation, and the poverty gap in deaths ran steeper outside cities. The authors blame uneven smoking, screening, and treatment.
europmc-pmc3323412:
Fischer Walker, Perin, Aryee, Boschi-Pinto, and Black estimated how often young children suffer diarrhea in poorer countries, in a 2012 review. Diarrhea remains a leading killer of children under five, yet planners lacked up to date counts of episodes by age and country. The team gathered long running studies that followed children over time and modeled rates for one hundred thirty nine low and middle income countries.

The typical child fell ill a little less often in 2010 than in 1990, though the average still approached three episodes a year. Babies between six and eleven months old suffered most, at more than four episodes a year. Across all countries, episodes still numbered well over a billion and a half in 2010. The authors say the sheer repeated burden on each child demands more money for prevention and treatment.
europmc-pmc3377712:
Srinivasan and co-workers profiled vaginal bacteria in 2012 from more than two hundred women with and without bacterial vaginosis. The condition is common and linked to many health problems, yet its microbial changes were poorly mapped. Deep gene sequencing let the team name bacteria down to the species level.

Women with the condition carried mixed communities rarely ruled by a single species, while healthy women were usually dominated by one of two Lactobacillus species. Only two bacteria tracked with all four clinical signs used in diagnosis. Groups of bacteria also appeared together, hinting at shared feeding. The maps help explain why two common diagnostic schemes often disagree.
europmc-pmc3398412:
Catalgol, Batirel, Taga, and Ozer revisited resveratrol in 2012, the red-wine compound behind the so-called French paradox. French eaters famously show good heart outcomes despite a rich, fatty diet. Resveratrol, a plant polyphenol, has since been tested across many diseases.

Studies credit it with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, growth-slowing, and vessel-blocking effects, the first of which may drive several others. Many signaling pathways sit among its molecular targets. The review follows those pathways into heart disease, cancer, brain degeneration, and possibly longer life. Where oxidative stress plays a central role, the authors argue, the compound's combined actions look most promising.
europmc-pmc3407712:
Stansley, Post, and Hensley compared laboratory systems in 2012 for studying microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, in Alzheimer's disease. Activated microglia join plaques and tangles as a hallmark of the disease, and interest in their biology has surged. Researchers grow them many ways, each with strengths and trade-offs.

The review covers freshly isolated primary microglia, virus-immortalized lines such as BV2 and N9, a human immortalized line, and rodent lines that immortalized on their own. It compares what each system needs to grow and how each behaves, especially when provoked by inflammatory triggers. Choosing the right system for the question, the authors stress, shapes what a study can honestly claim.

froude-history-england-vol-12:
Elizabeth's last years fill the twelfth and final volume of Froude's History, from 1865. The Earl of Essex rises, plots, rebels, and goes to the block. The old queen declines in body and spirit, and dies in 1603, ending the Tudor line.

Froude closes his vast epic with the passing of Gloriana herself. Grief, faction, and war with Spain cloud the reign's final seasons. He treats the queen with awe, yet shows the cost of her long rule. The volume ends both a reign and one of the great narrative histories in English, twelve books that made the Tudor century vivid for all later readers.
frus-1861-d112:
A dispatch from Mr. Jones reached Secretary of State William H. Seward under the date 15 April 1861. It is document 112 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Jones wrote three days after the fall of Fort Sumter opened the war. The heading gives no post, so his report must be read by its date and place in the file. It joins the flood of first week papers that told Washington how the world took the news. First week papers like this one set the tone of the whole year's foreign record. First week tone, set in haste, echoed through the whole year's file.
frus-1861-d12:
Baron von Gerolt, Prussia's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 July 1861. The letter is document 12 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Foreign envoys wrote to the Secretary as a matter of course, on claims, ships, and points of law. Gerolt's note came one day after Seward had written to him, a quick turn by the standards of the time. The pair of letters shows business between the two men moving at a brisk pace. Envoys' notes often dealt with the rights of their nationals caught in the war's net.
frus-1861-d212:
Writing from Washington on 9 May 1861, William H. Seward addressed Mr. Marsh. The printed record keeps it as Document 212 in the President's message volume for 1861. It belongs to the opening months of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d312:
21 October 1861 brought Mr. Harris a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 312 in the President's message volume for 1861. It belongs to the autumn of the war's first year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d112:
31 July 1862 brought Charles Francis Adams a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 112 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d12:
Seward's incoming mail for 31 January 1862 held a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 12 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d212:
On 19 March 1862 Lord Lyons sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a note that stands as Document 212 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The British legation in Washington traded such notes with the State Department all through the war.

By mid-March, Union armies were pressing in Virginia and the West, and foreign watchers had stopped expecting a quick end. Lyons's correspondence with Seward mixed formal protests, requests, and replies on the many small cases the war created. This note is one entry in that long, careful ledger between two governments at odds but not at war. Washington was a small town in 1862, and the envoys met socially as often as officially.
frus-1862-d312:
Document 312 is the second Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 19 September 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters in the same mail.

Post-Antietam letters from Washington had a new asset: proof the Union could stop the South's best army. That fact weakened the case for foreign action more than any argument. The second letter of 19 September belongs to the first wave of mail that carried the changed picture to Europe. In Paris, Dayton put it to work. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d412:
Carl Schurz, then American minister in Madrid, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 October 1861. It is Document 412 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, among the earliest Spanish papers in the file.

Schurz was a German-born reformer who had fled failed revolution in Europe and become a Union general and politician. From Madrid he reported on a Spain that held Cuba and was joining Britain and France in the move on Mexico. His early dispatches warned Washington how the war looked from a European court. They helped shape Seward's handling of Spain in the war's first full autumn.
frus-1862-d512:
James Shepherd Pike sent this report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 August 1862. It is Document 512 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Pike wrote as the Confederate cruiser Alabama was getting to sea, the start of a raiding war that would fill neutral-port files for two years. Dutch ports and colonies would face the same questions as British and Portuguese ones: coal, repairs, and the twenty-four-hour rule. His August report belongs to the moment when the maritime war widened. For Seward, reports from small posts helped him see the whole board before he drafted his protests to the great powers.
frus-1862-d612:
George G. Fogg, the American minister in Berne, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 October 1862. It is Document 612 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Swiss file's closing paper.

Fogg wrote a month after the emancipation order, news that a republic of Swiss cantons was well placed to appreciate. His report gave Washington the view from Berne: Swiss opinion, the war's standing in a neutral democracy, and the post's small formal business. The seven months between the Swiss file's two printed papers show how thin correspondence with the quietest posts could run. What survives still fixes Switzerland's friendly neutrality in the record of the Union's wartime world.
frus-1862-d712:
On 9 October 1862, William H. Seward wrote to Andrew B. Dickinson, the American minister in Nicaragua, three days after his last letter to him. The note is document 712 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It closes the Dickinson file in the volume.

Short follow-up letters let a secretary add a point, send fresh news, or fix a detail from the last sheet. Seward's note to Dickinson is one of those. Set beside the reports it answered, it rounds out a small, neat file. It holds an envoy's word from Nicaragua, and Washington's word back, in the middle of the Civil War.
frus-1863p1-d112:
A week after his dozen letters of 2 March, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams again, on 9 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 112 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, a week after Seward's dozen letters of 2 March.

A lone letter after a batch often dealt with what the batch had missed, or with news too fresh for it. Seward's 9 March sheet kept the London file warm in that way. It told Adams how his last reports had landed and what Washington wanted next. In the long exchange, such sheets are the stitches between the set pieces.
frus-1863p1-d12:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 December 1862. Adams was the American minister in London, and his mail anchors part one of the 1863 volume. The letter is document 12 in that part.

Adams wrote three days before the battle of Fredericksburg, though word of it would take weeks to reach him. His letters judged Britain by what he saw: the cabinet's care, the press's heat, the South's friends at work. This dispatch is one of his steady reports, the kind Seward read first when the London mail came in. Its worth grows from the run it sits in.
frus-1863p1-d212:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 10 June 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 212 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d312:
Mr. Stuart, an officer of the British legation in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 November 1862. His note is document 312 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For readers, the Stuart letters fill in the working level of the famous Lyons and Seward exchange. They show the legation's routine grind behind the headline crises. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d412:
The British minister in Washington, Lord Lyons, took up his pen on 7 March 1863 to write Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is document 412 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The channel between Lyons and Seward was the main safety valve of Anglo-American relations in the war. Papers like this one are the valve at work. It dates from the spring when British debate over aiding the South was still live, and every note counted. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d512:
Secretary William H. Seward wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 14 May 1863. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d612:
The letter printed as document 612 was written on 14 August 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d112: On November 10, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill, two days before sailing aboard the battleship Iowa. The letter is Document 112 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Final letters before a wartime voyage tended to mix the practical with the strategic, though this record names no topic. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, at the point where the correspondence gives way to the journey itself.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d12: On June 25, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt again, five days after his previous message in this series. The new note is Document 12 of the Cairo and Tehran volume in the Foreign Relations record. Late June brought allied argument over where to strike next in the Mediterranean, but the record for this item names no subject. The text itself, printed in full in the volume, is the only sound source for its errand.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d212:
A State Department memorandum dated at Moscow on 11 November 1943 sets out how Germany should be treated once it surrenders. Drawn up for the three big Allies to agree in advance, it starts from the declared aim of Germany's unconditional surrender.

The draft surrender terms demand an admission of total defeat, signed by both the German government and its military chiefs, with the Allies holding all the rights of an occupying power. Political prisoners must be freed, the camps emptied, and accused war criminals handed over. During the armistice, an inter-Allied Control Commission would rule Germany, British, Soviet, and American troops would occupy it, and Nazi officials at every level would be removed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d312:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued a secret note, paper C.C.S. 409, at Cairo on 25 November 1943 under the heading Overlord and the Mediterranean. It names the central quarrel of the Sextant Conference: how far the sanctity of Overlord must be preserved whole, whatever happens in the Mediterranean.

Much has changed since Quebec, the British argue: Russia advances beyond hope, Italy is out of the war, and Turkey may soon join. They do not recoil from a cross-Channel attack in late spring or early summer of 1944, but they refuse to treat a fixed date as the pivot of all strategy. German strength in France might make Overlord impossible, or make an early Rankin landing essential. Their policy is to stretch German forces everywhere and strike wherever the Allies hold superiority, letting Overlord follow from that pressure.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d412:
Howard Bucknell, counselor of the American embassy in London, sent the Secretary of State a short telegram, number 8476, on 4 December 1943. It reports how the news of the Tehran Conference reached the British public that morning.

Moscow radio's announcement of the conference, Bucknell writes, is carried in the late editions of the morning's London papers, though it arrived too late for editorial comment. Speculative stories over the past two days, he notes, had rested largely on a German press and radio campaign meant to prepare enemy populations for the expected news of the meeting. Senator Connally's speech at Fort Worth, in which he had spoken openly of a great conference in the Middle East, was also widely reported in Britain.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d512:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on December 9, 1943, three days after the Second Cairo Conference closed. The two leaders had spent most of a month traveling and conferring, from Cairo to Tehran and back to Cairo. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

By December 9 the alliance had settled its course for 1944, and the correspondence between the heads of government turned to carrying it out. Churchill's letters to Roosevelt mixed business, argument, and friendship in a way no later summary can reproduce. This one belongs to the immediate settling-up after the summits, when the decisions were fresh and the work was beginning.
frus-1944-quebec-d112:
President Roosevelt wrote to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on September 9, 1944, about lend-lease policy after Germany's collapse. Departments in Washington had been discussing the question on their own, and Roosevelt wanted it stopped. Identical letters went to the service chiefs, the Treasury, and the agencies that ran foreign aid and shipping.

Roosevelt ordered that no department act alone on lend-lease, since any step would affect national policy as a whole. Instructions already issued about aid after Germany fell were to be cancelled at once. He promised his own directions soon. The letter shows the president pulling a sensitive allied question back into his own hands before Quebec.
frus-1944-quebec-d12:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on June 28, 1944, as Cherbourg fell to American troops in Normandy. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, in the run of pre-conference correspondence.

Late June brought the alliance a working port in France and a grinding battle for the Norman countryside. Churchill's correspondence that week balanced celebration with argument about the next moves in Italy and southern France. For readers, the message belongs to the summer when victory in the West became a matter of time, and the leaders' letters began to carry more postwar business than battle plans.
frus-1944-quebec-d212:
The only source for this conversation, the editors note, is Eden's memoir. After the press conference of September 16, 1944, the Foreign Secretary said goodbye to Roosevelt alone. The president told him that he would visit England at the end of November whether he won or lost the election. It is a small, human entry amid the conference's military paperwork.

The note's footnote confirms the plan from another source. Churchill told Stalin on September 27 that Roosevelt intended to visit England, and thereafter France and the Low Countries, immediately after the election, win or lose. The editors cite both Churchill's memoir and the published Stalin correspondence for the message.
frus-1945-50-intel-d112:
Lyon, director of the State Department's Office of Controls, wrote to Neal, chief of the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, on 1 July 1946. Both offices handled sensitive paper at State. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Mid-level papers like this one show the intelligence system's undergrowth: offices with overlapping files learning to pass names and cases between them. Foreign activity correlation was the State desk that tracked foreign agents' doings in America, work that touched both controls and intelligence. Readers gain texture here. The grand contest of chiefs rested on hundreds of such small coordinations, and the volume's honesty in printing them is part of its value.
frus-1945-50-intel-d12:
Mathias Correa, special assistant to Secretary of the Navy James Forrestal, wrote to his chief on 19 September 1945. Correa handled intelligence matters for Forrestal, who took a deep interest in the subject. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The Navy had its own spies, codes, and claims in the coming fight, and Forrestal meant to defend them. A special assistant's memorandum shows the secretary being armed for the argument. This paper dates from the day before the OSS was dissolved, when every service was positioning for the scramble over its remains. Readers get the Navy's corner of that scramble, briefed by the man Forrestal trusted with the file.
frus-1945-50-intel-d212:
On 5 May 1947, Secretary of State Marshall sent a letter to Senator Chan Gurney. It stands as document 212 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

The letter form mattered in this world: it was signed, it was kept, and it bound the writer's office to what it said. Replies in the same file show the exchange from both sides. Gurney chaired the Senate Armed Services Committee, the panel then weighing the bill that would reshape the armed services and intelligence.
frus-1945-50-intel-d312:
On 6 October 1949, Secretary of Defense Johnson sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 312 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Reform talk filled the files that year, as the government weighed the Dulles team's harsh grades for the CIA.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d412: Document 412 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950 is a memorandum for the record dated 31 January 1950. The heading names no writer and no reader for the paper. Such notes fixed a talk, a choice, or an event in writing. The record of the young intelligence system would then hold it for later use.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d112:
On 19 January 1945 the Secretary of State pressed the President for a quick decision. The paper at issue is the draft pact on control machinery for Germany. It came out of the European Advisory Commission in London. Stettinius's note is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Britain gave its approval on 5 December 1944, and Soviet approval is expected at any moment. Without a word from Washington, the United States would sit in an awkward place in the commission. Stettinius notes that the heads of the War and Navy Departments both urged approval in a letter of 27 December. He asks the President to decide at the earliest chance.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d12: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on 22 October 1944, fresh from his own trip to Moscow that month. The message survives as document 12 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, issued by the Department of State. Churchill often reported his impressions of Stalin to the president, and this letter belongs to that candid channel between the two Western leaders.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d212:
Washington sent Paris a warm holding answer on de Gaulle's arms letter on 27 January 1945. Acting Secretary Grew's cable to Ambassador Caffery, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, carries a letter to be handed to the French foreign minister. It buys time without cooling the French.

De Gaulle's letter on the further arming of French forces, the reply says, is deeply appreciated. It now lies before the United States Chiefs of Staff for their study and advice, and a firm answer may soon be possible. In the meantime, Washington fully grasps France's fervent desire to strike at Germany with all she has. French troops fighting beside their allies are making an outstanding contribution, and earlier American arming, in North Africa and since, is recalled with pride.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d312:
For one Malta meeting, no official record survives at all, and the editors of this volume say so plainly. Their short note explains where the only account can be found. It sits in Secretary Stettinius's memoir, on two pages the note cites. The session ran late, ending close to midnight.

Notes like this one mark the honest gaps in the conference record. Where the files gave out, the editors leaned on a man who was in the room and later wrote about it. Readers are told exactly how much weight the evidence can bear, and no more.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d412:
Side by side with the delegation's other draft, this invitation text of February 9, 1945, shows the wording still in motion. It names the same five sponsoring powers, with the United States issuing the call. The conference date reads April 25 or soon after, with the place again left blank. The guest's name is a dash.
