The draft proposes that the conference take the Dumbarton Oaks plan as the basis for a charter. A copy of that plan, it notes, had already been sent to the invited government. Small changes between drafts — a word here, a date there — mark the last edits before the invitations went out to found the United Nations.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d512:
The veto question follows Stettinius to San Francisco in this cable to Grew of June 3, 1945. He asks Grew to pass his message to the President. The precise issue at present, he writes, has caused great confusion, especially in the press. It is whether a great power not involved in a dispute can use the veto to block mere discussion of a situation in the Council.

Discussion, in such cases, would only let the Council decide what action, if any, to take or recommend. All agreed, Stettinius notes, that unanimity of the great powers not involved should govern substantive decisions. The cable shows Yalta's voting bargain being defended at the conference it created.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d112:
Robert Murphy reported the Berlin timetable agreed with Marshal Zhukov in an urgent telegram from Hoechst on June 30, 1945. The message is document 112 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Generals Clay and Weeks had met Zhukov in Berlin the day before to plan the Allied move into the occupation zones.

The Soviets want a fast Western pullback starting July 1, with the withdrawal finished by July 4 and Allied troops entering Berlin on the last day. Murphy lists the agreed steps: scouting parties first, then main bodies moving in on July 3 and 4. Free use of the Hanau-Magdeburg-Berlin highway is granted, rail lines are assigned, and traffic on approved routes will pass without border searches. Zhukov also promised to meet reasonable transport requests tied to the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d12:
How to make Stalin ask for the meeting fills Grew's memorandum of a second conference on May 15, 1945. Eden, Balfour, Harriman, William Phillips, and Grew took part. Reference was made to a recent message from the President suggesting Stalin might take the initiative in calling the conference. Eden asked whether Truman had any idea how Stalin might be induced to do so.

Harriman thought it could readily be managed by Clark Kerr, the British ambassador. If Clark Kerr reached Moscow first, he could turn conversation so as to reveal whether Stalin would in fact take the initiative. Discussion then turned to the best place for the meeting. The extract shows diplomacy arranging even the invitation's authorship.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d212:
Ambassador Harriman confirmed the reparations discussion to Molotov in a letter dated July 12, 1945. The letter is document 212 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Molotov had asked about reparations when Harriman delivered the President's topic list on July 7.

Harriman explains that the President asked Pauley to come to Berlin to report on the state of the reparations commission's work in Moscow. He is satisfied, he adds, that the President will wish to discuss at the conference those reparations matters that remain unsettled. Pauley has confirmed this himself and has so informed Maisky, the Soviet chairman of the commission. The short letter locked reparations into the Potsdam program without adding it to the formal topic list.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d312:
Winant forwarded the British Foreign Office's formal reply from London on July 13, 1945. London had weighed Washington's letters of June 25 and July 9 on peace treaties with Bulgaria, Hungary, and Rumania. The reply, sent to the Department, was also repeated to Moscow.

Britain said it fully shared the wish for a real American and British part in the Control Commissions. It also wanted better political conditions in the three countries. But London confessed it still doubted the course Washington favored. The exchange shows the two allies entering Potsdam agreed on the problem, yet split on the remedy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d412:
Deadlock in London is the burden of Winant's cable of July 12, 1945. The European Advisory Commission held a long, inconclusive discussion of the new Soviet proposal on France's Berlin area. The Soviet delegation, Winant reports, had authority to conclude the French zone agreement only if its new formula was added.

The American and British representatives kept opposing any wording that stated the French area would be formed from the American and British areas alone. The French representative, Massigli, was eager to conclude the agreement on any basis the other three accepted. Winant also asks for fresh facts on destruction in Berlin, to offset Soviet claims relayed from Marshal Zhukov.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d512:
Territory Germany annexed from Poland in 1939 should simply go back, a briefing book paper of July 3, 1945 recommends. The territory of pre-war Poland annexed by Germany in 1939, it states, should be returned to Poland. Its basic data recall how Poland won that land after the first World War, through the Treaty of Versailles.

Poland then acquired the so-called Corridor, the Poznań area, and the major part of the Upper Silesian industrial area. President Wilson had played a prominent role in establishing an independent Poland with its outlet to the sea. Yet the United States, in its separate treaty with Germany of 1921, disclaimed any obligation for the territorial provisions of Versailles. The land had been a source of friction from 1919 to 1939.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d612:
An extract from Ambassador Harriman's Moscow wire of July 12, 1945, forms document 612 in the Potsdam papers. Addressed to the President and the Secretary of State, it is cut from the fuller report printed as document 577. It keeps one exchange from China's talks with Stalin.

In the passage kept here, T. V. Soong suggests going back to Chungking. He wants to consult the Generalissimo on the points still open in the Moscow talks. Stalin answers that a deal is better reached before he meets Truman at Berlin. He wishes to settle with Truman the date of Soviet entry into the war against Japan. The short extract thus ties the stalled China talks straight to the Potsdam timetable. What Soong could not close in Moscow, Stalin meant to settle with the President himself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1012: Walter Brown, special assistant to the Secretary of State, passed on a late-night Soviet message in this note of July 29, 1945. At 11:35 that night, Pavlov had called with word from Stalin. The Soviet leader named his two men for the committee on disposal of the German fleet. They are Admiral of the Fleet Kuznetsov and Mr. Sobolev. Brown's memorandum is only a few lines long. It simply asks that the appointments be transmitted to Secretary Byrnes, and the file copy is an unsigned carbon.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1112:
Washington answered its Rome embassy in this message of 19 July 1945, sent by the Acting Secretary of State to Ambassador Kirk in Italy. It followed two days after Kirk's own dispatch to Washington. The channel between the capital and the Rome post ran both ways through the summit.

Messages of this kind carried orders, answers, or fresh guidance as Italy policy was adjusted in real time. The quick turn shows choices being shaped while Potsdam was still in session. Read beside Kirk's reports, this message is the home office half of a running exchange. Together they show how one country's file was handled day by day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1212:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to President Truman on 16 July 1945, the day before the summit opened. It was written as the American team made ready for the talks. Stimson's counsel reached the president on the eve of his trip.

The War Department's chief writing on the eve of Potsdam framed the military picture for the whole trip. Forces in Germany, the war in the Pacific, and the new weapons all sat in his brief. This message is the Pentagon's voice in the president's ear before the bargaining began. It matches the companion Stimson letter printed near it in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1312:
A second Harrison note to Stimson bears the date 23 July 1945. The pair of same-day messages shows the Interim Committee channel under full load. Two days later the Allies would issue their terms to Japan, and the atomic choices stood behind that text.

Harrison wrote as the committee's working head, Stimson as its chief in title and in fact. Their traffic joined the laboratory, the committee room, and the summit in one line. This note is the day's closing link. It is part of the record of how the bomb's shadow fell across the peace talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1412:
Henri Bonnet, the French ambassador in Washington, wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 11 August 1945. Bonnet worked the American capital while Caffery worked Paris, the two ends of one tie. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

An ambassador's letter to a secretary of state is a formal act, weighed and drafted with care. Bonnet wrote after the Potsdam results were known, when France was pressing its claims in both capitals at once. Readers can pair his letter with Caffery's cables from the same days. The two files show an alliance being renegotiated in stereo, with each capital hearing the other's case in its own rooms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-112:
Delegation staff drafted this working paper at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. It belongs to the layer of rough texts beneath the conference's formal acts. Working papers let specialists shape options before ministers saw them. This one remained in the American files and was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

The interest of a working paper is its openness. Choices not yet narrowed stay visible on the page. Readers can compare its lines with the texts the conference finally approved. That comparison shows how bargaining trims a draft. The paper is a small window into the craft of writing agreements.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-12:
Thompson's minutes record the foreign ministers' meeting of July 18, 1945, at 11 a.m. at Potsdam. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Byrnes took the chair at Molotov's proposal, and the Council of Foreign Ministers was the business.

Molotov raised China again, but softened his objection with a condition. If the council dealt with more than European affairs alone, his doubts on China would drop. Byrnes proposed a five-power council with China's part limited in a set way. China would sit for Far Eastern problems and for questions of worldwide significance. That design, he argued, would leave a body ready for the peace in the Far East when the Japan war ended. Eden replied that for European work alone he would prefer four members.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d712:
Document 712 is the report of the Subcommittee on the Council of Foreign Ministers, dated July 18, 1945. The council was a new body the Big Three meant to create. It would draft peace treaties and carry work between summits. A subcommittee settled its shape early in the conference. The report entered the second Potsdam volume.

Few Potsdam ideas lasted as long as this council. It met for years and framed the postwar talks. Readers find here its birth certificate: who would sit, and what work it would take. The report shows the conference building tools for the future, not just dividing the spoils of the past.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d812:
Schuyler wrote to the War Department from Rumania on July 24, 1945, in document 812. The chief of the American military team on the Rumanian control commission reported mid-conference. His channel ran to the Army, not the State Department. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Military reports from the commissions have a harder edge. Schuyler wrote of orders, movements, and obstructions in plain terms. Readers see joint occupation as soldiers lived it. The document pairs with the diplomats' Rumanian letters to give a fuller picture. Together they show a country being pulled east, reported by men watching it happen.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d912: Edwin Pauley sent this urgent telegram from Babelsberg on July 22, 1945, to his reparations delegation in Moscow. He asks for four more sets of figures at once. The team must estimate the value of industrial and mining output in the Russian zone in 1938. They must also estimate farm production in that zone for the same year. Pauley wants each figure as a share of total prewar German production. He also asks what share of German industrial and mining output came from east of the Oder-Neisse rivers in 1939.
gao-gaoreports-b-296435-12: The Agriculture Department asked GAO to reconsider in this November 2005 call — the twelfth round — and the ruling is the answer. The agency challenged the prior call, and the ruling tests the request. Reconsiderations get the same full review. Reconsiderations get the same full review.
gao-gaoreports-b-297112: Carahsoft Technology took its November 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298912: Magellan Health Services took its January 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Health giants get the same fair hearing as the small firms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-212: Seven countries' food safety mergers got a GAO tour in 2005, and the report covers their consolidation experiences. The review crosses the borders for lessons. The dinner plates deserved the lessons. The lessons were gathered. The tour was global. The borders were crossed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-312: Tobacco settlement dollars got a GAO tally in 2005, and the report covers the states' 2004 and expected 2005 payments. The review counts the cigarette money state by state. The states' shares were weighed. The shares were weighed. The money was counted. The tally was GAO's.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-412: Bank customer ID checks under the Patriot Act needed sharper rules in 2005, and GAO's report says extra guidance could smooth the rollout. Congress got a roadmap for making the regulations work as intended, without tripping up lawful account holders. The guidance had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-612: Mercury control technologies showed promise in 2005, and GAO's report says emerging controls worked, though long-term data was lacking. The findings balance hope and caution. The report warns that the clean air deserved proven tech. The performance had to be proven.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-712: FAA air traffic system security needed better controls in 2005, and GAO's report says progress had been made, though controls needed improving. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the skies' data deserved protection. The controls had to be improved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-12: The health agency's tech spending needed guardrails in 2005, and GAO's report says the key money skills had to be built. The findings demand the framework. The report warns that the health agency's tech dollars deserved managing. The health agency's tech dollars deserved managing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-312: The conservation payments program needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says improved USDA handling was required despite cost controls. The findings demand the stewardship. The report warns that the farm stewardship dollars should go to the right fields. The management had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-512: The Pentagon's spare parts stockpile needed managing in 2006, and GAO's report says actions were required to improve inventory retention. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the warehouses should not hoard or starve. The inventory had to be managed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-612: Protecting federal buildings needed measuring in 2006, and GAO's report says guidance and standards were required to gauge agencies' facility protection. The findings demand the yardstick. The report warns that the guarded doors needed grading too. The effectiveness had to be measured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-712: FEMA and the Red Cross needed better teamwork in 2006, and GAO's report says coordination should improve for the coming hurricane season. The findings demand the partnership. The report warns that the next storm would not wait for better planning. The coordination had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-812: Special operations forces faced people problems in 2006, and GAO's report says several human capital challenges had to be addressed for the expanded role. The findings target the strains. The report warns that the elite needed steady ranks behind them. The challenges had to be met.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1012: Poor vets in poor housing — GAO's 2007 report looks at where low-income former troops lived and how HUD's programs reached them. The findings pair housing conditions with program take-up. The report asks whether the nation's housing aid found the veterans who needed it most.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-112: Tax collection appeals were mostly clean in 2007, and GAO's report says little evidence of procedural errors was found, though improvements were possible. The findings balance the good and the gaps. The report shows the due process mostly worked. The appeals deserved the check.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-212: Catching money launderers needed better teamwork in 2007, and GAO's report says the financial cops and the IRS had to coordinate compliance better. The findings demand the joint effort. The report warns that the dirty money moved faster than the paperwork. The hunters had to hunt together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-412: Ports needed better disaster playbooks in 2007 — GAO's report says more federal guidance would help them plan and recover from the worst. The findings press for the missing manual. The report's image: the harbor that plans together weathers the storm together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-712: A poison-gas scare at a nuke site got a weak investigation in 2007 — GAO's report says the phosgene probe fell short, though experts deemed workers safe. The findings fault the digging, not the conclusion. The report's standard: scary incidents deserve serious inquiries.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-912: The FBI's new case files system was minding some manners in 2007 — GAO's report says the bureau followed several key buying practices, with gaps left. The findings grade the post-Trilogy reboot of the bureau's computers. After the infamous tech flameout, the report asks: lesson learned, or lesson repeated?
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-112: The Government Accountability Office dug into veterans' Benefits: Improved Management Would Enhance VA's Pension Program in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-12: GAO published its findings on maritime Security: Coast Guard Inspections Identify and Correct Facility Deficiencies, but More Analysis Needed of Program's Staffing, Practices, and Data in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gaufridy-life-death-aix-1612:
Louis Gaufridy served as a priest at Aix-en-Provence until the law burned him for witchcraft in 1611. The Life and Death of Lewis Gaufredy, printed in English in 1612, spread his scandal abroad. A priest accused of bewitching nuns made news far past his own town.

The account tells how young nuns at a convent were said to be seized by devils who named Gaufridy. It follows his arrest, his confession, and his death by fire. French courts treated the case as proof that no rank stood above the charge. English readers got the whole lurid tale within a year.
geoffrey-histories-kings-britain-evans-1:
Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote his History of the Kings of Britain in Latin around 1136. Sebastian Evans translated it into English in 1912, in a version quite different from the older one by Giles. Geoffrey claimed to copy a very old Welsh book, a claim few now believe.

His chronicle runs from Brutus, the fabled founder of Britain, through Lear to Arthur himself. Arthur gets his first full life story here, complete with wars and a vast court. Much of it is invention, yet for centuries readers took it as true history. Almost all later Arthurian writing drinks from this spring.
giles-taoist-teachings-lieh-tzu-1912:
Lionel Giles translated Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzu in 1912, giving English readers the third Taoist classic in full. Lieh Tzu is named for a sage who, in legend, rode the wind. Giles's version was the first complete English rendering of the text.

The chapters mix short tales, dialogues, and musings on fate, dreams, and the vanity of striving. A famous passage asks whether a man who dreamed he was a butterfly should trust waking or the dream. The book completes the trio of Taoist works beside the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu.
glanvill-translation-beames-1812:
John Beames translated Glanvill's treatise into English in 1812, opening the oldest book of English law to modern readers. Ranulf de Glanvill, chief justiciar under Henry the Second, wrote the Latin original in the late twelfth century. His work describes the royal courts and writs that were then remaking English justice.

The treatise explains how a claim began with a writ from the king's chancery and moved through the courts step by step. It covers land disputes, inheritance, and the early forms of trial. Beames's version was the first full English dress for a text lawyers had read in Latin for six centuries. The book is often called the common law's birth certificate, and Beames made it legible to the age of reform.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-07-1912:
Volume 7 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1912, as Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild, Part 1. James George Frazer turned from dying gods to the spirits of the fields themselves. European harvest customs, gathered from many villages, form the core of the volume.

Frazer described the corn mother, the last sheaf, and mock killings and marriages at harvest time. He argued that farmers once believed a spirit lived in the grain and had to be caught, kept, or killed with care. Examples come from Britain, Germany, Scandinavia, and beyond. Part 1 shows his method working close to home, on customs still alive in living memory.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-08-1912:
Volume 8 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1912, completing Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild. James George Frazer ranged wider here, from European fields to the rice lands and forests of Asia, Africa, and the Americas. The corn spirit of Part 1 gains kin worldwide.

Chapters treat sacred trees, grove worship, and the spirits of wild animals and the hunt. Frazer matched harvest rites across oceans to argue for shared patterns in early religion. Later scholars trimmed his claims, but the gathered customs remain a vast record. The volume closes his long survey of plant and animal spirits in folk practice.
haanel-master-key-system-1912:
Charles F. Haanel sold The Master Key System as a mail course from 1912. The course ran to four and twenty parts, one a week. It taught the New Thought creed that mind makes the world of each man. Haanel wrote for men of trade who sought wealth and calm.

Each part pairs a talk with a drill for the mind. Still thought, clear scenes in the mind's eye, and firm will form the core. Haanel holds that thought draws like to like in the world. The book is a root text of the mind power school of the States.
harrison-themis-1912:
Jane Ellen Harrison was a Cambridge scholar who turned Greek studies toward ritual, art, and the life of the group. Her Themis, published in 1912, studies the social origins of Greek religion. It is the mature statement of the ritualist school she helped to found.

Harrison argues that rite came before myth: the dance and the sacrifice are older than the stories told to explain them. Her title names Themis, the goddess of settled custom, as the force beneath the shining Olympian gods. The book's mix of field reports, vase paintings, and bold theory still provokes classicists.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume twelve of Carlyle's great work: Frederick William I, the terrible father, and the making of Prussia. The giant grenadiers, the Tobacco Parliament, and the son who survived it all. Carlyle's portrait of the old king is one of his most vivid. History with the bark on.
hocking-meaning-god-1912:
The Meaning of God in Human Experience, published in 1912, is William Ernest Hocking's philosophy of religion. It is one of the most respected American works in its field. Hocking, a Harvard thinker formed by Royce and James, asks how God can be known in and through experience.

He argues that worship and mystic experience give real knowledge, not mere feeling. God is met as the other self who makes community possible. The book balances argument with testimony drawn from prayer and practice. Its tone is earnest and elevated. It represents American idealism turning, in its last strength, toward religion.
hodgson-night-land-1912:
Far in the years ahead, the sun has died in William Hope Hodgson's huge novel The Night Land, from 1912. The last folk of earth live in a vast fort of stone and steel. Great beasts and still, dread forms roam the black waste past its walls.

One man leaves the fort to seek a lost love from a past life. His trek is long, harsh, and full of dread sights. The book helped found the dying-earth tale. Its scale and gloom still stun new fans. Great Watchers stand still for ages past the walls, which adds dread. The love quest at its core keeps the huge tale warm and human.
huygens-treatise-on-light-1912:
Christiaan Huygens's Treatise on Light appeared in English in 1912, translated by Silvanus P Thompson from the French work of 1690. Huygens, a Dutch scientist, rivaled Newton in the study of light. Where Newton pictured particles, Huygens pictured waves spreading through an unseen medium.

Huygens explained reflection, refraction, and the strange double refraction of Iceland crystal by waves alone. His principle, that each point of a wave starts fresh waves, still bears his name in physics classrooms. Thompson's version was the first in English, more than two centuries after the original. The book is the founding text of wave optics, clear and brief beside its great influence.
jachin-and-boaz-1812:
Jachin and Boaz, first published in 1762, is the most reprinted Masonic exposé of all. This edition of 1812 represents the text that defined public knowledge of Masonic ritual for over a century. Its title takes the names of the two pillars at the porch of Solomon's temple, words heavy with meaning in the Craft.

The book styles itself an authentic key to the door of Free-Masonry. Degree by degree, it prints the questions, signs, and obligations of the lodges. Masons raged, answered, and could not outsell it. Edition followed edition on both sides of the Atlantic. Any reader curious how the general public pictured Masonry between 1762 and the modern era will find the answer shaped by Jachin and Boaz.
james-essays-radical-empiricism-1912:
Essays in Radical Empiricism, published in 1912, collects the papers in which James stated his final philosophy. His student Ralph Barton Perry gathered them after James's death, giving form to a system its author left scattered in journals.

Radical empiricism holds that pure experience is the one stuff of the world, and that relations are as real as the things they join. Famous essays here deny that consciousness is an entity at all. The doctrine underlies his pluralism and his late metaphysics. These short papers, dense and bright, are among the most argued-over in American philosophy.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-12:
Quebec's yearbook for 1637 fills Volume 12, published by Thwaites in 1898. One year of a small colony gets a full, careful annual report. Converts are counted, setbacks are owned, and small brave acts are set down plainly.

Daily life along the St. Lawrence comes through in quiet detail. Readers see sowing, building, teaching, and care for the sick. The priests praise help from France and beg for more hands. No bragging inflates these modest pages from the frontier. Each small gain is weighed with care. Few records show so well how a colony of faith took root in wild country.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyons-10212:
Lyons, the French city on the Rhône, is given a long Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews lived in the surrounding region from an early date. By the ninth century they formed a prosperous community in Lyons itself. They lived in their own quarter at the foot of the Fourvière hill. One street there is still called Rue Juiverie.

The article describes royal protection and church hostility side by side. Kings Louis and Judith shielded the Jews, while Bishop Agobard fought them and failed. In 1245 a council at Lyons moved against them, and the archbishop soon expelled them from the city. For nearly a century almost no Jews remained in the district. Records from 1364 show Jews living in Lyons again, in their old quarter. The entry gives a full picture of a medieval community's rise, fall, and return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makkedah-10312:
Makkedah, a city of the Judah foothills, is described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Joshua's book places it among the hill towns reaching toward the coastal plain. It was a stronghold of some importance. The narrative names it beside Libnah, Lachish, and Hebron.

The article retells the cave story from Joshua's campaign. Five allied kings hid in a large cave near the city during their rout. Joshua had the cave sealed with boulders and guarded while the army finished the pursuit. On its return the kings were led out and executed. The writers then take up the city's lost site. Warren identified it with Al-Mughar, the cave, southwest of Ekron. Conder noted it as the only cave site in the Shephelah. Eusebius put it eight miles east of Eleutheropolis, which the entry doubts. The piece leaves readers with a famous story and an open map.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayer-abraham-1:
Abraham Mayer was a Belgian physician. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Düsseldorf on July 10, 1816, studied medicine at Bonn, and took his degree in 1839. He settled at Antwerp in 1848 and practiced there for the rest of his life, dying on March 1, 1899. He served for a time as assistant surgeon in the Belgian Hussars of the Guard.

The entry presents him as a working doctor who wrote up what he saw. He sat on the board of medical inspectors for the schools of Antwerp. He also led several medical societies. His case reports run from a death caused by a burn that perforated the intestine to an odd poisoning traced to lead in snuff. They also include studies of London hospitals, puerperal illness, and a note on treating cholera.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-memel-10612:
Memel was an East Prussian port in the district of Königsberg. Gotthard Deutsch and Hermann Vogelstein give its communal history in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its 19,796 people in 1900 included 1,214 Jews. But settlement was long at risk. The first mention, in 1567, is a decree of expulsion by Duke Albrecht. In 1664 the Great Elector let one Dutch Jew live and trade there. He was Moses Jacobsohn de Jonge. When his affairs failed, Jews were admitted only for the fairs. They dealt in furs and Hebrew books.

The Prussian edict of 1812 reopened the city. The timber trade with Russia drew Polish and Russian Jews in. Yet the community formed only in 1862. Its first rabbi was Dr. Isaac Rülf, who served from 1865 to 1898. He founded the religious school and the hospital. He championed the Russian Jews and made their cause his own. Dr. Emanuel Carlebach followed him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-i:
Meshullam ben Israel was a Talmudic scholar of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 enters him through the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn. He is entered for one useful book: the "Mar'eh Mekom ha-Dinim," an alphabetical index to the Shulhan Aruk, printed at Cracow in 1647. Finding-aids rarely make reputations, but in a code of that size an index was a working tool every rabbi could use.

Fürst adds the personal details the title page omits. Meshullam was known also as Phoebus. He died at Amsterdam in 1652. The poet David de Barrios praised him. That is the whole of the notice: two sentences of fact and one of bibliography. The bibliography points to Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue. The notice reminds readers of one thing. The encyclopedia recorded the makers of scholarly instruments as faithfully as scholars themselves.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-midrashim-small:
Beyond the famous midrashic collections stands a crowd of smaller, mostly later works, catalogued in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and J. Theodor, published in 1906. These are the midrashim too small or too late for the main articles on Midrash Haggadah and Midrash Halakah. Many survive only in pieces.

The first example shows the pattern. Midrash Abkir, a set of homilies on Genesis and Exodus, is lost as a book; more than fifty excerpts live on inside the Yalkut anthology and in quotations by other writers. Even its name is a reconstruction, taken from the closing formula of its homilies as reported by Eleazar of Worms. The article works through the rest of the list in the same careful way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mo-ed-feasts-10:
Mo'ed, feasts, is the second order of the Mishnah. It is the volume of laws for Sabbath and festivals. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach map it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Talmud itself uses the name. Twelve treatises in eighty-eight chapters belong to it. They run from Shabbat and Pesaḥim to Ta'anit, Megillah, and Ḥagigah.

The article fixes the order's anatomy and its textual oddities. Sheḳalim has no Babylonian Gemara. Probably none ever existed, so editions print the Palestinian one instead. The Palestinian Gemara to Shabbat's last chapters is missing. Frankel's Hodegetica is the single cited guide. The entry is a reference for anyone opening the Mishnah's festival volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morenu-lit-our-:
Morenu, our teacher, is the title German Jewry began giving its ordained rabbis in the mid-fourteenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia explains it in 1906. It hides inside the famous acronyms. MaHaRaM is Morenu ha-Rab Rabbi Meïr, and MaHaRiL is Morenu ha-Rab Rabbi Jacob Levi. The title rides on ordination, semikah, revived at Vienna by Meïr ben Baruch ha-Levi.

Its first bearers, by David Gans's account, were Shalom of Austria and Jacob Mölln. Why this word was chosen, the article admits, cannot be determined. Abravanel guessed the German rabbis wanted a degree to match the universities' doctorate. Zunz thought plain rabbi had lost its scholarly shine and needed reinforcing. A small word marks the professionalization of the rabbinate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-kalfo-111:
Moses Kalfo was an Italian scholar who taught at the yeshiva of Bari at the start of the eleventh century. Solomon Schechter and Max Schloessinger wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. No book of his survives under his own name.

He is known only through word explanations quoted by Nathan ben Jehiel in the Aruk, the great Talmudic dictionary. Nathan probably studied under Kalfo for some time at Bari. Three entries of the Aruk carry his explanations of hard words. The notice shows how a teacher's learning can survive inside a pupil's book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muller-joel-112:
Joel Müller was a German rabbi and Talmudist born in Moravia in 1827 and dead at Berlin in 1895. Isidore Singer and Thomas Seltzer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He succeeded his father as rabbi of his native town, then held the rabbinate of Leipa in Bohemia. Later he taught Talmud at Berlin's Lehranstalt for Jewish learning.

Müller's scholarship centered on the old responsa, the written rulings of the rabbis. He edited the Masseket Soferim and collections of French, eastern, and pre-Geonic responsa. His chief work is the Mafteah of 1891, a key that summarizes the contents of the Geonim's responsa. After his death his edition of Saadia's halakic writings appeared in Saadia's collected works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nedarim-vows-11:
Nedarim is the Mishnah treatise on vows. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands in the Mishnah, Tosefta, and both Talmuds. Its base text is Numbers chapter thirty, verses two to seventeen. It usually ranks third in the order Nashim. Eleven chapters hold ninety paragraphs in all.

First come substitute words that still count as vows. Slurred forms of korban or oath words bind the speaker. Then oaths and vows are set side by side. Food vows get long lists: boiled, roasted, meat, fish, milk. Time limits and loose wording are weighed with care. Later chapters cover release of vows by a scholar. Wives' and daughters' vows close the treatise's work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novokonstantino: Novokonstantinov is a Russian town in Podolia. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It holds 2,855 people, of whom 1,825 are Jews. Jewish artisans number 245 in the town. Nineteen ḥadarim give schooling to 310 pupils. Three houses of prayer serve the community. Its dark hour came in the Cossack war of 1649. Cossacks and Tatars burned the town marching to Zborov. Its Jews and Poles were put to the sword.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-onkelos-commonl:
Onkelos was a convert to Judaism and a sage of old. Wilhelm Bacher and Louis Ginzberg wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the close of the first century. Men oft mix him up with Aquila, a like convert. The chief Aramaic version of the Bible bears his name.

That version is called Targum Onkelos, from the mix-up. Yet a sage named Onkelos did live, the piece argues. He taught that the cherubim bent their heads back. They bent as a pupil turns from his teacher. Onkelos was famed for strict care in laws of purity. He kept in daily life the rules set for gifts at the altar. In this he passed even Gamaliel the Second, a chief sage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paris-11912:
Paris is the chief city and the heart of France. Gotthard Deutsch, Louis Germain Lévy, Joseph Jacobs, and Moïse Schwab wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived in Paris before the Frankish hosts came. Church councils of the fifth century set laws against them. Those laws hint that Jews lived in north France then.

From the first Frankish kings, Paris had a Jews' street. It was called the Rue de la Juiverie in that age. That street ran from the town core to the palace gate. In 582 a synagogue was built on that same street. Till the sixth century, Jews in Paris lived in fair ease. They kept their faith in full freedom in those years. They held friendly ties with the Christians of the town. Some of them held posts of trust in public work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pentecost-fifti:
Pentecost is the Greek name for a feast fifty days after Passover. Four writers shared this article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were Kaufmann Kohler, J. L. Magnus, the Executive Committee, and Judah David Eisenstein. In Hebrew the feast is called Shabuot, or Weeks.

The count starts with a sheaf of barley at Passover. Seven weeks of grain harvest follow that offering. The feast closes the season with ripe wheat. Its other names tell the same story. Jews called it the Feast of Harvest and the Day of First-Fruits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-morris:
Morris Phillips was an American editor born in London. He was born on May 9, 1834, and schooled in Cleveland. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied law before he found his true trade. New York tutors finished his schooling after Cleveland.

In 1854 Phillips joined Nathaniel Parker Willis in New York. The two men ran the New York Home Journal together. When Willis died in 1867, Phillips took full control. He became the paper's chief editor and sole owner. He traveled widely and wrote for many magazines.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plowing-12212:
The Bible never describes the plow it so often names. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The tool matched the simple plow of Palestine's fellahin. A long pole, a crosspiece, and an iron share.

The share ran only eight centimeters deep. Stones stayed in the field to hold moisture. One hand could lift the light plow out. Oxen drew it, or an ass on light soil. Yoking ox and ass together was forbidden. The plowman steered with one hand, goaded with the other.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-possart-ernst-v:
Ernst von Possart was a German actor and author born at Berlin in 1841. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At seventeen he was placed in a Berlin book and art shop. There he met the actor Kaiser. Kaiser offered to teach him speech for free.

Possart studied with Kaiser for three years. In 1861 he made his first stage trial at Berlin. He played Riccaut in one play and Iago in Othello. The trial went so well that Breslau hired him at once. He took second character parts at its city theater. The entry traces his rise from that small start. He became one of the known actors of Germany.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinovitz-shal:
Shalom Rabinovitz, known by the pen name Shalom Alekem, was a Russian novelist. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Pereyaslav in 1859. At twenty-one he became crown rabbi of a small town. Later he settled at Kiev and lived there still in 1905.

Rabinovitz wrote without pause for the Hebrew journals of Russia. His Hebrew novels ran in papers such as Ha-Asif. Shimele came out there in the year 1889. Shoshannah ran in Ha-Zefirah that same year. One tale casts a Jew as a Don Quixote of Mazepowka. The entry lists his tales as they stood at that date.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-revelation-book:
The Book of Revelation is the last book of the New Testament. Crawford Howell Toy and Kaufmann Kohler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Yet the writers call it one of the oldest such books. They call it a surviving Judaeo-Christian work.

The article says the book has a complex makeup. Its first verse presents two frames at once. One frame names God as the giver of the revelation. Another names Jesus revealing truth to his servant John. Recent study says a compiler joined two sections together. The main apocalypse runs from chapter four onward. Letters to seven churches form the other section. Vischer showed the main part fits Jewish apocalyptic writing. That finding makes the book vital for Jewish students.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romanin-samuel-:
Samuel Romanin was an Italian historian born at Triest in 1808. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Venice on September 9, 1861. He lost his parents at an early age.

The article says he became head of his family young. In 1821 the family removed to Venice. He tutored French and German in a private home. His first work translated Hammer-Purgstall's Ottoman history into Italian. A prose version of a German poem followed. His history of European peoples filled three volumes by 1844. In 1847 he began his great history of Venice. Its first volume appeared in 1853. The full work was finished in manuscript at his death. He also translated Talmudic legends into Italian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salaman-annette: Annette A. Salaman was an English authoress who died on April 10, 1879. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote her entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Bedridden for a time in girlhood, she compiled Scripture texts teaching Judaism's precepts. They appeared as Footsteps on the Way of Life, in a second London edition in 1874. She also wrote Aunt Annette's Stories to Ada, a series of tales for children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jehi:
Samuel ben Jehiel was a martyr of Cologne in the First Crusade, on June 25, 1096. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Cologne's Jews had fled to villages under Archbishop Hermann's protection.

Crusaders hunted the refugees out of those villages without mercy. At Wevelinghoven, standing in a marsh, Samuel blessed God before killing his own son. The boy answered Amen, and the onlookers took up the Shema. They threw themselves into the water rather than be taken. Samuel then gave the knife to Menahem, the sexton, to be killed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sason-aaron-ben:
M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Aaron ben Joseph Sason, a rabbi of Salonica. He worked across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. He died shortly before 1626. Sason studied under Mordecai Matalon. In time he taught Ḥayyim Shabbethai.

Sason wrote works on both rabbinic law and the Cabala. Most of them burned in the Constantinople fire of 1606. His son Joseph published some of his responsa at Venice in 1626. That book is called Torat Emet. His model texts for renting houses survive in another man's book. A work named Sefat Emet holds his readings on the Tosafot. The entry also untangles a catalog error. Two old bibliographers confused that book with a work by Moses Ḥagiz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schreiber-emanu:
Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Emanuel Schreiber. He was an American rabbi. Schreiber was born at Leipnik, in Moravia, on December 13, 1852. He studied at Eisenstadt and at Berlin's Hochschule. He took his doctorate at Heidelberg in 1873. He taught at Wolfenbüttel, then served as rabbi at Elbing and Bonn.

In 1881 Schreiber crossed to the United States. He led congregations at Mobile and then Denver. Los Angeles, Little Rock, Spokane, Toledo, and Youngstown followed in turn. Since 1899 he has led Congregation Emanu-El in Chicago. He edited Jewish papers in Germany and in Chicago. His books compare the principles of Judaism and Christianity. Others treat Abraham Geiger, the Talmud, and Reform Judaism's pioneers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semikah-laying-:
Semikah was the act of laying both hands on an animal before it was offered in sacrifice. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The owner had to press his bare hands, with full force, between the animal's horns. The rite took place in the Temple court.

During the act, a person bringing a sin offering confessed his sins aloud. He said he had done wrong, had repented, and hoped for forgiveness. For thank offerings, hymns took the place of confession. The entry, drawn from rabbinic rules and Maimonides, shows how sacrifice joined body, words, and repentance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shrimski-samuel:
Samuel Edward Shrimski was a New Zealand politician born at Posen, Prussia, in 1828. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He went to London in 1847 and became a merchant. In 1859 he emigrated to Melbourne, in Australia.

Two years later Shrimski moved on to New Zealand. At Oamaru he served as government land auctioneer. Voters elected him mayor of Oamaru again and again. He also led in education and charity work locally. In 1875 he entered the House of Representatives for Oamaru. Reelected three times, he rose to the Legislative Council in 1885. That upper house seat was a life appointment. He died at Auckland in 1902, a pioneer settler turned statesman.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-pazzi-:
Simeon ben Pazzi was a Palestinian amora of the third generation of teachers. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. In Palestine people called him just Simon, the Greek form. In Babylon he went by his full name instead.

Scholars dispute whether Pazzi was his father or mother. Bacher takes it as a family name borne by several teachers. The Pazzi family lived at Tiberias and was highly respected. Simeon was, so far as known, its most important member. He studied under Joshua ben Levi in the south. He kept friendly ties with Tiberias school leaders too. For a time he also lived at Babylon. There he stayed in the house of the exilarch. The entry follows a respected scholar between two centers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-smolenskin-pete:
Peter Perez ben Moses Smolenskin was a Russian writer born in 1842. Isidore Singer and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Monastyrshchina in the government of Moghilef. At ten he lost his father. At eleven he entered the yeshivah of Shklov for five years.

There he secretly learned Russian with his brother's help. When found reading profane books, he was persecuted and left. He later earned his living as a synagogue singer and preacher. In 1862 he went to Odessa and taught Hebrew. His great aim was to edit a Hebrew periodical. At Vienna he founded Ha-Shahar to fight obscurantism. He also sought to stir Jewish national feeling and love of Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-son-of-god-1391:
Son of God is a term used in several senses in the Bible. Kaufmann Kohler and Emil G Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It can name angels or mythic beings in Genesis. It can name a judge or ruler over men. It can also name the king over Israel, as with David.

Sons of God can also mean Israel as a people. The term can even mean all members of the human race. It never means physical descent from God, the article stresses. The Hebrew idiom conveys godlikeness, not shared essence with God. In Jewish literature the term rarely means the Messiah. Piety, not birth, places a person in a filial bond with God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steiner-kilian-:
Kilian von Steiner was a German financier born at Laupheim in 1835. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steiner died at Stuttgart on September 24, 1903. He began work as a lawyer before moving into banking. He rose to lead finance in Württemberg as president of its union bank.

In 1871 Steiner founded the Württemberg note bank. He was a patron of science and art throughout his life. He was also a close friend of the writer Berthold Auerbach. His role in founding the Schiller society and museum won him honorary citizenship. That honor came from Marbach, the birthplace of Schiller. The entry honors a banker who backed culture as well as finance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sun-hebrew-shem:
The sun holds a high place in Hebrew thought and speech. Emil G. Hirsch, Joseph Jacobs, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its Hebrew name is shemesh, with poetic names for heat. Genesis counts it among the two great lights. God gave the greater light rule over the day.

Hebrews pictured the sun as a torch in the firmament. Psalms give it a tent and a bridal chamber. It comes forth at dawn and returns at dusk. East means the place of rising in Hebrew idiom. West means the place of coming back. The phrase under the sun simply means on earth. Ecclesiastes favors that phrase above other books. The entry gathers how one body shaped a language's map of the world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talmid-hakam-pl:
A talmid hakam is a scholar honored for mastery of the Law. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The title names one well versed in Torah. Such scholars formed a kind of aristocracy in Jewish society. Their rank rested on learning, not birth or wealth.

The Mishnah ranks a learned bastard above an ignorant high priest. Communities trusted scholars in worldly as well as spiritual matters. A scholar oversaw worship and checked weights and measures. Law freed him from taxes so he could study. He owed the community his full devotion in return. Modesty was required, yet he must guard his dignity. Slighting him meant slighting the Law itself. The entry weighs privilege and duty in one title.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temurah-exchang:
Temurah, meaning exchange, is a tractate in the Mishnah, Tosefta, and Babylonian Talmud. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It deals with rules in Leviticus about swapping consecrated things. The tractate has seven chapters and thirty-four paragraphs.

Chapter by chapter, the article lays out the rules. Who may make an exchange, and what may be swapped, comes first. Later chapters treat sin-offerings, first-born animals, and unborn young. Some chapters ask what may go on the altar. Others ask what must be burned or buried. Readers get a clear map of a dense legal text. The Tosefta part adds still more cases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-titus-full-name:
Titus, son of Vespasian, was Rome's emperor from 79 to 81. Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in 39 or 41 and died in 81. He was schooled at the courts of Claudius and Nero. He served in Germany and Britain under his father.

In Judea he helped his father crush the Jewish rebellion. He reduced Jotapata, Tarichaeae, and Giscala with bold courage. Josephus credits him with a prophecy of Vespasian's rise. When Vespasian left for Rome, Titus took over the war. He reached Jerusalem just before Passover in 70. His ride ahead of the army nearly ended in capture. The article follows his siege in personal detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trier-salomon-m: Salomon Meyer Trier was a Danish pharmacist born in Copenhagen in 1804. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He graduated from the Copenhagen College of Pharmacy in 1826. From 1830 to 1856 he owned a pharmacy at Lyngby. For over twenty years he published Archiv for Pharmacy. In 1868 he helped compile the Pharmacopea Danica. That official drug book remained in use in Denmark and Norway. He died at Copenhagen in December 1888.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiesner-adolf-1:
Adolf Wiesner was an Austrian journalist and author. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Prague in 1807. He died in New York on September 23, 1867. His birth name was Wiener. Barred as a Jew from legal careers, he converted. He took the name Wiesner on converting.

Wiesner practiced law briefly in Vienna's criminal court. He then turned to writing and the stage. His drama Inez de Castro reached Vienna's Burgtheater in 1842. His book on Austrian censorship is now a key source. In 1848 voters sent him to the Frankfort Parliament. He sat with the extreme Left there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worm-15012:
Worm, in the Bible, is a broad word for small things that crawl. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Two Hebrew words carry most of the sense. They are rimmah and toleah in the old text.

Those words cover more than the earthworm of our fields. They cover grubs, moth young, and things that eat rot. The worms in the manna were of that sort. So were the worms that ate vines and a gourd. In dead flesh the words mean grubs that feed there. As a figure, the worm stands for low rank and weak state. One verse joins worm and fire as signs of pain that lasts. The Talmud uses the same broad words for crawlers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhaki-abraham:
Abraham ben David Yizhaki (1661-1729) was a rabbi of Jerusalem who fought a false faith. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. On his mother's side he came from Abraham Azulai. He was a pupil of Moses Galante in his youth.

He stood firm against the sect of Shabbethai Zevi. He urged the rabbis of Smyrna to probe one man's books. In 1708 he signed the ban on Nehemiah Hayyun in Jerusalem. He then went to Europe to raise funds for the poor. At Leghorn and Amsterdam he fought Hayyun in the open. His chief book is a set of court replies in two books. It treats all four parts of the great law code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zederbaum-alexa:
Alexander Zederbaum (1816-1893) was a Russian Hebrew news man of note. Joseph Jacobs and S. Hurwitz wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Samostye in Lublin, he was the son of poor kin. As a boy he was bound to a tailor for his trade.

By grit he taught himself Hebrew books in his spare hours. He learned the tongues of Russia, Poland, and Germany as well. In 1840 he left his home town for Odessa in the south. That town was the heart of the new light move then. He took a trade post and kept up his self school. In time he ran a clothes shop with his own hands. In 1860 he won leave to print a Hebrew paper. That paper, Ha-Meliz, was the first of its kind in Russia.
johnson-ex-colored-man-1912:
James Weldon Johnson published his novel in 1912 without putting his name on it. The narrator is a light-skinned Black man who works as a musician. He grows up in the South, moves north, and later travels to Europe. At each step he faces a hard choice about race and safety.

Over time the narrator decides to live as a white man and give up his music. He marries, works in business, and keeps his past secret. The ending leaves him full of regret for what he traded away. Readers still value the novel as an early and honest look at passing in America.
journal-of-discourses-vol-12:
Steel rails reach Utah in the discourses of Volume Twelve, from 1869. The railroad ends the kingdom's long desert isolation at a stroke. Young greets the new era with mingled hope and sharp warning.

The world is coming to Zion now, for good and for ill. Sermons weigh trade, mines, and strangers against the Saints' pure ways. Speakers urge the flock to sell labor, not land or faith. An age closes in these talks, and a riskier one begins. The end of the desert refuge gives the volume its elegiac, wistful pull. Young knows the trains will change his people, and says so.
kalidasa-shakuntala-ryder-1912:
Arthur W. Ryder's verse translation of Kalidasa appeared in Everyman's Library in 1912. Alongside Shakuntala it holds Kalidasa's two other dramas, Malavika and Agnimitra and Urvashi, plus three long poems. The Dynasty of Raghu, The Birth of the War-God, The Cloud-Messenger, and The Seasons complete the volume.

Ryder, a Sanskrit scholar at Berkeley, aimed for poems that sing in English as they do in Sanskrit. His Shakuntala became the standard modern counterpart to Jones's pioneering version of 1789. The Cloud-Messenger, a lover's message sent by cloud, shows Kalidasa's lyric gift at its purest. Readers can compare two ages of translation in the library's pair. Ryder's notes stay light, letting the verse carry the learning.
keeping-up-appearances-sailor-s-knots-pa:
Keeping Up Appearances gathers sea-shore stories by W. W. Jacobs, from his book Sailor's Knots of 1909. A night-watchman tells the tales, starting with a one-eyed black cat ashore near the wharf. The title story concerns Bill Burtenshaw, whose superstitious mother heard three taps. Once, she insisted, the taps came from a neighbor hanging pictures at three in the morning.

Men who killed a black cat, the watchman says, swore they saw its ghost while drunk. Jacobs builds his comedy on such small terrors and tall talk. His watchman narrates with a straight face and perfect timing. These stories of sailors, wives, and village sharpers show Jacobs's dry humor at its best.
king-richard-ii-pg1512:
This edition of Shakespeare's King Richard the Second prints the full cast and scene plan. Richard heads the list, with John of Gaunt and the Duke of York as his uncles. Henry Bolingbroke and the Duke of Aumerle stand among the younger lords. Thomas Mowbray, Bushy, Bagot, and Green fill out the court.

The contents move from the lists at Coventry to Gaunt's house and the Wolds in Yorkshire. A camp in Wales, Flint Castle, and a garden at Langley follow. Westminster Hall hosts the deposition, and a dungeon at Pomfret closes the plan. Gaunt's famous speech on England belongs to this play's second act. The apparatus here maps Richard's fall stage by stage, from quarrel to murder.
l-alchimie-et-la-medecine-etudes-sur-les:
René-Félix Allendy wrote this study of alchemy and medicine as his Paris medical thesis. He defended it at the University of Paris in 1912. Allendy had been born in Paris in February 1889.

His subject is the role of hermetic theories in the history of medicine. He asks how alchemy shaped doctors' ideas over time. The thesis was printed by Bibliothèque Chacornac in Paris. It serves readers who study how old occult thought and real medicine once mixed. A thesis format gives the study a strict, ordered shape. Allendy moves through medical history with a young scholar's care.
la-toyson-d-or-ov-la-flevr-des-thresors-:
Salomon Trismosin's La Toys on d'Or appeared in French in 1612. Its title means the golden fleece, or the flower of treasures. The book promises a brief and methodical treatment of its subject.

That subject is alchemy, the search for the philosophers' stone. Trismosin was famed as a teacher of Paracelsus in alchemical lore. Works under his name gathered recipes, symbols, and hidden doctrine. This French printing spread that lore to new readers. It now helps students trace how alchemical teaching passed across Europe in print. Its old spelling and long title page suit its age. Few English readers meet Trismosin outside such rare reprints.
lamettrie-man-machine-bussey-1912:
Julien Offray de La Mettrie, a French army doctor, published Man a Machine in 1747 and fled two countries for writing it. The Open Court translation of 1912, by Bussey and Calkins, is the text here. Frederick the Great's Eulogy of La Mettrie and extracts from his Natural History of the Soul travel with the main work.

La Mettrie's manifesto denies the soul any life apart from the body's machinery. Thought, feeling, and morals all rise, he argues, from organized matter in motion. Fever, food, and sleep change the mind because the mind is the body at work. The claim enraged church and state in his day. Man a Machine remains materialism's founding firecracker, witty and unrepentant.
lancre-tableau-de-linconstance-1612:
Pierre de Lancre was a French judge sent by the king to the Labourd country in the Basque lands in 1609. His Tableau de l'Inconstance des Mauvais Anges et Demons, published in 1612, reports the witch-hunt he led there. It is the fullest French demonological report of the Basque trials.

De Lancre describes sabbaths on the shore, dances, feasts with demons, and the testimony of hundreds of accused villagers and children. He believed nearly all of it, and his court sent scores to the stake on such evidence. Historians read his Tableau as both a record of the trials and a window into the judge's own fevered mind.
lancre-tableau-inconstance-french-1612:
Pierre de Lancre's Tableau de l'inconstance des mauvais anges et démons appeared in 1612. De Lancre had judged the great witch trials of the Labourd, the Basque country under Bordeaux, in 1609. His book paints those trials in sensational detail, sabbaths, pacts, and demonic marks across hundreds of pages.

It is often called the most infamous French demonology. De Lancre describes the sabbath as a vast, inverted court, with a connoisseur's relish for the strange. His purple prose serves a judge who ordered burnings. The Tableau preserves the persecution's own imagination at full stretch. Historians still quarry it for the Labourd trials and for the mind of their judge.
lawrence-trespasser-1912:
The Trespasser, Lawrence's second novel, appeared in 1912, drawn from the experience of a friend whose love affair ended in death. Its hero, Siegmund, is a violinist and married man who escapes to the Isle of Wight with his pupil Helena.

For a few days the lovers live in a haze of music, sea, and summer light. Then Siegmund must return to his wife, his children, and the life he fled, and he cannot bear what waits. The novel moves toward its fatal end with the certainty of weather. Already the early Lawrence is present: desire and doom locked together.
loeb-mechanistic-life-1912:
Jacques Loeb was a German-born physiologist who wanted biology run with the strict methods of physics and chemistry. His 1912 book The Mechanistic Conception of Life states that program as a manifesto. Living things, he argues, are machines whose moves can be forced and forecast.

Loeb reports tadpoles and sea creatures made to turn toward light or chemicals by set drives he calls tropisms. He also cites artificial parthenogenesis, eggs made to grow without fertilization by a salt bath. His bold claims thrilled some readers and angered others, but they set a research agenda for decades.
mann-death-in-venice-1912:
Thomas Mann published Death in Venice in 1912, a German novella about a writer on holiday. Gustav von Aschenbach is a famed author known for discipline and hard work. He travels to Venice and becomes obsessed with Tadzio, a beautiful Polish boy at his hotel. He watches from afar and never speaks to the boy.

A cholera outbreak spreads through Venice while officials hide the truth. Aschenbach stays, decays in spirit, and neglects his health and dignity. Mann sets Apollonian order against Dionysian passion, in Greek terms. The prose is stately and exact. The novella is a perfect, troubling study of art, beauty, and decline.
manners-makyth-man-ship-s-company-part-1:
Manners Makyth Man is a tale by W. W. Jacobs, part twelve of Ship's Company. The night-watchman tells it, and he is out of sorts tonight. He bursts out against play-acting, which he never held with. Dressing up and pretending, he says, is a kid's game.

He chews his tobacco and stares across the river at the wharves. A lighterman's antics in mid-stream fail to stir him. He owns that hurrying to do good to others undid him. From that hint the watchman's comic confession unfolds. Jacobs's wharfside philosopher is one of his beloved creations. The tale mixes dry humor with a small moral sting.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-12: Volume twelve of the Napoleon memoirs is etext 3562. Louis Antoine Fauvelet de Bourrienne is listed as its author there. A date label in the head reads 1814, beside the title. Widger is credited as producer, in the eleventh edition. All of that comes from the file head, because the sample holds only the head. No memoir prose follows it in the portion preserved, so contents stay unstated here.
moore-ethics-1912:
Moore published his short Ethics in 1912, restating the doctrine of his Principia Ethica of 1903 for general readers. The Principia had made him the leading voice of a new moral philosophy at Cambridge. The smaller book brings the same teaching to readers without technical training.

Moore holds that good is a simple quality that cannot be defined in other terms, and that we know it by direct insight. Attempts to define good as pleasure, or as any natural thing, commit what he named the naturalistic fallacy. The book then weighs conduct, free will, and the kinds of things that are good in themselves. Twentieth-century moral thought begins in large part from Moore's pages. The Ethics remains his clearest and shortest statement, written in plain and honest English prose.
murray-five-stages-greek-religion-1912:
Gilbert Murray, Oxford's great humanist and translator of Greek drama, published Five Stages of Greek Religion in 1912. The lectures trace Greek faith from early nature worship to late philosophy. Murray writes for general readers in lucid, graceful prose.

He moves from the Olympian gods in their bright order to the failure of nerve he saw in the later ancient world. Mystery cults, astrology, and world-weariness fill his fourth stage before reason makes its last stand. His humane, skeptical survey long served as the standard short account of Greek religion in English. Murray never hides his own loves and doubts behind his learning.
my-novel-volume-12:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's twelfth book brings the Caxton family back. Mr. Caxton speaks for them as a chorus to the drama. They ring the altar, eager to ask and judge. Yet they do not know how the skein will unravel.

Mrs. Caxton hopes Violante was deceived, not willing, in her flight. Her husband cites old novels where such girls must die. The captain protests they have had enough of tombs. Poor Nora's grave, he notes, began the whole tale. The final volume gathers family and fate together, closing Lytton's long panorama of English hearts and homes.
nasa-tm-19720008496-inexpensive-programm:
James E Vrancik of the Lewis Research Center built this low cost clock and reported it in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2500. It served the PDP-12, a small twelve bit digital computer. Laboratory computers need a clock they can set and read under program control. Commercial units cost more than many labs could justify. Vrancik's design filled that gap cheaply, and an errata sheet later restored a missing page.

The instruction list stays short and practical. One instruction tests and clears the clock's flag. Others clear or stop the clock on command. A preset instruction loads the counter from the computer and starts it. The clock then counts at a fixed rate for timing tasks. Test setups could time events without costly gear.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-12:
Chrysostom's homilies on Paul's two letters to the Corinthians fill volume twelve of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, from 1886. The Corinthian letters gave a preacher rich ground: a gifted, quarrelsome church much like Chrysostom's own. Philip Schaff edited the series.

Through forty-four homilies on the first letter and thirty on the second, he treats factions, lawsuits, marriage, and the collection for the poor. The great chapter on love gets his full rhetorical power. In the second series he defends his ministry and consoles a church under strain. Readers meet Paul filtered through the finest pulpit of the ancient world.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-12:
Leo the Great and Gregory the Great, two popes who remade their office, fill volume twelve of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890. Leo ruled Rome as the empire cracked in the 440s and 450s. Gregory, a century and a half later, ruled it as a plague- and war-worn city. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Leo's Tome on the two natures of Christ settled the council of Chalcedon, and his sermons and letters run the volume's first half. Gregory's pastoral rule for bishops and his letters, which managed estates, missions, and kings, fill the second. Between them, the volume shows the papacy becoming the West's steady center.
northamptonshire-witches-1612:
The Witches of Northamptonshire records a group trial held in 1612, the same summer as the famous Pendle case. Agnes Browne stands among the accused in this Jacobean pamphlet. The charges grew out of deaths and harms laid at the doors of the accused.

The pamphlet sets down the proof the court heard and the ends the accused met. Such prints let readers far away follow a trial they could never attend. They also spread stock ideas of what a witch did and how she was caught. This case ranks with the major witch trials of King James's reign.
odonnell-werwolves-1912:
Elliott O'Donnell ranges the whole wolf lore in Werwolves, his survey of 1912. O'Donnell was a famed ghost hunter of his day in London. His book runs through scores of short parts. Wolf men of old lands sit by fresh tales from guests. One part e'en tells how a man might turn wolf by rite, herb, or curse.

He writes for thrills, with a show man's flair. Sages doubt much of it, yet crowds ate it up. The book is the theme's vast fair ground. It shows the lore at its most lush.
openalex-w1694905212:

One channel yields two photons from the Higgs decay. The other yields four leptons through Z bosons. A joint fit matched the mass peaks from both channels. The separate measures agreed well with each other, they report. The abstract gives a combined mass near one hundred twenty-five GeV. That value is stated there in plain numeric form. Precise mass anchors all other Higgs property tests.
openalex-w1858542512:
G. Aad and the ATLAS Collaboration reported this landmark search. It appeared in Physics Letters B in the year 2012. The team hunted the standard model Higgs boson at the LHC. Data came from proton collisions in 2011 and 2012. The paper's title announces observation of a new particle.

The hosted sample preserves the journal front matter and citation. It lists the paper across pages one to twenty-nine. The dedication honors ATLAS colleagues who died before publication. The old abstract describes data sets at two collision energies. This paper is the ATLAS announcement of the Higgs discovery. It completed the standard model's roster of particles.
openalex-w1974613712:
José María Gutiérrez and the Global Snakebite Initiative wrote this appeal. It appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013. Snakebite envenoming kills and maims many poor people yearly. It sat apart from the main neglected disease strategy. The authors call that separation a costly mistake.

Full integration into the global strategy is their demand. Snakebite shares victims, places, and needs with those diseases. Shared programs could improve antivenom access and care. The paper is a viewpoint, setting out the way forward. It asks funders and health leaders to act together. Snakebite belongs on the global health agenda, they argue.
openalex-w2128606612:
Joëlle Amselem, Christina Cuomo, Jan van Kan, and colleagues published this genome study in PLoS Genetics in 2011. Both attack an unusually wide range of host plants and persist well in the environment, yet they differ in mating and spore production.

The team compared the two genomes with each other and with other fungi. The genomes are close in size and share most of their genes in the same large-scale order. One fungus carries far more jumping DNA elements than the other. Their toolkits of genes tied to killing plant cells look broadly similar despite their differences.
openalex-w2159327312:
John Wieczorek, David Bloom, Robert Guralnick, and colleagues published this paper in PLoS ONE in 2012. They describe Darwin Core, a community-built standard for sharing biodiversity data. Species records sit in countless formats on many systems, and common term definitions are the first step toward joining them into one view.

The paper traces how the standard grew and how its terms are organized. It contrasts the simple flat form with a relational form for richer data. Case studies show the standard stretching into new fields like metagenomics and genetic resources. Records shared this way combine into products such as species range maps that track change under environmental pressure.
openalex-w2223575612:
John Powers, Maria Guerrero, Nancy Leidy, and colleagues published this study in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2015. First, phone interviews with forty-six confirmed flu patients in the United States and Mexico harvested symptom descriptions. Patients named cough, tiredness, sore throat, congestion, headache, chills, and aches most often. A draft instrument was then tested on thirty-four more patients, who understood it easily and added nothing new. The resulting thirty-seven-item tool proved content valid, with formal reliability testing to follow.
openalex-w2254159412:
Martín Caldarola, Pablo Albella, Emiliano Cortés, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2015. That heating can warp the antennas, boil nearby liquid, and damage the very molecules under study.

The team built antennas from silicon instead of metal, arranging them as paired dimers on arrays. Guided by computer calculations, they designed the silicon pairs for the near infrared range. Tests checked their light enhancement against predictions. Because silicon avoids the loss channel that heats metals, these non-plasmonic antennas promise surface-enhanced measurements with ultra-low heat conversion, protecting delicate samples.
openalex-w2524066112:
Zichen Wang, Caroline D. Monteiro, and Kathleen M. Jagodnik, with a very large group of contributors, published this 2016 Nature Communications paper. It concerns the Gene Expression Omnibus, a public storehouse of gene expression data from thousands of studies. Such data record which genes are turned up or down in cells under different conditions. The title announces its method: extracting gene signatures from the archive with help from a crowd.

The authors explain that these archives hold far more information than the original studies extracted. Reusing the data is hard, because formats differ and required background details are often missing. Combining many studies takes heavy manual cleanup before any joint analysis can start. Careful annotation, they argue, could power a search engine working directly on the data. That would help researchers find gene signatures across tissues, diseases, and treatments.
openalex-w2549196812:
Tung Gia Phan, Federico Giannitti, and Stephanie Rossow, with colleagues, reported a new pig virus in Virology Journal in 2016. Using deep sequencing, they pieced together the genome of a new circovirus, named PCV3. Its key proteins matched a bat-associated circovirus only loosely, and pig circoviruses even less. All three pigs shared heart lesions, and viral RNA sat inside the damaged heart cells. Other viruses also appeared in the tissues, which clouds the picture. The authors say PCV3's role in disease, alone or with co-infections, needs further study.
openalex-w2890167612:
