The field uses materials at the nanoscale to diagnose disease or ferry drugs to precise targets. It is young but develops fast. Such targeted delivery promises stronger effects with fewer side effects.

The review updates advances across nanomaterials for medicine. Uses include chemotherapy agents, biological drugs, and immune therapies. It looks at how nanocarriers improve both new and old drugs, including natural products. Disease-marker tests also get coverage. Chances and challenges are weighed together, from lab discovery to clinical use. It closes with trends and outlook. For chemists and clinicians, it maps where nano delivery is actually heading.
openalex-w2983201012:
Daniel Conroy-Beam, David Buss, Kelly Asao, and colleagues published this study in Scientific Reports in 2019. It tests rival computer models of how people combine their wishes when choosing a mate. People weigh many traits at once, such as kindness, looks, and status, and models differ on how those wishes add up.

The team drew on survey data from forty-five countries, giving the test a rare worldwide reach. Each model was asked to reproduce how real preferences hang together in actual partner choices. Comparing the models shows which simple rule best matches human behavior across cultures. The work links everyday ideas about attraction to formal models that can be checked against data from thousands of people.
openalex-w3032218712:
Kenneth Aamodt, A. Abrahantes Quintana, D. Adamová, and colleagues of the ALICE collaboration published this letter in Physical Review Letters in 2011. It measures how many charged particles spray out when lead nuclei collide at the Large Hadron Collider. The count is taken at midrapidity, straight out from the beam line.

Earlier work covered only head-on collisions, so this study extends the count to glancing ones. Collisions are sorted into nine classes by how central they are, covering the most central eighty percent of cases. The particle density is scaled by the number of nucleons that took part, estimated with a standard geometry model. The pattern shows how particle production grows as collisions become more violent.

Governments had acted on an unprecedented scale, and clear records were lacking.

From January 2020 the tracker logs closure, health, and economic measures for more than one hundred eighty countries. Nineteen policy areas are scored on ordered scales, so a partial school closure sits below a full one. The authors show the timing of adoption, easing, and reimposition. Anyone can now test how policies related to cases, deaths, and welfare with the same ruler.
openalex-w3216620312:
Shuai Li, Valentina Silvestri, Goska Leslie, and colleagues estimated cancer risks from faulty BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. Their study appeared in the Journal of Clinical Oncology in 2022. These inherited faults are famous for raising breast and ovarian cancer risk. Far less was known about their links to other cancers. Precise, age-specific figures are needed for honest counselling and screening plans.

The team analysed more than five thousand families carrying these variants, gathered by an international consortium. They estimated relative and absolute risks for twenty-two first cancers, adjusting for how families were recruited. Separating risks by gene and by age matters, because a young carrier faces different choices than an older one. The estimates give clinics firmer ground for risk management.
openalex-w4407684012:
Soomin Kim and Hiroshi Kori study synchronised states in rings of oscillators. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2026. Many oscillator networks are multistable. The same network can settle into different patterns depending on where it starts.

The authors add two realistic features: uneven natural frequencies and a phase lag in the coupling. They compute numerically how large each state's basin of attraction is. A larger phase lag widens the basins of states with higher wave numbers, up to a point. Slight frequency unevenness instead favours the more synchronised low-numbered states. Knowing which state wins from which start helps engineers control networks from power grids to robots.
openalex-w4416338912:
Shunichiro Kittaka, Yohei Kono, Toshiro Sakakibara, and colleagues measure magnetostriction in the superconductor Sr2RuO4. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. The material is a famous puzzle in superconductivity. Its upper critical field seems limited by the Pauli effect.

That effect can create a rare modulated superconducting state, predicted decades ago. Evidence includes a first-order transition and a drop in spin signal. Magnetostriction, the tiny length change in a magnetic field, senses such transitions sharply. The team's high-resolution measurements probe the field-driven state precisely. Pinning down this state would settle long debates about how the material's electron pairs break and rearrange.

perry-present-philosophical-tendencies-1:

Perry expounds each school fairly before judging it from his new realist position. His account of pragmatism, learned from James yet critical of it, is especially valued. Charts match sign to sign through the ages. His claim sparked rows, yet parts of it have worn well. The tract is the root text of one school on the ABC's birth. It shows Petrie at his most keen.

Philostratus tells how Apollonius healed the sick and faced down emperors. Travels to India, debates with priests, and miraculous escapes fill the narrative. The imperial family commissioned the biography a century after Apollonius died. Readers have long treated it as a pagan answer to the Gospels. History or holy fiction, it shows what a divine man looked like then. Conybeare's edition made the full text handy for English readers.

Volume two of Conybeare's Loeb Apollonius appeared in 1912 alongside the first. It completes Philostratus's Life of Apollonius of Tyana in Greek and English. The sage's surviving letters and a famous controversy fill the back.

The letters show Apollonius advising cities, rulers, and friends in his own voice. Eusebius's treatise against Hierocles then attacks a comparison of Apollonius with Christ. Hierocles, a Roman official, had praised Apollonius above Jesus. Eusebius answers fiercely, giving readers the early Christian backlash in full. The volume thus preserves both a pagan legend and its rebuttal. Few books stage an ancient religious rivalry so directly.
pico-mirandola-strix-latin-1612:

Pico writes as a humanist confronting the witch craze in Italy. His speakers debate confessions, flights, and the value of testimony dragged out by fear. He finds demonology wanting in places, a brave stance for his time and place. The Strix shows Italian humanism measuring the witch belief with classical tools. plos-pbio-0020212:
Niels C. Rattenborg, Bruce H. Mandt, William H. Obermeyer, and their team studied sleep in migrating sparrows for PLOS Biology in 2004. White-crowned sparrows fly long distances at night during migration. In cages, they enter a restless state at night in migration season and sleep far less, yet stay alert.

Wild birds cannot afford to be drowsy on long flights, and this species seems to cut sleep without the usual cost. The birds remained able to learn and perform during the day. How they do it is still an open puzzle. The work points to a natural model of sleeplessness without harm, a state sleep science would love to understand.
plos-pbio-0020312:
Paul D. N. Hebert, Mark Y. Stoeckle, Tyler S. Zemlak, and Charles M. Francis tested a DNA identification method for birds in PLOS Biology in 2004. A short, standard stretch of DNA can act as a barcode: read it, match it to a reference list, and name the species.

The team showed the barcode separates bird species with high accuracy, even close kin. One small tissue sample can thus name a bird without an expert eye. That promise has since grown into global libraries used for wildlife trade checks, food fraud, and biodiversity surveys. This bird paper was one of the early proofs that the scheme works at scale.
plos-pbio-0020412:
Jonathan B. Alberts and Garrett M. Odell built a computer model of a moving bacterium in PLOS Biology in 2004. Listeria, a germ that causes food poisoning, hijacks a host cell's actin to push itself around. It rides a comet tail of actin filaments, hopping in small jumps the authors call nano-saltation.

Their in silico model rebuilds that motion from the known parts and reproduces the jerky hops seen under microscopes. A model that matches real motion can be pushed further than any single experiment. It tests which parts matter most and predicts what changes would do. Listeria's trick is also a clean window on how all cells use actin to move and change shape.
plos-pone-0000012:
Don Klinkenberg, Christophe Fraser, and Hans Heesterbeek asked in 2006 how well contact tracing really works when a new epidemic breaks out. Contact tracing means finding the people an infected person has exposed, then isolating or treating them before they spread the disease further. It is slow, costly work.

Using models of emerging infections, the team tested when tracing can hold an outbreak down and when it falls behind. Speed, the share of contacts found, and how fast the disease spreads all change the answer. Their results help health officials judge whether tracing is worth its heavy cost in the first weeks of an epidemic, the moment when control is still possible.
plos-pone-0000112:
Bryant F. McAllister and Amy L. Evans published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It looks at Drosophila americana, a North American fruit fly, and asks why some stretches of its DNA carry more variation than expected. The focus is on genes linked to the Y chromosome only part of the time.

Genes on a Y chromosome usually show little variety, because the Y rarely swaps DNA with a partner chromosome. The authors measure diversity in this fly to see what changes when that linkage is only temporary. The work bears on a basic question in evolution: how the layout of chromosomes shapes the genetic variety a species holds.
plos-pone-0000212:
Clément Nizak, Robert J. Fitzhenry, and Richard H. Kessin published this amoeba study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dictyostelium caveatum is a social amoeba, a microbe that lives in soil and feeds on other microbes. The authors report that it exploits other social amoebae, taking advantage of its relatives rather than only hunting bacteria.

Social amoebae gather and build fruiting bodies together, which creates room for cheating. A species that exploits its cousins shows how far such exploitation can go in microbial societies. The work feeds the wider study of cooperation and conflict among microbes, a model for social evolution at its simplest.
plos-pone-0000312:
Angus M. Tester, Jennifer H. Cox, Andrea R. Connor, and colleagues published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. LPS is a bacterial molecule that triggers strong immune reactions, and neutrophils are the first-responder white blood cells. The authors show that responses to LPS, and neutrophil movement toward infection sites in living animals, require MMP-8. MMP-8 is an enzyme from the neutrophils themselves.

An enzyme best known for cutting tissue proteins turns out to be needed for the cells to arrive and respond at all. The paper pins that requirement down in vivo. The result matters for understanding inflammation, where MMP enzymes are often drug targets.
plos-pone-0000412:
Martin Wasser and William Chia studied a fly protein that lives outside the chromosomes, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, called EAST, is extrachromosomal, meaning it is found in the nucleus away from the DNA strands themselves. In the fruit fly Drosophila, it can associate with the giant polytene chromosomes of larval glands.

Beyond sitting on chromosomes, EAST can regulate gene expression, changing which genes are turned on. Proteins that organize the nucleus may control genes by shaping the space they sit in. This work adds to the picture of the nucleus as a structured place, not a bag of loose DNA.
plos-pone-0000512:
Isaac Amela, Juan Cedano, and Enrique Querol tested a reassuring idea about immunity with computation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. When the body makes antibodies against a pathogen, one worry is cross-reaction. The antibody might also attack the host's own proteins. That can happen if the two share epitopes, the small patches antibodies recognize. Their bioinformatics approach compared pathogen proteins that elicit antibodies with host proteins.

The title states their conclusion: such pathogen proteins do not share epitopes with host proteins. If true broadly, the immune system's targeting is cleaner than feared, and vaccine design faces one less hazard. Computational claims of this kind invite experimental spot-checks, which the paper's clear statement makes easy to design.
plos-pone-0000612:
Caroline Fasano, François Tercé, Jean-Pierre Niel and their co-authors reported in PLOS ONE in 2007 on an unusual route for nerve signals. Their study asks whether neurons can pass on excitation without action potentials, the classic electrical spikes. The proposed route rests on ceramide, a fatty molecule made by the cell.

Working with an in vitro model, meaning a lab setup outside a living body, the team tracked how excitation moved along neurons. Action potentials normally lead, after synaptic transmission, to other neurons switching on and networks working as a whole. A ceramide-based path would add a second way for that spread to happen. Readers get a challenge to the standard picture of how nerve cells talk.
plos-pone-0000712:
Srinivasan Ramachandran, Lai-Hua Xie, Scott A. John and co-authors found a new role for a channel protein in cell injury, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen, is linked to ischemia, atherosclerosis, and neurodegenerative disorders. How it kills cells at the molecular level was poorly understood. Connexin hemichannels, half-channels in the cell membrane, are their focus.

The authors demonstrate a role for these hemichannels in oxidative stress and in smoking-induced cell injury. Channels that open at the wrong time can leak a cell's contents and flood it with harmful ions. A named culprit gives drug designers a target for limiting tissue damage.
plos-pone-0000812:
Manisha Chandalia, Ping Lin, Thanalakshmi Seenivasan and colleagues compared body fat and insulin resistance in South Asian and Caucasian men, for PLOS ONE in 2007. South Asians are susceptible to insulin resistance even without obesity, a pattern that makes standard weight cutoffs misleading. The team examined body fat content, distribution, and function in South Asian men, and their relationships to insulin resistance, against a Caucasian comparison group.

The groups studied numbered 29 South Asian and 18 Caucasian men, as reported in the abstract. Where fat sits, belly versus limbs, and how it behaves may matter more than how much there is. Findings like these argue for ethnic-specific risk screening in diabetes.
plos-pone-0000912:
Chunxia Chen and Andrew Wells compared the cancer linked power of the E2F factor family, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. The E2F family has nine members with jobs that are partly distinct and partly shared. These factors sit below growth signals and help decide whether a cell grows and divides.

Because they control genes tied to cell growth, some members may push cancer more than others. Chen and Wells set the members side by side to compare their oncogenic activity, their ability to drive tumor like growth. A clear ranking helps cancer research focus on the members that matter most, instead of treating the family as one block.
plos-pone-0001012:
Saeid Naderi, Hamid-Reza Rezaei, Pierre Taberlet and colleagues surveyed the DNA of domestic goats worldwide, in PLOS ONE in 2007. From the start of farming, moving livestock around reshaped their genes and numbers. Present day genetic patterns still carry the record of those journeys.

In a large scale analysis of mitochondrial DNA, the team found six haplogroups, six deep maternal branches, with high diversity among goats. High diversity suggests goats were domesticated broadly, or kept mixing, rather than passing through one narrow bottleneck. The goat's family record helps historians of farming trace early herding routes. It also matters for conserving rare local breeds.
plos-pone-0001112:
Min-Hyuk Yoo, Xue-Ming Xu, Bradley Carlson and colleagues showed that lowering a redox enzyme stalls cancer cell growth, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Thioredoxin reductase 1 is a major redox regulator and an antioxidant selenoprotein. It is thought to help prevent cancer, yet many cancer cells overproduce it, and numerous cancer drugs inhibit it.

The team targeted reduction of TR1 in cancer cells and report it inhibits self sufficient growth and DNA replication. A protein can guard normal cells and serve cancer at once; context decides. Cutting TR1 tests the cancer side of that bargain. The result supports TR1 as a drug target with a clear rationale.
plos-pone-0001212:
Nef is a small HIV protein that helps the virus thrive by rewiring the cells it infects. Claudia Haller, Susanne Rauch, and Oliver Fackler describe two of its tricks in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Nef modulates host cell vesicle transport and signaling. Recent studies also suggested it alters the formation and function of immunological synapses, the contacts between immune cells.

The authors show that Nef uses two distinct mechanisms to move the signaling protein Lck within the cell. It also reshapes actin remodeling after T-cell receptor stimulation. Both moves can blunt the T cell's response. Understanding Nef in this detail matters for any drug aimed at it.
plos-pone-0001312:
A gel women could use to protect themselves from HIV was a major prevention hope of the 2000s. Leigh Peterson and colleagues report a phase 3 trial of one candidate in Ghana, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The candidate was SAVVY gel, containing 1.0 percent C31G. The trial's objective was to determine whether the gel prevents male-to-female vaginal transmission of HIV among women at high risk.

The study was double-blind, randomized, and placebo-controlled, the strongest trial design. Participants were followed for up to twelve months. Trials like this one, whatever the outcome, settled whether microbicide gels of this type could work.
plos-pone-0001412:
Vincent Dietemann and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on fights between honeybee queens. In most species, fights settle who gets to breed. Smart fighters cut the cost of a clash by sizing up the rival first. In some species, though, fights still turn lethal. The team asked whether bee queens know their own strength.

By staging queen duels and tracking the acts of each bee, they tested self sizing in a strict way. Queens did act as if they weighed their own odds. The work adds bees to the list of animals that gauge self before a fight. It helps explain how lethal fights can still be a sound strategy.
plos-pone-0001512:
Takeshi Egawa, Taras Kreslavsky, and Dan Littman wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how T cells pick their fate. In the thymus, the grip of a young T cell's receptor sets its path. Some become helpers, others killers. Mouse models with fixed receptors let labs watch that choice. The team used fate maps to trace it in a new way.

Their maps show some cells veer from the path their grip would predict. That veer, called lineage diversion, refines the standard model of choice. Sharp models of T cell growth guide vaccine and immune therapy design. They also help explain immune ills where the mix of T cells skews.
plos-pone-0001612:
Peter Janson and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how to tell true regulator T cells in people. These cells hold the immune system back from attacking the self. A factor called FOXP3 is their hallmark, but standard cells can wear it briefly too. That blur made counts of the true cells hard to trust.

The team show a chemical change on the FOXP3 gene marks the true, committed cells alone. Brief wearers lack the mark. A clean mark lets clinics count these cells with faith in trials and in immune ills. It also helps sort which cell therapies truly hold regulator cells.
plos-pone-0001712:
Taras K. Oleksyk, Kai Zhao, Francisco M. De La Vega, and their co-authors presented a way to spot selected DNA regions in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. When natural selection sweeps a helpful gene variant through two recently split populations, it leaves marks. Variation near the gene drops, and the gap between the populations there rises or falls sharply.

Their method reads those marks from light-coverage genome data, cheaper partial sequencing from two human populations. The full text gives the statistics, the populations used, and the regions flagged. Finding selection's footprints with light data lowers the cost of scanning whole populations for genes shaped by local pressures such as diet, climate, and disease.
plos-pone-0001812:
Oliver W. Morgan, Boaventura Rodrigues, Tony Elston, and their co-authors studied how severe a dangerous gut infection strain is in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Clostridium difficile is a leading cause of diarrhoea tied to health care. Several rich countries had reported more cases and outbreaks, blamed on the new PCR ribotype 027 strain.

Their study compared how sick ribotype 027 patients got with patients infected by other types. The full text gives the patient groups and how each group fared. Whether 027 is truly more harmful, or just more common, decides how hospitals should spend on separate rooms and testing for this strain.
plos-pone-0001912:
Sarah Meadows and co-authors showed that blood gene patterns can flag exposure to radiation, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Past work had hinted that the set of genes switched on in blood shifts with disease or with contact with harmful agents. The team asked whether those shifts could track one known exposure: ionizing radiation.

They tested how traits such as dose and time changed the blood gene pattern, in both mice and humans. They report that the radiation response pattern is specific, lasts, and reads out with accuracy. A blood test that proves recent exposure could help sort patients fast after an accident or attack.
plos-pone-0002012:
Lucius Chiaraviglio, Daniel Brown, and James Kirby showed that the Legionnaires' bacterium can infect vessel-lining cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Legionella pneumophila is a bacterium that causes a severe pneumonia called Legionnaires' disease. It was known to grow inside lung immune cells, which was thought to be its main home in the body.

The team report, for the first time, that the bacterium infects and grows within cultured human endothelial cells, the cells that line blood vessels. If it does so in patients, vessel infection could add to lung harm. A new host cell type widens the picture of how this disease unfolds.
plos-pone-0002112:
Gary Bren and co-authors studied why HIV kills the very cells it infects, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Acute HIV-1 infection of CD4 T cells often results in the apoptotic death of the infected cells. What evolutionary advantage that offers the virus was unclear, since a virus that kills its host cell seems to cut its own life short.

The team tied two past observations together: infection switches on NF-kappaB, a master immune switch, and it arms a death enzyme, caspase 8. As the title states, killing by the HIV protease promotes NF-kappaB dependent replication. Death of one cell may seed more virus in the next.
plos-pone-0002212:
Timothy Hallett and co-authors modeled what male circumcision programs could do to HIV in southern Africa. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Three randomized trials had shown clearly that circumcising adult men cuts their chance of catching HIV. What mass programs would achieve at the scale of whole countries, alone or with other measures, was not known.

The authors used models to project the impact of circumcision programs across the region. Their work weighs how fast programs would need to roll out and how they might combine with existing prevention. Model results like these guide one of the largest HIV prevention decisions African health systems have faced.
plos-pone-0002312:
Michael Thaut, Martina Demartin, and Jerome Sanes mapped the brain networks that let people keep a beat, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Moving in time with an external pace requires the brain to fuse sensory input with motor commands. Musicians go further, performing layered polyrhythms, and the machinery behind simple beat keeping and complex rhythm may differ.

The team studied brain networks for integrative rhythm formation in their subjects. Their recordings separate the systems that lock movement to a beat from those that combine several rhythms at once. Understanding this circuitry also serves therapy, since rhythmic cues help patients with movement disorders walk.
plos-pone-0002412:
Matigian and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Nicholas A. Matigian, Richard D. McCurdy, François Féron, and others. Its subject is fibroblast and Lymphoblast Gene Expression Profiles in Schizophrenia: Are Non-Neural Cells Informative?. Lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) and fibroblasts provide conveniently derived non-neuronal samples in which to study the aetiology of schizophrenia (SZ) using gene expression profiling.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002512:
Led by Matarese, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Its subject is relationship between Quality and Editorial Leadership of Biomedical Research Journals: A Comparative Study of Italian and UK Journals. The quality of biomedical reporting is guided by statements of several organizations.

Although not all journals adhere to these guidelines, those that do show “editorial leadership” in their author community. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002612:
Research by Rodriguez-Feo and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Juan A. Rodriguez-Feo, Willem E. Hellings, Frans L. Moll, and others. Its subject is caveolin-1 Influences Vascular Protease Activity and Is a Potential Stabilizing Factor in Human Atherosclerotic Disease. Caveolin-1 (Cav-1) is a regulatory protein of the arterial wall, but its role in human atherosclerosis remains unknown.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002712:
Research from Yvonne J. K. Edwards and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers a Meta-Analysis of microarray gene expression in mouse stem cells: redefining stemness. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Yvonne J. K. Edwards, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. While much progress has been made in understanding stem cell (SC) function. The authors add a further point. This lack of knowledge is a major barrier holding back the discovery of therapeutic uses of SCs. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002812:
Work by Abigail Manson McGuire and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with conserved secondary structures in aspergillus. The catalog record names Abigail Manson McGuire first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Recent evidence suggests that the number and variety of functional RNAs (ncRNAs as well as cis-acting RNA elements within mRNAs ) is much higher. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002912:
Eric Nicholson, Brian Brunelle, Juergen Richt and co-authors reported a heritable variant in cattle prion protein genes in 2008. BSE, or mad cow disease, is a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy of cattle. Classic BSE comes from eating contaminated feed, while rare atypical forms differ in key ways.

Published in PLOS ONE, the study identifies a polymorphism in the bovine PRNP gene tied to genetic transmissible disease. In plain terms, some cattle may carry an inborn risk in their own genes. That changes how surveillance and breeding advice for BSE need to be framed. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003012:
Charles Plessy, Michela Fagiolini, Akiko Wagatsuma and co-authors built a resource for gene analysis in the mouse brain in 2008. The cerebral cortex transcriptome is remarkably uniform, with variation stronger between individuals than between areas. Many distinct cell types are mixed in each sample, so signals from one type can be averaged away.

Their resource aims to let researchers analyze expression in the mouse brain with that problem in mind. Published in PLOS ONE, a shared reference dataset saves repeated profiling. Neuroscientists studying cortex development or disease can compare new samples against a common baseline.
plos-pone-0003112:
André Boorsma, Xiang-Jun Lu, Anna Zakrzewska and co-authors inferred transcription factor activity in yeast from gene expression in 2008. A key systems biology goal is understanding how genome-wide expression is controlled by transcription factors in a condition-specific way. Factor activity is often modulated after the protein is made, by ligand binding or chemical modification.

Direct activity cannot be read from the factor's own RNA level in those cases. Their regulon-based analysis infers activity from the behavior of each factor's target genes. Published in PLOS ONE, the method lets one dataset answer condition-by-condition questions about control.
plos-pone-0003212:
Sabrina Bonde, Kun-Ming Chan and Nicholas Zavazava test stem cell derived blood cells for transplant tolerance in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Bone marrow cells can induce stable mixed chimerism under proper conditioning of the host, mediating transplantation tolerance. Their strong immunogenicity, however, precludes routine clinical use due to the need for harsh preconditioning and related risks.

The authors test whether hematopoietic cells derived from embryonic stem cells can induce the same tolerance. Readers see an attempt to keep the benefit of bone marrow while cutting its dangers. A renewable cell source for tolerance would be valuable for organ transplant patients.
plos-pone-0003312:
Sherry T. Hikita, Kenneth S. Kosik, Dennis O. Clegg and colleagues study a cancer protein's role in stem cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The MUC1 protein is aberrantly expressed on an estimated seventy-five percent of all human solid tumour cancers. The team recently reported that a transmembrane cleavage product, MUC1*, is the predominant form of the protein on cancer cells, with evidence it functions as a growth factor.

The title reports that MUC1* mediates the growth of human pluripotent stem cells. Readers see a tumour-associated protein act as a stem cell growth signal. That dual role may explain part of why MUC1 is so common in cancers.
plos-pone-0003412:
Thomas F. Clarke and Patricia L. Clark studied word choice inside genes in this 2008 paper. Most amino acids can be spelled by more than one DNA codon. Some codons are used often, while others are rare. Though rare and common spellings build the same protein, they are not placed at random.

The authors found that rare codons tend to cluster together in genes. These clusters show up across many kinds of organisms. Their placement may affect how a protein folds while it is built. The finding gives gene readers a new pattern to explain.
plos-pone-0003512:
Susanne Diekelmann and co-authors tested what lost sleep does to memory in this 2008 study. People sometimes recall events that never happened, with full confidence. Such false memories grow from strong links to real events. Sleep normally helps sort real memories into long-term storage.

After sleep loss, subjects produced more of these false memories. Their brains seemed to file suggested events as truly seen. Rest appears to guard the line between real and imagined events. The finding warns that tired witnesses and tired students may misremember. False memories matter in courtrooms, where tired witnesses may swear to false events.
plos-pone-0003612:
Yong Wang and Frederick C. C. Leung compared fish and sea squirt genes in this 2008 paper. Sea squirts carry methylation on only part of their DNA. Fish evolved global DNA methylation across the genome. Methylated CpG sites mutate in context-dependent ways over time.

Fish genes showed more GC content at positions flanking CpG sites. Sea squirt counterparts kept lower GC in those spots. The shift may reduce the impact of heavy methylation. Genome chemistry thus records how a silencing system spread. Sea squirts are close kin of backboned animals, which makes the contrast sharp.
plos-pone-0003712:
Po-Shun Lee, Sanjay R. Patel, David C. Christiani, and colleagues published this pilot study in PLOS ONE in 2008. In sepsis, the blood protein gelsolin falls to low levels. Gelsolin normally sweeps up actin, a cell protein spilled into the blood when tissue is damaged. The team studied septic patients.

They tested whether the depth of gelsolin loss tracks with how patients fare. They also checked whether free actin in the blood is a sign of the septic state. The pilot weighs a cleanup protein as a possible marker of sepsis severity and outcome.
plos-pone-0003812:
Shuguang Jiang, Alexis S. Bailey, Devorah C. Goldman, and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The lymphatic system grows out of veins in the embryo and drains fluid from tissues all life long. Little was known about whether circulating progenitor cells help maintain its lining in adults.

The authors investigated whether hematopoietic stem cells, the bone marrow cells that make blood, can form lymphatic endothelium. They report that these stem cells do contribute to the lymphatic lining. The finding extends the blood stem cell's resume well beyond blood itself.
plos-pone-0003912:
Tamami Nakano, Fumitaka Homae, Hama Watanabe, and co-authors recorded brain activity in sleeping babies in 2008. Babies learn links between events and act ahead of what they expect. Behavior studies had shown that skill, but its brain basis was unknown. Imaging work in adults offered hints about how prediction works.

The team measured cortical activity while infants slept and sounds played. Activity rose before expected sounds, showing the brain prepared in advance. That early response suggests prediction machinery works very early in life. The study gives a window on how learning starts in the infant brain.
plos-pone-0004012:
Yufeng Shen, Sumeet Sarin, Ye Liu, and co-authors compared genome sequencing machines in worms in 2008. Whole-genome sequencing promises a shortcut to finding mutations. It could replace slow genetic mapping for mutant hunts. The roundworm C. elegans is a classic model for such work.

Their PLOS ONE article tests two leading high-throughput platforms head to head. Both were used to find chemically induced mutations in worms. Knowing each platform's strengths helps labs pick the right tool. Faster mutant finding speeds gene function studies across biology. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004112:
Peter Vogel, Michael S. Donoviel, Robert Read, and co-authors partially blocked a lipid enzyme in mice in 2009. S1P is a fat signal that modulates many body processes. Its levels must be tightly regulated inside and outside cells. The enzyme S1PL destroys S1P in the final breakdown step.

Their PLOS ONE article reports incomplete S1PL inhibition reshapes immune function. Partial blocking avoided the early death and organ lesions of full loss. That window matters for drugs that target this enzyme. It suggests immune benefits may come without the worst side effects. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004212:
Sumiyo Morita and colleagues published this pancreas study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dicer1 is an essential part of the microRNA pathway, the system of tiny RNAs that fine-tune gene activity. Mice lacking Dicer1 die early in embryonic life, so its role in adult tissues could not be studied with ordinary knockouts.

Using a targeted approach, the team removed Dicer1 in the adult pancreas. They report that Dicer is required for maintaining the adult pancreas. The result shows that microRNAs are not just building instructions for embryos but upkeep instructions for grown organs. The pancreas makes both insulin and digestive juices.
plos-pone-0004312:
Namasivayam Ambalavanan and colleagues published this pilot trial in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inhaled nitric oxide is a proven treatment for pulmonary hypertension in newborns, usually given through a ventilator. The team's earlier animal work showed that nitric oxide given by a simple oxygen hood reduces pulmonary hypertension.

Here they tested the feasibility of that hood delivery in human neonates with an elevated alveolar-arterial difference, a sign of poor oxygen transfer. A hood that works would bring the treatment to babies who are not on ventilators. The pilot checks safety and practicality before any larger trial.
plos-pone-0004412:
A common diabetes measure may misstate future risk. Marcus Lind, Anders Odén, Martin Fahlén, and co-authors test HbA1c in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. The updated mean HbA1c is used in risk estimates for diabetic complications.

That mean ignores the temporal relationship between HbA1c and complications. The authors used simulations of HbA1c variables to ask whether the updated mean underestimates risk. Timing of high values may matter beyond the average. Their work helps clinicians judge what a patient's history really predicts. Simulations let the authors vary histories that real patient records rarely capture fully.
plos-pone-0004512:
Friendly bacteria protected the gut wall in rats with inflamed pancreases, report Femke Lutgendorff, Rian Nijmeijer, Per Sandstrom, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Acute pancreatitis is a sudden, severe inflammation of the pancreas. During an attack, oxidative stress helps break down the intestinal barrier, letting gut contents leak where they should not.

The team gave multi-species probiotics to rats with the condition and studied the ileum, part of the small intestine. The probiotics prevented barrier failure, in part by inducing the gut lining to make more glutathione, a natural antioxidant. Dozens of rats were split into groups for comparison. If the effect holds in people, probiotics could become a simple support therapy in a dangerous illness.
plos-pone-0004612:
The walking motor protein kinesin keeps its two feet in step by a precise coupling, dissect Sarah Adio, Johann Jaud, Bettina Ebbing, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kinesins are motor proteins that move stepwise along microtubules, the cell's rail tracks, hauling cargo. Processivity, taking many steps without falling off, requires the catalytic steps in the two heads to be coupled exactly.

The team shows that these functions, chemical coupling and mechanical coordination, can be separated. In other words, the motor's grip timing and its power strokes are distinct mechanisms that can be studied apart. Pulling a machine apart conceptually, without breaking it, is how engineers and biologists alike learn how it works. The findings refine models of all walking motors.
plos-pone-0004712:
Vanessa Delfosse and colleagues reported the first shape of a new self enclosed protease from archaea, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some proteases hide their cutting site inside a closed chamber. Only proteins that enter the chamber get cut, which keeps the cell safe from stray cutting.

The archaeal protein forms a cube shaped ring of eight parts. Its shape starts a new family in this class of enzymes. Knowing the shape helps explain how the chamber opens and picks its targets. It also adds a piece to the story of protein cleanup in early life forms. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004812:
Phuong Mai and colleagues studied potential excess mortality in BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carriers beyond known cancers, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Increased risk of breast, ovarian, and prostate cancer in carriers has been studied extensively. Its impact on mortality is not well quantified. Possible effects on non cancer mortality risk have not been examined in large carrier families before this analysis.

The team asked whether carriers die earlier from other causes. Answering that shapes counseling and screening advice. Carriers need clear total risk pictures. The study expands outcomes beyond cancer incidence alone. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here.
plos-pone-0004912:
Fiona Lovegrove and colleagues showed serum angiopoietin levels discriminate cerebral malaria and predict outcome in African children, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Limited tools find which people infected with Plasmodium falciparum risk serious complications such as cerebral malaria. The objective was to assess serum biomarkers differentiating cerebral from uncomplicated malaria, with long term goals of triage, and Targeted care in resource limited hospitals where many children present with fever.

Angiopoietins reflect blood vessel dysfunction central to disease. Bedside prediction could save lives quickly. Biomarkers beat medical signs alone in accuracy. Malaria triage needs such tools. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0005012:
The social amoeba Dictyostelium lives alone, then teams up into a slug. A protein called CbfA regulates its genes in both phases. Jörg Lucas and colleagues dissected that protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. CbfA has several domains and belongs to a family of gene regulators. They tested its carboxy-terminal domain on its own.

That tail domain works as an independent gene regulatory entity. It does not need the rest of the protein. One protein's job splits into separate modules. The finding matters for understanding how regulator proteins evolve. Dictyostelium is a favorite model for such questions. Its switch from solo life to teamwork makes gene control especially interesting.
plos-pone-0005112:
Mitochondrial DNA passes from mother to child. One lineage, macro-haplogroup R0, dominates West Eurasia. Its best-known branch, haplogroup H, covers about forty percent of people there. Vanesa Álvarez-Iglesias and colleagues refined R0's family tree in PLOS ONE in 2009. R0's sub-lineages were badly defined in the control region. Coding-region markers offered sharper resolution.

The study reports new population and phylogenetic features. R0's internal variation is now better resolved. Ancestry researchers gain a clearer maternal map. Finer branches mean more precise origin stories. The work serves population genetics and genealogy alike. It shows why whole coding regions matter. Control-region data alone blur the tree's finer twigs.
plos-pone-0005212:
Making proteins with errors is usually harmful, since faulty proteins can kill cells and damage nerves. Yet yeast has a longevity gene, PNC1, that responds to stress. Silva and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that protein-making errors switch that gene on.

When messenger RNA is mistranslated, more faulty proteins appear and the cell senses trouble. That alarm raised PNC1 activity in their tests. A gene tied to longer life answering to errors is a surprise, and it hints that mild stress signals can prime cells to protect themselves.
plos-pone-0005312:
Babies born to HIV-positive mothers carry their mothers' antibodies for up to eighteen months. A positive antibody test therefore cannot prove the baby is infected. Peltier and colleagues checked the World Health Organization's 2006 prediction scores for this problem in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Where PCR testing is unavailable, the WHO suggested clinical criteria for starting treatment. The study validated those scores in children under eighteen months with positive serological tests. A validated score lets clinics act on time instead of waiting for tests they do not have. In towns where the lab is a day's walk away, that gap matters most. A score card a nurse can use at the bedside can mean care in time, not care too late.
plos-pone-0005412:
Borrelia burgdorferi, the Lyme disease bacterium, grips host tissues with surface proteins that bind fibronectin, a matrix protein. One such protein, BBK32, is a known virulence factor. Prabhakaran and colleagues found a new binding motif in these proteins in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The novel fibronectin binding motif targets the F3 modules of fibronectin. These grip proteins belong to a family called MSCRAMMs, surface components that recognize adhesive matrix molecules. Knowing the exact grip could let drugs or vaccines block the bacterium's hold. A tick bite is small and the rash can be missed, so a drug or shot that keeps the germ from its first grip could guard hikers. Dogs, and farm hands in the wide woods of the north.
plos-pone-0005512:
Andre Kalil and co-authors reviewed a drug used after organ transplants in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. A virus called CMV can cause serious illness in transplant patients whose defences are lowered by drugs. Valganciclovir is the drug most often used to prevent it, and also the most costly option.

The authors gathered the trial evidence on how well the drug works and how safe it is. A clear summary helps transplant teams weigh benefit, harm, and cost. It also shows where cheaper options might serve patients just as well. Prevention also spares patients the illness and extra hospital time that a CMV infection would bring.
plos-pone-0005612:
Damon Ellison and co-authors studied a tick-borne germ's response to its surroundings in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Rickettsia bacteria live only inside other cells and cycle between ticks and mammals. Germs that move between hosts usually reshape their gene activity for each place.

The team exposed the germ to changes meant to mimic host shifts and read its gene activity. The responses were surprisingly limited, as the title reports. A germ that barely adjusts may rely on a fixed toolkit, which shapes how vaccines and drugs should target it. A fixed toolkit may also mean fewer surprises when the germ meets new drugs or vaccines.
plos-pone-0005712:
Simon Donner projected in 2009 how much heat stress coral reefs will face under different climate paths. Warm spells in the ocean bleach corals, killing the algae they depend on. Past work warned that human-driven warming will make such spells far more common.

Donner tested what happens if nations keep the pledges they have made, and under other futures. The spread of outcomes shows how much choices today matter for reefs. Even strong cuts may not spare all reefs, but they change the odds. The study gives reef planners a clear view of the stakes.
plos-pone-0005812:
Pudota Bhaskar and co-authors gave potato researchers a fast gene-testing tool in 2009. Potato is the world's third most important food crop, yet its genetics lag behind other staples. Its genome is doubled and highly mixed, which slows classic studies.

Their method uses Agrobacterium bacteria to deliver genes into potato tissue for quick, temporary tests. Genes can be switched on or silenced within days rather than seasons. Fast assays let breeders screen candidate genes for blight resistance and quality traits. The paper details the setup so other labs can adopt it directly.
plos-pone-0005912:
Xiangming Wang and co-authors studied in 2009 what a spindle checkpoint gene does across the whole life of a worm. The gene bub-1 was first found in yeast, where its faults let cells divide despite lost microtubules. Its broader developmental roles were only partly known.

In C. elegans, the team traced bub-1's function beyond the checkpoint itself. Worms offer a full life cycle in days, so effects from embryo to adult can be watched. A checkpoint gene moonlighting in development would link division control to body building. That link interests both cancer and developmental biology.
plos-pone-0006012:
Sex costs a species twice over, since males make no young themselves. Alexander Feigel, Avraham Englander and Assaf Engel asked in 2009 why that cost is worth paying. Their PLOS ONE paper weighs the classic puzzle of sex against its gains: wider variety among offspring, which improves defense against parasites, shifting surroundings and harmful mutations.

Their answer, stated in the title, is that sex is always well worth its twofold cost. A model that reaches so firm a verdict gives the long debate a clear claim to test. The work speaks to one of evolution's oldest questions: why nearly all complex life pays for sex when cloning looks cheaper.
plos-pone-0006112:
Type 2 diabetes care climbs a ladder, from diet to pills to insulin. Christine Clar, Pamela Royle and Norman Waugh reviewed one rung of that ladder in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper is a systematic review and meta-analysis of adding pioglitazone, an oral agent licensed for use with insulin when metformin cannot be taken, to insulin-containing regimens.

Pooling every sound trial gives a fairer answer than any single study can. Prescribers need that pooled view, since the combination is common and its gains and harms must be weighed together. The review stands as a reference for diabetes guidelines, the kind of summary that busy clinics actually act on.
plos-pone-0006212:
Kidney transplants can fail slowly through chronic damage called chronic allograft nephropathy. Sunil Kurian and colleagues hunted for warning signs in blood in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Surgery and anti-rejection drugs have improved, yet this slow failure remains a major problem for transplant patients.

The team combined protein and gene profiling of peripheral blood to find markers of early and late stages. A blood test that flags damage early could spare patients invasive biopsies. It could also let doctors adjust treatment before the graft is badly hurt. The study maps marker candidates for later, larger checks.
plos-pone-0006312:
Transplanting insulin-making islet cells across species usually fails as inflammation destroys the graft. Chunguang Chen and colleagues tested thalidomide in such a xenogenic transplant model in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The drug is known for both anti-inflammatory and anti-vessel-growth properties.

Thalidomide improved the survival and function of the islet grafts in mice, per the title. Calming inflammation around foreign tissue can outweigh the drug's other effects. Islet transplantation is a hoped-for cure for some diabetes patients. Repurposed drugs that protect grafts could widen its use.
plos-pone-0006412:
Immune cells inside ovarian tumors can signal better survival, but their functional status was poorly understood. Katy Milne and colleagues systematically analysed immune infiltrates in high-grade serous ovarian cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Tissue microarrays covered this subtype alongside other epithelial ovarian cancer types and risk categories.

CD20, FoxP3, and TIA-1 emerged as positive prognostic factors, per the title. Those markers identify immune patterns tied to longer survival. Prognostic immune signs can guide treatment intensity and trial design. The study strengthens the case for immunotherapy research in ovarian cancer.
plos-pone-0006512:
Emma Nickerson and co-authors studied severe staph infections in a developing country setting for PLOS ONE in 2009. Invasive Staphylococcus aureus infection is increasingly recognized as an important cause of serious sepsis across the developing world. Mortality rates there are higher than in wealthy countries. The team examined factors predicting death in patients with this disease.

They also looked at factors that reduce mortality. Knowing who is most at risk helps hospitals triage scarce resources. Simple changes with proven benefit can save lives where intensive care is limited. The study gives local evidence rather than importing conclusions from richer health systems.
plos-pone-0006612:
Indrani Rajan and co-authors studied a brain enzyme's partial loss in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Histone deacetylase 4, HDAC4, has been associated with muscle and bone development. Its N-terminal domains bind the MEF2 and RUNX2 transcription factors. The team examined loss of the putative catalytic domain of HDAC4.

Their title reports reduced thermal nociception and seizures, while other functions are allowed. In plain terms, mice feel heat pain less and show seizures when only part of the protein is lost. Separating the protein's jobs helps explain the human syndromes linked to it. It also cautions drug developers targeting HDAC enzymes.
plos-pone-0006712:
Edyta Pawelczyk and colleagues tracked labeled transplanted cells inside living tissue in PLOS ONE in 2009. Researchers often load cells with visible labels before transplanting them. Labels include iron oxide particles, chemical tags, and green fluorescent protein. Imaging then follows where the transplanted cells go. The team used labels carried inside bone marrow stromal cells.

They implanted the labeled stromal cells locally in tissue. Later, the labels appeared inside resident tissue macrophages instead. The cells' own labels had transferred to the host's scavenger cells. That transfer can fool researchers into misreading cell survival. The finding is a caution for imaging studies of cell therapy everywhere.
plos-pone-0006812:
Natalia Scaglia, Jeffrey W. Chisholm, and R. Ariel Igal blocked a fat-making enzyme in cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer cells ramp up production of fatty acids. New membranes are needed for rapid cell replication. The enzyme studied is stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1. Earlier knockdown work had shown its importance to cancer cells.

Inhibiting the enzyme inactivated acetyl-CoA carboxylase, another fat-pathway enzyme. Proliferation of the cancer cells was impaired. A protein called AMPK played a role in the shutdown. AMPK acts as a cellular fuel gauge. Linking fat synthesis to that gauge reveals a vulnerability in cancer metabolism worth exploiting.
plos-pone-0006912:
Chen Song and Haishan Yao studied what happens when the two eyes see different images in PLOS ONE in 2009. Perception is usually stable and accurate. Conflicting eye inputs produce binocular rivalry instead. Perception alternates spontaneously between the two images every few seconds. Neither image wins permanently.

The authors found a duality in how rivalry responds to imbalance. Percept sequence and percept duration reacted with distinct sensitivities. One measure changed while the other held steady. That split shows rivalry is not a single simple process. Separate mechanisms may control switching order and switching speed. The result sharpens models of how consciousness selects between competing inputs.
plos-pone-0007012:
Pooneh Mokarram, Krishan Kumar, Hassan Brim, and colleagues searched for colon cancer marks in PLOS ONE in 2009. Colorectal cancer advances through gene mutations and through methylation that silences genes. A known set of candidate cancer genes offered a place to look. The team suspected these genes are shut off by epigenetic silencing in tumors.

They profiled methylation across those candidate genes. The pattern differed in high-risk patient groups, forming a distinct high-profile set. Methylation marks can appear early and can be shed into stool or blood. Distinct profiles could support earlier, less invasive screening for colorectal cancer.
plos-pone-0007112:
Alex Bullock, Santina Russo, Ann Amos, and colleagues solved a cancer drug target's shape in PLOS ONE in 2009. PIM2 is a kinase found at high levels in leukemias and lymphomas. It helps tumor cells survive and multiply. Its varied ATP site makes it a promising but tricky drug target. Structural knowledge of it was thin.

The team crystallized PIM2 bound to an organoruthenium inhibitor. The structure shows exactly how the metal-based compound fits. That fit guides chemists toward stronger, more selective drugs. It also proves unusual metal compounds can be shaped for kinase pockets.
plos-pone-0007212:
Alejandra Rodriguez, Tiina Luukkaala, Robert E. Fleming, and colleagues mapped gene activity in iron overload in 2009. Iron is essential, but the gut normally controls its absorption tightly. In hereditary hemochromatosis, low levels of the hormone hepcidin let too much iron enter the body.

The authors study mice lacking a working Hfe gene, plus mice fed extra iron. They measure gene responses across the whole liver and duodenum. Their PLOS ONE paper compares genetic deficiency with dietary overload. The comparison helps separate effects of the gene defect from effects of iron itself.
plos-pone-0007312:
Henry T. Robertson and David B. Allison asked whether suicidal thoughts predict suicide attempts across drugs in 2009. In randomized trials, some drugs raised suicidal ideation, meaning thoughts of suicide. Obesity drugs that block CB1 receptors were one example that drew regulatory concern and public attention at the time.

A key question was whether more ideation also means more attempts. The authors compare drugs on both measures. They report that drugs associated with more suicidal ideations are also associated with more suicide attempts. Their PLOS ONE finding supports using ideation as a warning signal in drug safety reviews.
plos-pone-0007412:
Toshiyuki Hayakawa, Nobuko Arisue, Toshifumi Udono, and colleagues identified a human malaria parasite in chimpanzees in 2009. Human malaria parasites were widely believed to infect only humans as natural hosts. Earlier microscope observations suggested great apes might also be natural reservoirs, which would complicate malaria eradication efforts in Africa.

The authors screen sixty imported chimpanzees for malaria parasites. They identify Plasmodium malariae, a human malaria species, in the apes. Their PLOS ONE result is reported as an identification in imported chimpanzees. Evidence of ape reservoirs changes how scientists think about malaria's natural history.
plos-pone-0007512:
Julián Pardo and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how the immune system controls mousepox. Ectromelia virus causes that disease, a natural and often deadly mouse infection. Killer T cells release a weapon called granzyme B, which is known to matter for control. How it stops the virus was the open question. The team traced the chain using immune cells taken from infected animals.

Granzyme B works by triggering the caspase pathway, the controlled self-destruction program inside infected cells. That self-destruction, in turn, chokes off virus replication. So the kill chain runs from immune attack, through the cell's own death machinery, to virus shutdown. Tracing it exactly matters for understanding poxvirus infections generally. Mousepox is a close model for smallpox, which gives the finding added weight.
plos-pone-0007612:
Longjiang Fan and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on what changed in maize genes after the crop was first tamed. Taming was only the first round of choice. Farmers kept picking better plants for years after, a phase scholars call post-domestication selection. Chinese waxy maize is a clean case: it arose from plain tamed corn and is prized for its sticky starch. The team traced signs of that later choice along the genes that make starch.

Gene marks show the starch path was reshaped well after taming. Breeders picking for texture were, without knowing it, picking gene forms too. Reading those marks shows how long use rewrites a crop's inner chemistry. The waxy trait is a human taste made plain in DNA. Work like this rebuilds the second, quieter half of a crop's past. It also shows breeders which starch genes still hold untapped range.
plos-pone-0007712:
Nazzareno D'Avanzo and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares two channel families that sit in cell membranes. Potassium channels select their ion with great precision. Their cousins, HCN channels, look similar in build but are far less picky.

A short stretch of the pore, called the P-loop, helps set that precision. The authors moved key P-loop parts into a rabbit HCN channel, HCN4. The swap failed to make HCN4 selective. That negative result is useful: selectivity must depend on more of the channel's structure than the filter alone.
plos-pone-0007812:
Jean Lud Cadet and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines how prior small doses of methamphetamine change the rat brain's response. Methamphetamine is an illegal drug that is toxic to the brain. Repeated large doses cut dopamine and serotonin levels sharply.

Earlier exposure can precondition the brain, changing later reactions. The authors measured gene activity in the midbrain after injurious doses. They compared preconditioned rats with naive ones in their striatum responses. The transcriptional patterns differed between the groups. The work may help explain why drug history shapes brain damage.
plos-pone-0007912:
Eliana Marengo and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a leprosy protein in a mouse model of eye inflammation. Heat shock proteins are abundant in chronic inflammation and autoimmune disease. The model, experimental autoimmune uveitis, is driven by T cells inside the eye.

The team gave mice rHsp65, a heat shock protein from Mycobacterium leprae. Instead of calming the disease, the protein aggravated it. The result warns that such proteins can fan autoimmunity, not just soothe it. It bears on trials that use heat shock proteins as therapy. Dose and context decide friend from foe.
plos-pone-0008012:
Nicolas Guex and colleagues won a prediction contest with a gap-filling trick, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. The contest, DREAM3, hands teams fresh data on protein networks and scores how well they rebuild the network. Real data always have holes where measures failed.

Instead of discarding rows with holes, the team filled each gap many times over with sound guesses and pooled the results. That care with missing values beat fancier models. The lesson travels well: in messy biology data, how you treat the holes can matter more than the model you fit.
plos-pone-0008112:
Sharon Bewick and colleagues put forward a danger-based account of immune firing in PLOS ONE in 2009. The immune system must strike fast and hard at invaders, yet spare the body it guards. Old accounts leaned on the split between self and foreign; this one leans on signs of damage.

In their model, growing danger signals, not mere foreignness, set the size of the response. Tissue harm thus calls the tune, which fits cases the older account strains to explain. The paper is a theory piece, meant to be tested, and it reframes how tolerance might be taught.
plos-pone-0008212:
Gijs Kooij and colleagues studied a transport protein in multiple sclerosis in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Multiple sclerosis is an inflammatory disease that damages the protective coating of nerves. Rogue T cells that attack myelin cause much of that damage. These cells are first primed outside the brain by antigen-presenting cells. The team focused on P-glycoprotein in that process.

P-glycoprotein is better known for pumping drugs out of cells. Here it acted as a modulator of immune activity during neuroinflammation. That role could change how the disease unfolds. It might also matter when patients take drugs this pump handles.
plos-pone-0008312:
Lukasz Kozera, Ed White, and Sarah Calaghan studied heart cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Many ion channels sit in caveolae, tiny pockets in the cell membrane. There, scaffolding partners regulate channel activity. Mechanosensitive channels may also depend on the membrane's mechanical state. The team studied a swelling-activated chloride channel in rat heart cells.

They found caveolae act as membrane reserves during swelling. Extra membrane unfolds from the pockets, limiting channel activation. That mechanism protects heart cells when they swell under stress. It links membrane structure to electrical stability in the heart.
plos-pone-0008412:
Xiaoxi Li, Yixin Xu, and Ling Ma studied sex hormones and immune cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Gender differences in immune capability suggest sex hormones regulate immune competence. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are thought to play a pathogenic role in lupus, or SLE. Whether estradiol affects these cells was unclear. The team tested 17 beta-estradiol on their response to CpG, an immune stimulant.

Estradiol enhanced the response of plasmacytoid dendritic cells to CpG. Stronger responses from these cells could help explain why lupus is far more common in women. The finding links a hormone directly to a suspect cell type.
plos-pone-0008512:
Tracy Richmond and co-authors ask why asthma rates vary by school in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Childhood asthma prevalence and severity vary by neighborhood. Less is known about variation between schools. A school's rate may just reflect which students attend it. Higher-risk students may simply cluster in certain schools. Or the school setting itself may add risk. The team separate those two explanations.

They test if between-school variation persists after accounting for student mix. Compositional effects come from the students themselves. Contextual effects come from the school environment. Knowing which dominates guides where to intervene: at enrollment patterns or at school conditions.
plos-pone-0008612:
Ramin Farzaneh-Far and co-authors track telomere length over time in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Leukocyte telomere length is an emerging marker of biological age. It predicts cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in prior studies. However, its natural history in coronary artery disease was unstudied. The team use the Heart and Soul Study, a cohort of such patients. They measure telomeres longitudinally and seek its determinants.

They chart the trajectory of telomere shortening in these patients. Certain factors predict faster shortening over the follow-up. A trajectory view is more informative than a single measure. It may refine how telomeres are used to forecast heart disease outcomes.
plos-pone-0008712:
Meka Aruna, Theeya Nagaraja, Sadaranga Andal, and colleagues checked a hormone gene in women with repeated miscarriages. Their Indian case study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Progesterone helps hold a pregnancy in place. Its receptor reads the hormone signal inside cells. Small variants in the receptor gene might weaken that reading.

The team compared variant patterns in women with recurrent losses and in controls. They focused on three linked single-letter changes plus one inserted segment. Any link would mark a useful risk clue for doctors. Genetic clues like this may someday guide closer care in early pregnancy.
plos-pone-0008812:
Martin Allgaier, Amitha Reddy, Joshua Park, and colleagues hunted plant-fiber enzymes in compost. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Biofuels from crop waste need enzymes that chew tough plant walls. Compost microbes already do that job in nature. The team adapted a compost community to switchgrass, a biofuel crop. Adapted microbes should carry enzymes tuned to that feedstock.

Targeted gene hunting in the adapted community found new glycoside hydrolases. Those enzymes snip the sugars that lock plant walls together. Matching enzymes to feedstock could cut biofuel costs. The compost heap becomes a prospecting site for industry.
plos-pone-0008912:
Christina Hutson, Jason Abel, Darin Carroll, and colleagues matched two monkeypox virus strains against two mouse strains. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Monkeypox viruses from West Africa cause milder disease than Congo Basin ones. Most past work used wild rodents or primates, which are hard to standardize. Common lab mice offered a controlled comparison. BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice differ in immune style, adding a second axis.

Disease severity separated by both virus origin and mouse strain. The mouse system reproduced the known strain difference. A tractable model lets researchers test virulence factors one by one. It also suits trials of vaccines and treatments for monkeypox.
plos-pone-0009012:
Dina Dechmann and co-authors wondered whether hunting together explains why some bats live in groups, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many bat species roost socially, some in highly organised colonies. The benefits of bat social life are still debated. One idea: bats share news about short-lived swarms of insects.

The study followed molossid bats, fast fliers that chase insects on the wing. If group hunting paid, bats could find patchy food faster by following roostmates. The team tested whether their foraging matched that prediction. Answering this helps explain social life in a whole order of mammals.
plos-pone-0009112:
Ping Yuan and co-authors argued that a stem cell gene marks the birth line of one lung cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Non-small cell lung cancers make up about 85 percent of lung tumours. The two main kinds are adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. They grow through different early stages in the airways.

SOX2, a gene that keeps stem cells in their youthful state, ran high in squamous tumours. Its pattern followed the cells these tumours descend from. A lineage gene left switched on may drive the cancer's growth. That makes SOX2 both a signpost and a possible drug target.
plos-pone-0009212:
Bonnie Joubert and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It draws on research in Malawi on how HIV passes from mother to child. A cell-surface protein called CCR5 helps HIV enter cells. Gene variants that lower CCR5 were linked to lower transmission, but the link to actual levels in the body was murky.

The team studied how CCR5 levels are controlled in the placenta, the organ linking mother and baby. They connected gene variants to the amount of CCR5 the placenta actually makes. That in-body check matters because the placenta is where much transmission risk is decided. The findings clarify one route by which genes may protect babies from infection.
plos-pone-0009312:
Pengxiu Cao and co-authors published this worm study of Parkinson's disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. In Parkinson's, the neurons that make dopamine die off first. One suspect is alpha-synuclein, a protein that builds up in those neurons. Messing up dopamine balance may itself help kill the cells.

The team put human alpha-synuclein into the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. The worms' dopamine neurons degenerated, as in the human disease. The work ties the protein to broken dopamine handling in a simple animal. Worms like these give researchers a fast way to test what protects the vulnerable neurons.
plos-pone-0009412:
Theetha Pavankumar, Anurag Sinha, and Malay Ray published this Antarctic bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pseudomonas syringae strain Lz4W lives in the cold of Antarctica. Its RecBCD enzyme repairs broken DNA through recombination. One part, RecD, when missing, left the bacteria sensitive to DNA damage and unable to grow at four degrees.

The team tested all three parts of the enzyme. Each subunit proved essential, both for DNA repair and for growth in the cold. Repair machinery that doubles as cold survival gear shows how extreme life links the two jobs. The finding helps explain how microbes persist where damage is constant and warmth is absent.
plos-pone-0009512:
Benjamin Cohn and co-authors studied a diarrhea causing parasite in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cryptosporidium parvum spreads as a tough cyst. Once swallowed, it wakes and infects the gut, a step called excystation. During waking, its heat shock genes switch on. Those genes help it cope with sudden change. The team hunted for DNA elements that control that switch.

They found candidate control elements near the heat shock genes. Such elements are where the cell's machinery starts reading a gene. Knowing them shows how the parasite times its waking. That moment may be its weakest point, so the elements could serve as targets for new treatments.
plos-pone-0009612:
Andreas Wilting and co-authors mapped the range of a rare wild cat in PLOS ONE in 2010. The flat headed cat lives in Southeast Asia and is classed as endangered. It is small, secretive, and seldom seen. Records of where it occurs are scattered. The team built a species distribution model from known records and habitat data.

The model shows where the cat can still plausibly live. It also shows where its habitat has been lost or broken up. Such maps guide surveys to the most promising ground. They also tell planners which wetlands and forests matter most if this little known cat is to survive.
plos-pone-0009712:
Cell lines grown from human breast cancers are workhorses of cancer research. Qingbei Zhang and colleagues checked which identity markers those cells carry. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Markers are proteins that reveal what kind of cell a cell resembles.

The lines carried markers of nerve cells, skin-like epithelial cells, and pigment cells at once. The mixed pattern showed in dishes and in living tissue alike. Such mixed identity challenges simple ideas of what a breast tumor cell is. It also warns researchers to read cell line results with care.
plos-pone-0009812:
H5N1 bird flu worries health officials because it can kill people it infects. Srinivas Rao and colleagues compared three gene-based vaccine designs against it in animals. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ferrets are a standard stand-in for people in flu research.

Each vaccine carried a different flu protein gene: hemagglutinin, nucleoprotein, or matrix 2. The team tested how well each protected mice and ferrets. Comparing the three head to head shows which targets work best. Results like these guide vaccine design before human trials. Mice and ferrets often give different answers, so both were used.
plos-pone-0009912:
Resistin is a hormone linked to insulin resistance, and its gene answers to several controllers. Anil Singh and colleagues traced one control meeting point for the human resistin gene. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Transcription is the copying of a gene into RNA, the first step of using it. The work shows transcription involves an interaction of Sp1 with PPAR-gamma. Both are proteins that bind DNA and tune gene activity. PPAR-gamma is also the target of some diabetes drugs. Mapping that meeting clarifies how resistin output is set.
plos-pone-0010112:
The authors were Eva Jimenez-Guri, Frederic Udina, Jean-François Colas, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study traced cell lineages in the mouse hindbrain. The hindbrain forms in segments called rhombomeres, with sharp boundaries between them. Boundaries stop cells from wandering, so each segment keeps its identity and follows its own path.

By marking clones of cells and following their spread, the team tested how strong that restriction is. Their results underline the importance of rhombomeric boundaries during segmentation. The work helps explain how the early brain builds orderly regions without constant signals from neighbors.
plos-pone-0010212:
The authors were Anastasia Rozhdestvenskaya, Artem Totolian, and Alexander Dmitriev. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study worked on Streptococcus agalactiae, a bacterium that colonizes many tissues. Such bacteria use two-component systems to sense their surroundings and switch genes on or off. Those systems control virulence genes, the tools a germ uses to cause disease in its host.

The team switched off a response regulator called Sak189 in this species. Doing so stopped production of the beta-antigen and changed the bacterium's virulence. The result names one control point a future drug might attack.
plos-pone-0010312:
The authors were Jun Hou, Joachim Aerts, Bianca den Hamer, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study classified lung cancers by gene activity rather than appearance. Non-small cell lung cancer treatment still depends on how tumors look under a microscope. That histology approach poorly predicts each patient's outcome, leaving many patients on standard therapy that may not fit their tumor's biology.

Gene expression profiling promised better clinical stratification of these cancers. The team built a classification from expression data and tested survival prediction. Sharper classes could pave the way for individualized lung cancer treatment choices.
plos-pone-0010412:
Marit Kramski and co-workers built a primate model for poxvirus infection, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2010. Smallpox was wiped out, but its virus could in theory be released on purpose. Related poxviruses from animals also sicken people, sometimes severely. Testing vaccines and drugs needs an animal model that behaves predictably. The team sought a model that was both reliable and lethal, to mirror grave disease.

A model that gives the same result every time is vital for fair drug tests. Their primate system was designed for that consistency. Such work supports biodefense planning without waiting for a real outbreak. It also helps with natural pox threats like monkeypox. Preparedness research, this study argues, needs models ready before they are needed.
plos-pone-0010512:
Görel Sundström and co-workers dated the copying of pain and reward genes in PLOS ONE in 2010. The copies arose before jawed vertebrates appeared. Opioids govern pain relief and reward in the brain. In mammals the system uses four receptors and several peptide signals. Those signals come from four precursor genes. The team traced when those genes were duplicated during evolution.

The duplications happened together, before jaws evolved in vertebrates. That timing ties the opioid system's birth to a major genome event in early vertebrates. An ancient origin explains why the system is so deeply built into brain function. It also guides comparisons with jawless fish alive today. Evolution here illuminates why pain and reward share machinery.
plos-pone-0010612:
Raphael Bueno and colleagues read the full genome of a mesothelioma tumor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mesothelioma is a cancer of the lining around the lungs, often tied to asbestos. Older studies checked only a few genes at a time.

New sequencing machines let the team scan the tumor genome far more broadly. They catalogued its mutations and structural changes in detail. Some changes pointed to pathways that existing or future drugs might block. A wide genome view gives future studies a fuller list of suspects than gene-by-gene work ever could.
plos-pone-0010712:
Megan Landsverk and colleagues charted message variants of a cell-division gene family in zebrafish, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Septins help cells divide and keep their shape. In people, changed levels of one family member, SEPT9, appear in several cancers, and gene faults cause a nerve disorder.
