General Assembly Resolution 112, adopted on 14 November 1947, dealt with the future of Korea after the end of Japanese rule. The Assembly held that Korea's freedom was a matter for the Korean people. It held that elected Korean voices had to take part. It also held that national independence should be restored and occupying forces withdrawn, as soon as could be done.

The text created a United Nations Temporary Commission on Korea. It was made up of nine named states. It was to travel and observe across the country. The text called for elections by adult vote and secret ballot, no later than 31 March 1948. It also called for a National Assembly. A National Government was to take over from the military commands.

General Assembly Resolution 12, adopted on 1 February 1946 at the twenty-first plenary meeting, dealt with the temporary staff who had served under the Executive Secretary. They had served while the United Nations was being set up. The Assembly praised their able and faithful work. It let the Secretary-General keep them on under their current terms until 1 April 1946. He could keep them until that date, or until he made new arrangements with them under the provisional staff regulations.

General Assembly Resolution 2012 (XX), adopted on 12 October 1965, answered threats by the authorities in Southern Rhodesia to declare independence on their own. The Assembly noted Britain's stand that such a step would be rebellion, and that any act to carry it out would be treason.

The text condemned any bid to seize independence by unlawful means in order to keep minority rule. It said such rule clashed with equal rights and self-rule under the Charter. All states were asked not to accept or recognize any such declaration. Britain was called on to stop it. If it came, Britain was to end the rebellion and hand power to a government of the majority.

Resolution 712 (VII), approved by the General Assembly on 28 August 1953, marks the armistice that had just halted the fighting in Korea. The Assembly salutes the soldiers of the Republic of Korea and of the countries that fought under the United Nations Command. It pays tribute to those who died. It also records its satisfaction that collective action under the Charter had, for the first time, successfully repelled armed aggression. That was the principle on which the United Nations had intervened.

Adopted at the sixty-ninth session, Resolution 69/12 of the General Assembly records and encourages cooperation between the United Nations and the Collective Security Treaty Organization. The Assembly notes the organization's practical work on regional security and counter-terrorism. It notes its 'Kanal' anti-drug operation against Afghan opiates. It notes new cooperation between its secretariat and the United Nations peacekeeping department. It invites regular consultations between the two secretaries-general. It invites continued joint work on the Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy. It invites a report to the seventy-first session.
un-sc-res-12: Four Balkan states were called to speak, without a vote, under Security Council Resolution 12 of 1946. Greece and Yugoslavia are invited to take part in the Council's talks in full. Albania and Bulgaria are invited so the Council can hear such words as they wish to give. If the matter later proves to be a true dispute, the last two will gain the same right to sit in on the talks. The vote is a small step in the Greek border fight that then filled the Council's plate.
un-sc-res-1312: The catalog's entries for 2000 include Resolution 1312 of the United Nations Security Council. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1412:
Angola's long civil war had just ended when the Council met in May 2002. On 17 May 2002 it suspended some sanctions on UNITA for ninety days. The government and UNITA had signed a memorandum on 4 April. That deal closed the military side of the Lusaka peace process. The Council had earlier voiced readiness to ease the measures if peace took hold.

The pause covered the travel limits set in resolution 1127 of 1997. Before the ninety days ran out, the Council would judge the peace process again. Angola's government would supply much of the evidence. The step rewarded a real ceasefire without dropping the sanctions outright.
un-sc-res-1512:
On 27 October 2003, the Council acted on the Rwanda tribunal by adopting Resolution 1512. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda was trying those accused of the 1994 genocide. Its leaders asked for more judges to finish trials faster. The plan was to complete all first-instance trials by the end of 2008.

The text amends the tribunal's statute under Chapter VII. The number of temporary, or ad litem, judges serving at one time rises from four to nine. Those judges also gain the power to handle pre-trial work in cases beyond their own trials. Trial chambers keep sixteen permanent judges, and sections of three judges can hear cases on their own.
un-sc-res-1612:
Children caught in armed conflict gained a watching system on 26 July 2005. The Council restated its child protection texts from 1261 (1999) to 1539 (2004). It noted gains in standards but deplored the lack of progress on the ground. Parties to conflict still broke the law shielding children, and few faced any penalty. The Secretary-General's report of 9 February 2005 proposed a monitoring plan.

The Council strongly condemned the recruitment and use of child soldiers. It told the Secretary-General to put his monitoring and reporting mechanism to work without delay. Its findings would feed his reports and could point the Council toward steps such as sanctions. UNICEF and other United Nations bodies were praised for their field efforts. The Council set up a working group of its members to review reports and recommend action. Governments were reminded that ending impunity for crimes against children was their first duty.
un-sc-res-1712: Resolution 1712, from 2006, is a formal act of the Security Council preserved through a Wikisource transcription of the record. Its opening clauses do the framing work, naming the situation and the principles at stake. Its closing clauses do the deciding. The entry holds the whole arc, which is what gives a resolution its force.
un-sc-res-1812: Adopted in 2008, Resolution 1812 is part of the Security Council's numbered record kept in this collection through English Wikisource. The act follows the standard internal order: matters recalled, facts noted with concern or welcome, steps decided. The preservation of the whole order matters, because the decisions only make sense standing on their stated grounds.
un-sc-res-1912:
A Council decision on Timor-Leste took shape as Resolution 1912, adopted on 26 February 2010. Village elections in October 2009 had gone well. All camps for displaced people had closed. National police were taking back patrol duties step by step. Yet joblessness and poverty stayed high across the country.

The text extends the United Nations Integrated Mission in Timor-Leste, called UNMIT, until 26 February 2011. Its police wing will shrink in step with the handover to national police. The mission keeps training police, judges, and lawyers. It will back town elections if the government asks. Reports are due in October 2010 and January 2011, the last with ideas for the mission's size and shape.
un-sc-res-2012:
Haiti drew a formal Council decision in Resolution 2012, adopted on 14 October 2011. Security had improved, though it stayed fragile, since the great earthquake of January 2010. Power had just passed peacefully between elected presidents for the first time. Forming a government, though, was stuck in a standoff between president and parliament.

The Council extends the stabilization mission, called MINUSTAH, until 15 October 2012. Part of the post-quake surge now goes home. Authorized strength falls to 7,340 troops and 3,241 police. The cut should finish by June 2012. Haitian leaders are urged to end their deadlock and agree a way forward. Police training stays central, so the state can hold security alone in time.
un-sc-res-212:
Security Council Resolution 212, adopted on September 20, 1965, recommended the Maldives for membership in the United Nations. The island chain in the Indian Ocean had gained full independence from Britain less than two months before, on July 26. Its government moved fast to take a place in the world body alongside other new states of the decade.

The Assembly seated the Maldives the next day, making it one of the smallest members of the time. The resolution follows the usual pattern: a finding that the applicant accepts the Charter, then a referral to the Assembly. For a nation of scattered atolls, membership gave a voice far beyond its size.
un-sc-res-312: Acting formally, the Security Council produced the decision numbered 312, catalogued under 1972. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-412: Filed in the official record under number 412, this Council resolution is catalogued with a 2021 date. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-612:
Chemical weapons use in the Iran-Iraq war was condemned by the Security Council on 9 May 1988. A mission sent by the Secretary-General had reported on 25 April 1988. Its findings showed that chemical weapons were still being used in the conflict. Worse, their use had grown more intensive than before, the mission concluded.

The Council affirmed the urgent need to observe the Geneva Protocol of 1925, which bans poison gas and similar weapons in war. It condemned vigorously the continued use of chemical weapons against the duties owed under that protocol. Both sides were told they were expected to refrain from any future use. All states were called to keep or set strict controls on exports to the two belligerents of chemicals that serve to make such weapons. The Council stayed seized of the matter and said it would review how the resolution was applied.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Sudan became independent on the first day of 1956. It shed joint British and Egyptian rule after decades as a condominium. An application for UN membership followed at once. Resolution 112 was adopted unanimously on 6 February 1956. The paperwork was filed as document S/3543.

The Council recommended that the Sudan be admitted. The General Assembly approved that November. Sudan entered during the same large intake as Morocco and Tunisia. Its membership made it one of Africa's earliest UN voices. Civil conflict between north and south already loomed. Even so, this brief resolution marks the peaceful, legal birth of Sudanese statehood inside the postwar system.

Security Council resolution 12, from the Council's first year, is a short procedural decision on the Greek question then before it. It invites the representatives of Greece and Yugoslavia to take part in the discussion without a vote. It invites Albania and Bulgaria to come and make whatever statements they wish. If the Council later finds the matter is a dispute, the Albanian and Bulgarian representatives will also join the discussion without a vote.

Peace between Ethiopia and Eritrea takes its first United Nations step here, on 31 July 2000. The two countries had signed a ceasefire, the Agreement on Cessation of Hostilities, in Algiers on 18 June, with help from the Organization of African Unity. Both governments then asked the United Nations to help carry the deal out.

The Council set up the United Nations Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, starting with up to 100 military observers and civilian support staff, to serve until 31 January 2001. It also cleared mine experts to judge the danger from mines and unexploded shells. The small mission was meant as a bridge to a larger peacekeeping force.

Resolution 1412 is a UN Security Council reward for peace in Angola, adopted unanimously on 17 May 2002 under Chapter VII. Weeks earlier, the government and the UNITA rebel movement had signed a memorandum completing the Lusaka Protocol, ending hostilities after the death of UNITA's leader and decades of civil war.

The resolution suspends for ninety days the travel restrictions imposed on UNITA officials in 1997, so its members can move freely for the peace process, demobilization, and national reconciliation. It stresses that UNITA must cooperate fully with disarming and reintegrating its soldiers. The suspension, later extended and then lifted, marked the sanctions regime's conversion from pressure into an incentive for peace.

The Rwanda tribunal's bench is enlarged by Resolution 1512, adopted on 27 October 2003. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda aimed to finish all first-instance trials by the end of 2008 under its Completion Strategy. Its President had asked for changes to help it get there. Ad litem judges at the time had narrower powers than permanent judges.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council amends articles 11 and 12 quater of the tribunal's Statute, replacing them with annexed texts. The number of ad litem judges who may serve at one time rises to nine. Up to six may sit in each Trial Chamber. Trial Chambers may split into sections of three judges with full powers. Ad litem judges gain the power to handle pre-trial proceedings in cases other than their own trial. They still may not vote for the tribunal President, adopt the rules of procedure, or review indictments.

Resolution 1612, passed on 26 July 2005, builds a watch system for children in war. Five past texts had set the rules to guard children in armed strife. Yet armed groups kept breaking them, the Council said, and paid no price. States bear the chief duty to shield children. They must also bring to court those who commit grave crimes against them.

The new system's heart is a watch and report chain. It tracks six grave wrongs against children in war, from forced service as troops to strikes on schools. A team of the Council's own members sifts the facts. The flow of reports feeds the UN chief's yearly list of armies and armed groups that harm children.

Liberia's mission, UNMIL, is extended on 29 September 2006, and its gradual drawdown is endorsed. Liberia's government was fighting corruption and rebuilding after the civil war, with regional and world support. Hard tasks remained, including reintegrating former fighters, repatriating refugees, and restructuring the security sector in depth.

The mandate is extended, and the Secretary-General's plan for a phased, gradual reduction of the force, tied to benchmarks of stability on the ground, is approved. Progress against those benchmarks is to be closely monitored. Liberia's government is called on to work with UNMIL on security reform and on completing the reintegration of former combatants, so the state can hold its own security as the mission shrinks.

Sudan's mission, UNMIS, is extended until 30 April 2009 on 30 April 2008. The mission supports the 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement between north and south. It had also helped the African Union force in Darfur hand over to the joint UNAMID operation at the start of 2008.

The mission's work and the states supplying its troops are praised. Reports are asked for every three months, and all parties are called on to give UNMIS full, unrestricted cooperation. The parties are urged to settle their open disputes under the peace deal, including borders and oil wealth sharing, by agreement. The mission is also asked, within its mandate and means, to be ready to support the coming referenda preparations.

Timor-Leste's UN mission is extended in Resolution 1912, adopted on 26 February 2010. Village elections in October 2009 had gone well, all displaced-persons camps had closed, national police had resumed primary policing in several districts, and a new Anti-Corruption Commission had its first commissioner. Poverty and unemployment stayed high, and accountability for the 2006 crisis crimes was incomplete.

The Council extends UNMIT until 26 February 2011 at current strength. It backs the phased handover of policing to the PNTL against agreed criteria and endorses reconfiguring and drawing down the UNMIT police component as the handover proceeds. UNMIT must keep supporting security-sector reform — a clear split between the army, F-FDTL, and the police, with civilian oversight — plus justice reform and the 2006 inquiry's prosecutions. A report on mandate adjustments is due by 26 January 2011.

Haiti's mission begins drawing down its earthquake surge in Resolution 2012, adopted on 14 October 2011. Haiti had achieved its first peaceful transfer of power between democratically elected presidents. Security had improved, though gangs and rising crime persisted. Over 600,000 people remained displaced amid a cholera epidemic. The Secretary-General's August 2011 report recommended a drawdown.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MINUSTAH's mandate until 15 October 2012. It sets its strength at up to 7,340 troops and 3,241 police, a first step down from the post-earthquake surge. Future adjustments must rest on conditions on the ground and on growing Haitian state capacity, above all the Haitian National Police under its next five-year development plan. MINUSTAH must support the political process and the legislative and local elections. It must help build rule-of-law institutions and the resettlement of displaced persons and coordinate with the OAS and CARICOM.

A chain of low isles in the Indian Ocean joined the UN in 1965. The Maldive Islands had just left British shelter. They were among the world's least lands by size and folk count. Their bid reached the Council that fall. Resolution 212 passed with no dissent on 20 September 1965. It shared a meet with Singapore's bid.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit the Maldive Islands. The Assembly did so the next day. Some doubted so small a state could bear a seat's costs. The isles proved the point moot. In time, their voice grew loud on the sea's rise, a threat to their very soil. The seat that this text gave them in 1965 became their chief stage to plead that case to the world.

The African territories under Portuguese rule came under full review in February 1972. The territories were Angola, Mozambique, and Guinea-Bissau. Portugal was using military repression against the African peoples of those colonies. It was also raiding neighboring independent states. Resolution 312 was adopted on 4 February 1972.

The Council restated the right of the peoples of Angola, Mozambique, and Guinea-Bissau to govern themselves and be free. Their struggle was backed as just. Portugal was condemned for refusing to carry out the Council's orders to end colonial rule. The Council voiced deep concern at reports that chemical substances were being used in the colonial wars. All states were called on to stop giving Portugal help that made the repression possible. Arms sales to Portugal also had to be blocked.

A small state on the Red Sea coast sought its United Nations seat just days after its independence in 1977. Resolution 412, adopted unanimously on 7 July 1977, takes up the Republic of Djibouti's bid to join. The Council looked at the bid. It then recommended to the General Assembly that Djibouti be admitted to membership in the United Nations. That single act is the whole text of the resolution.

Chemical weapons in the Iran-Iraq war are condemned in Resolution 612, adopted on 9 May 1988. A mission sent by the Secretary-General had investigated claims of poison gas use and reported back in April. Its findings shocked the Council: chemical weapons were still being used, and on a more intensive scale than before.

The Council stated the urgent need to obey the 1925 Geneva Protocol, which bans poison gas in war. It vigorously condemned the continued use of chemical weapons by the parties and said it expected both sides to stop. All states were called on to control strictly the export of chemical products that could serve to make such weapons, a step toward cutting off supply.
varro-de-re-rustica-storr-best-1912:
Marcus Terentius Varro, the most learned Roman of his age, wrote On Farming in his eightieth year. Varro on Farming, in Lloyd Storr-Best's 1912 English rendering, gives his De Re Rustica whole. The work is the oldest complete Roman book on the farm to survive.

Varro sets his lessons as talks among landowners at a country house. Crops, soils, cattle, sheep, bees, and farm hands each get their due in turn. His voice is dry, shrewd, and full of the lore of the old Roman farm. Later writers on husbandry all drank from this spring.
waverley-novels-volume-12: This volume of the collected Waverley Novels continues Walter Scott's great series in the handsome uniform edition Victorian readers treasured. Scott's historical romances — the books that taught Europe to love the past — appear here as his devoted public knew them. A fine way to meet the Wizard of the North in his classic form.
webster-white-devil-1612:
John Webster wrote The White Devil early in his career, and it reached print in 1612. The play draws on recent Italian scandals around Vittoria Accoramboni, a famous beauty murdered in 1585. Its first London production failed, but Webster defended the play in print with pride.

Vittoria is tried for adultery and murder in a corrupt court that already knows its verdict. Her lover, the duke Bracciano, plots fresh murders with the villain Flamineo, her own brother. Poisonings, ghosts, and a storm of revenge follow until nearly everyone of rank lies dead. Webster paints a whole society rotted by lust and ambition. The trial scene, where Vittoria out-faces her judges, is the play's blazing center.
wharton-reef-1912:
Edith Wharton published The Reef in 1912, writing much of it in France, where she then lived. The American widow Anna Leath has settled in a French country house with her stepdaughter. Wharton called it, in effect, a story told almost entirely through shifting feelings and half-spoken truths.

Anna is engaged to George Darrow, a diplomat she loved in her youth. Before the wedding she learns that Darrow recently had an affair with Sophy Viner, the girl now hired as her stepdaughter's companion. Doubt works on Anna like acid as she questions both lovers. Nothing is ever stated plainly, and every talk shifts the ground. Wharton builds her most psychologically intricate novel out of hints, pauses, and dread.
wunsch-antike-fluchtafeln-1912:
Richard Wunsch selected the most vivid ancient curse tablets for his 1912 German volume. The slim book belonged to the Kleine Texte series for students. German explanations accompany the chosen Greek and Latin texts.

Love spells gone wrong make painful reading in these pages. Chariot-race sabotage and courtroom curses show competition turning to magic. Wunsch chose examples that bring the ancient practice alive quickly. His collection is far more approachable than Audollent's massive scholarly corpus. Students still use it as the friendliest doorway into binding magic. The tablets reveal losers, lovers, and litigants hiring the gods against each other.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol12:
Volume XII of the Journal of Discourses came out at Liverpool in 1869, the year rails finally crossed the continent. Brigham Young, his counsellors, the Twelve, and other elders preach in its pages. Shorthand reporting keeps the sermons close to the moment of delivery, rough edges and all.

A railroad at the doorstep meant new goods, new strangers, and new tests for a separated people. The pulpit answers run through these discourses, mixed with the faith's standing doctrines. Volume XII shows the record doing its work: one voice of counsel for a church entering a changed age.
